notes.title: Classify site salinity and select concrete strength and cover for residential slabs and footings
notes.body:
# Classify site salinity and select concrete strength and cover for residential slabs and footings

> **Source:** `INDUSTRY_GUIDE_T56_Residential_Slabs_and_Footings_in_Saline_Environments.pdf` (Sections 3.5-3.6 (Tables 1-2, pp. 4-5) and 6.1-6.2 (Table 4 and cover recommendations, pp. 9-11)), held in the local reference library — see
> [[Reference library]]. This note is a paraphrased working aid, not the
> document. Values, clauses and criteria must be read from the source before
> they are relied on, and engineering conclusions need qualified review.

**Outcome.** A concrete grade and reinforcement cover matched to the site's ECe salinity class so slabs and footings achieve their design life in saline ground.

## Inputs

- Soil ECe values with depth (from EC1:5 x texture factor or saturation extract)
- Soil permeability class (sands vs silts/clays) and pH
- Footing system type (stiffened raft with membrane, strip/pad footings, retaining walls)
- Design life expectation (nominal 50 years for houses; 10-20 years may suffice for sheds/small walls)

## Procedure

1. Establish the salinity class from ECe in dS/m per the Richards-based table (T56 Table 2, p. 5): non-saline <2, slightly saline 2-4, moderately saline 4-8, very saline 8-16, highly saline >16; soils are generally regarded saline above ECe 4 dS/m.
2. Select minimum concrete grade from the salinity class (T56 Table 4, p. 10): N20 for non-saline and slightly saline, N25 moderately saline, N32 very saline, above N40 for highly saline.
3. Select cover to reinforcement (T56 Section 6.2.3, p. 11): membrane-protected slabs/internal beams 20 mm to internal surfaces and 30 mm to the membrane face; unprotected perimeter beams/strip footings 40 mm non-aggressive, 45 mm moderately saline, 50 mm very saline, 55 mm highly saline.
4. For strip and pad footings (rarely membrane-wrapped), design the concrete itself for site exposure; only reduce strength/cover if the member is completely encased in membrane.
5. Check pH/acidity separately: the strength table is a saline-conditions guide and may be inadequate in highly acidic soils; AS 2159 treats permeability classes differently (the guide notes ~25 MPa minimum in low-permeability silts/clays vs ~32 MPa in permeable sands where groundwater replenishes at the concrete face).
6. Where salt type matters (e.g. suspected magnesium/ammonium sulphates, classified as more severe than calcium/sodium/potassium sulphates), commission ion analysis rather than relying on total-EC alone.

## Decision rules

- Treat the plastic membrane as an additional safeguard, not the primary durability measure — codes permit 20 MPa on the basis of a perfect membrane, but specifying strength/cover for the actual exposure is the more robust approach, especially for strip/pad footings.
- Because standard concrete grades step ~25% apart, small ECe uncertainties rarely change the selected grade — do not over-refine the salinity estimate for this purpose.
- For sites with potential (not current) salinity hazard, design for the hazard to exist within the 50-year design life rather than betting on guarantees that conditions will not change.
- Urban saline groundwater is typically well below seawater concentration (worst Wagga Wagga bores ~33% of seawater chloride) — design for measured site exposure, not marine defaults, unless data says otherwise.

## Checks

- EC measurement method (EC1:5 vs ECe saturation extract) and conversion factors documented before classification.
- Aggressivity classification cross-checked against AS 2159 exposure tables and the project spec.
- Cover selections compatible with AS 2870 details for the chosen footing system.

## Common errors

- Classifying from raw EC1:5 without texture conversion, understating the class.
- Relying on the membrane to justify minimum-grade concrete in strip/pad footings that cannot practically be wrapped.
- Ignoring soil permeability: the same salinity is more aggressive in sands (replenished exposure) than clays.
- Applying the saline-soil table to acid sulfate or highly acidic ground without additional measures.

## Caveats

- Classification and aggressivity calls must be verified against the source document, current AS editions and the project specification — T56 tables are industry recommendations, not code minima.
- The guide itself flags that an arbitrary ECe cutoff is a simplification of building impact; salt type, water movement and wetting/drying govern actual attack.
- EC vs ECe distinction: T56 uses ECe for classification but quotes some comparators (drinking water 2.5 dS/m, seawater ~59 dS/m) as plain EC — do not mix these scales.
- Related guidance merged from building-in-saline-environment-080145.pdf (Australian Standards section, pp. 16-17).

## Standards cited

AS 2870 Residential Slabs and Footings, AS 3600 Concrete Structures; AS 2159 Piling - Design and Installation; AS 3735 Concrete Structures for Retaining Liquids, AS 1379 Specification and Supply of Concrete, National Construction Code Vol 2; BRE Special Digest 1 (aggressive ground, for sulfate-dominated cases)

- [[Library - RMS and TfNSW specifications]]

notes.title: Classify Sydney sandstone and shale with the Pells three-criteria system and state the controlling criterion
notes.body:
# Classify Sydney sandstone and shale with the Pells three-criteria system and state the controlling criterion

> **Source:** `PELLS MOSTYN WONG (2019) CLASSIFICATION OF SANDSTONES AND SHALES IN THE SYDNEY.pdf` (Australian Geomechanics Vol 54 No 2, June 2019; Section 3 and Tables 2a-2c (p 33), misuse guidance in Section 2.2 (pp 31-32)), held in the local reference library — see
> [[Reference library]]. This note is a paraphrased working aid, not the
> document. Values, clauses and criteria must be read from the source before
> they are relied on, and engineering conclusions need qualified review.

**Outcome.** A defensible Class I-V assignment for Hawkesbury Sandstone or Ashfield Shale, with the rock volume and controlling criterion recorded, and misuse of the system avoided.

## Inputs

- Saturated substance unconfined compressive strength (UCS) data
- Defect (joint and bedding) spacing measured as true spacing in core or exposure
- Percentage of seams (clay, fragmented, highly weathered zones) within the defined zone of influence
- Definition of the rock volume being classified

## Procedure

1. Assemble quantitative data for all three criteria: saturated UCS, defect spacing, and % seams in the vertical interval of influence.
2. Assign the class from Tables 2a (sandstone) and 2b (shale) of the 2019 paper; the class thresholds differ between sandstone and shale, so use the correct table.
3. Apply the rule that all three criteria must be satisfied; the worst criterion governs the class.
4. Describe defect spacing with the ISRM / ISO 14689 terms tabulated in Table 2c.
5. When reporting, state the volume of rock mass the classification covers and which criterion (strength, spacing or seams) controlled the class.

## Decision rules

- Never classify from pile-rig cuttings or from drilling resistance; the system needs quantitative strength, spacing and seam data.
- Do not apply the system to small components of the rock mass, to major fault zones, or to zones affected by dykes and sills.
- Do not use the system for slope stability, excavatability or rock-cutting assessments; use the Bertuzzi & de Ambrosis ground-type matrix instead of the foundation classes when linking to tunnel support design.

## Checks

- UCS values are for saturated substance, not dry.
- Defect spacing is true spacing, not apparent spacing in inclined core.
- Seam percentage is computed over the correct zone of influence (1.5 times least footing dimension for pads; socket length plus footing width for sockets).

## Common errors

- Attaching engineering properties to a class without supporting lab or field data.
- Reporting a class without stating the rock volume or the controlling criterion.
- Using the sandstone table thresholds for shale or vice versa.

## Caveats

- Zone-of-influence definitions come from the companion 1998 paper; cross-check both documents.
- Design reference only: class thresholds and their application must be verified against the source tables and reviewed by a qualified engineer before use.

## Standards cited

ISO 14689 / ISRM defect spacing terminology, AS 1726 (geotechnical site investigations), Pells et al (1978) and Pells, Mostyn & Walker (1998) original classification papers

notes.title: Classify unsuitable material into NR44's three categories before directing removal
notes.body:
# Classify unsuitable material into NR44's three categories before directing removal

> **Source:** `nr44 Earthworks Specification.pdf` (Guide commentary to Clause 2.4 (NR44 Ed 2 Rev 0, April 2013; based on R44 Ed 4 Rev 1)), held in the local reference library — see
> [[Reference library]]. This note is a paraphrased working aid, not the
> document. Values, clauses and criteria must be read from the source before
> they are relied on, and engineering conclusions need qualified review.

**Outcome.** Faster, better-costed decisions on foundation material: spoil, treat in place, bridge over, or accept - instead of defaulting to blanket removal.

## Inputs

- Foundation inspection observations after topsoil strip or at cutting floor level
- Moisture condition and any in-situ test results (CBR, strength)
- Embankment height over the area and distance below the Selected Material Zone
- Earthworks balance and program context

## Procedure

1. Sort the suspect material into NR44's three working categories: inherently unsuitable (peat, muck, some silts - cannot go in the works at all), unsuitable by virtue of position (e.g. low CBR at cutting floor - fine elsewhere in general fill), and unsuitably wet (problem is moisture, not the soil).
2. For inherently unsuitable ground, prefer designs/directions that bridge over it with embankment height rather than excavate; NR44 notes removal under adverse conditions typically multiplies cost several-fold versus raising grade.
3. For position-based unsuitability over extensive areas, use the standard foundation treatments (e.g. excavate-and-replace or working platform types) rather than ad-hoc removal, and reuse the material in general earthworks.
4. For unsuitably wet material, weigh drying, stabilising, spoiling or using as-is deep in fills based on earthworks balance, drying sites, climate and long-term performance.
5. Where embankments are high (roughly above 1.5 m per the guide), judge the foundation mainly as a working platform; where the foundation is close beneath the Selected Material Zone (within about 1.2 m) or at cutting floor level, allow program time for in-situ testing.
6. Decide quickly - exposed foundations wet up in rain and the delay costs usually exceed the cost of removing a bit more material.

## Decision rules

- A quick decision with a small extra removal cost usually beats a delayed optimal decision.
- Material wet but sound can often be placed deep in high fills with geotechnical concurrence; monitor heave and pore pressure dissipation rather than rejecting it.
- Where a treatment can be designated pre-tender, specify it - removing offending material as general earthworks avoids stop-and-test cycles.

## Checks

- Hold point discipline retained: Principal inspects before each lot of unsuitable is replaced
- Before/after surveys captured for quantity measurement
- Category decision recorded with its basis (inspection, testing, judgement)

## Common errors

- Testing obviously inherently-unsuitable material instead of directing spoil immediately
- Removing position-unsuitable material to spoil when it is acceptable general fill
- Leaving foundations exposed awaiting decisions through wet weather

## Caveats

- NR44 is a guide, not a contract document - it explains intent and never overrides R44 or the contract.
- Based on R44 Ed 4 Rev 1; verify commentary still matches the R44 edition current for the project.

## Standards cited

RMS R44, RMS Q

notes.title: Classify vibration and select assessment criteria
notes.body:
# Classify vibration and select assessment criteria

> **Source:** `vibrationguide0643.pdf` (Sections 1.1, 2.1-2.2, Table 2.1 (DEC NSW, February 2006)), held in the local reference library — see
> [[Reference library]]. This note is a paraphrased working aid, not the
> document. Values, clauses and criteria must be read from the source before
> they are relied on, and engineering conclusions need qualified review.

**Outcome.** The correct human-comfort vibration criterion (continuous, impulsive or intermittent/VDV) selected for a source, with excluded cases routed to the right framework.

## Inputs

- Source character and event count per assessment period
- Receiver type (critical area, residence, office/school/place of worship, workshop)
- Assessment period (daytime vs night-time)

## Procedure

1. Classify the vibration: continuous (uninterrupted over the period), impulsive (rapid build-up and decay, no more than three events per period), or intermittent (interrupted continuous, repeated impulses such as pile driving, or strongly varying continuous).
2. Route excluded cases elsewhere: blasting to the ANZECC blasting framework; structural damage, occupational exposure and motion sickness are outside this guideline.
3. Select the matching criterion set: weighted rms acceleration tables for continuous/impulsive; vibration dose values for intermittent.
4. Identify the governing axis convention relative to occupant posture (standing, seated, lying) and take the conservative case where posture is unknown.

## Decision rules

- Three or fewer events per assessment period: assess as impulsive; more: assess as intermittent via VDV (vibrationguide0643 Section 2.1, Table 2.1).
- Daytime is defined 7 am to 10 pm, night-time 10 pm to 7 am (vibrationguide0643 Table 2.2 note).
- Criteria are preferred/maximum goals, not mandatory limits; exceedances beyond maximum values after all feasible and reasonable mitigation trigger community negotiation (vibrationguide0643 Sections 2.3-2.4, 3.6).

## Checks

- Assessment location is where people are affected (inside buildings), with a justified transfer function if measuring outside.
- Building resonance considered - indoor values can exceed external ground values.

## Common errors

- Assessing pile driving against impulsive criteria when event counts make it intermittent.
- Applying human-comfort criteria to building-damage questions (different frameworks, e.g. DIN 4150-3).
- Assessing blasting under this guideline.

## Caveats

- Guideline is dated (2006, framed as interim pending BS 6472 revision); check for current NSW EPA policy before relying on it.
- Criteria are amenity goals; consent conditions and contract documents override.

## Standards cited

BS 6472-1992, BS 6841-1987, ISO 2631.1/2631.2, ANZECC 1990 blasting guideline, DIN 4150

- [[Soil description order]]

notes.title: Clean, pack and store PLT equipment after testing
notes.body:
# Clean, pack and store PLT equipment after testing

> **Source:** `050-Setup Proceedure for PLT Draft 4 Feb 2024.pdf` (Sections I-J, p. 8), held in the local reference library — see
> [[Reference library]]. This note is a paraphrased working aid, not the
> document. Values, clauses and criteria must be read from the source before
> they are relied on, and engineering conclusions need qualified review.

**Outcome.** The engineer can decommission the kit in a way that avoids corrosion and sensor damage, and route the day's data to the supervising engineers.

## Inputs

- Completed test, equipment still in the field
- Dry cloths
- Transport cases
- Completed datasheets and stored electronic data

## Procedure

1. Wipe the base plate and the electronic box feet with a dry cloth only; remove or let any water dry off.
2. Clean the displacement transducer with a dry cloth and stow it in its dedicated compartment in the measuring device.
3. Check the case interior is dry before packing; never pack wet materials or damp cloths, because trapped moisture plus cement- or lime-treated soils promotes alkali attack on the metal finish. If the case is damp, leave it open in a climate-controlled space to dry first (p. 8).
4. Pack everything into the carrying cases and store the device somewhere dry and environmentally controlled.
5. Complete any remaining datasheet fields, then back in the office download the test data and pass it to the supervising geotechnical engineers.

## Decision rules

- If moisture is found in the case, dry the open case indoors before storage rather than packing wet.

## Checks

- Case interior and equipment are dry before closing.
- Datasheet is fully completed and data has been handed to the supervising engineers.

## Common errors

- Using cleaning agents or lubricants - lubricants can impair moving parts and distort measurements (p. 8).
- Leaving damp cloths or wet material in the transport case, inviting alkali corrosion after work on cement/lime-stabilised ground.

## Caveats

- The reporting workflow (Section J Step 2) is marked 'to be determined' in this draft.

## Standards cited

None cited in the source passage.

## Related

- [[Library - plate load testing]]
- [[Skills]]

notes.title: Compile excavation submission package for road authority
notes.body:
# Compile excavation submission package for road authority

> **Source:** `RMS_ Attachment A_ GTD 2012-01.pdf.pdf` (Submission to RMS, Technical Requirements and Hold Points sections (GTD 2012/001, 27 April 2012)), held in the local reference library — see
> [[Reference library]]. This note is a paraphrased working aid, not the
> document. Values, clauses and criteria must be read from the source before
> they are relied on, and engineering conclusions need qualified review.

**Outcome.** A complete concurrence submission (dilapidation survey, design documentation, drawings, specifications, monitoring plan) lodged with the road authority ahead of construction.

## Inputs

- Structural and geotechnical design reports with analysis output (moment/shear envelopes, deflections)
- Drawings showing the works relative to road assets with construction sequence
- Instrumentation layout, monitoring frequency, trigger levels and response actions
- Dilapidation survey scope for sensitive assets in the influence zone

## Procedure

1. Assemble design documentation with accurate retention geometry, load/design assumptions, load cases, section/material properties, analysis outputs, and critical cross-sections showing the geotechnical model; attach the underlying geotechnical report; cover temporary and permanent works.
2. Prepare drawings locating all affected road assets, longitudinal and cross sections at critical locations, and the construction sequence.
3. Include the instrumentation layout, monitoring frequency, trigger levels and actions on the drawings; include specifications needed to interpret the design.
4. Undertake a dilapidation survey of authority assets in the influence zone where damage risk exists.
5. Lodge the package with the required lead time before construction; refer any post-acceptance design modification back for concurrence; submit work-as-executed drawings (including rock stabilisation measures) at completion.

## Decision rules

- Submission is required at least six weeks before construction commencement (RMS_ Attachment A_ GTD 2012-01.pdf submission section).
- In the 2012 direction, no part of a ground anchor may be shallower than 2 m below surface within the road reserve (later superseded by a different depth in GTD 2020/001) - always apply the current direction (ground anchors section).
- Construction may not proceed past staged hold points without chartered-engineer certification.

## Checks

- Design report addresses ruptured-utility or underpinning scenarios where utility-owner requirements are not established.
- Damming effects on groundwater considered in design levels.
- Authority site access for compliance review is provided for.

## Common errors

- Lodging drawings without the construction sequence or trigger levels shown.
- Modifying the accepted design during construction without re-referral.
- Omitting the dilapidation survey and losing the pre-existing-condition baseline for later damage disputes.

## Caveats

- This direction is SUPERSEDED by GTD 2020/001 - use it only as historical context and follow the current direction for technical values.
- Contract/DA documents and current authority directions override.

## Standards cited

AS 5100, AS 1726, AS 1170, AS 3600, AS 2159

## Related

- [[AS 1726 soil and rock description]]
- [[AS 2159 piling]]
- [[Library - RMS and TfNSW specifications]]
- [[Skills]]

notes.title: Compile positioned core photographs into a per-borehole core-photo deliverable
notes.body:
# Compile positioned core photographs into a per-borehole core-photo deliverable

> **Source:** [Google Drive — Core Photos (MP4 compilation)/MP4 Core Photos.pdf + MP4 Core Photos.docx + MP4-BH01.jpeg; Core Photo/Positioned/ (MP4-BHxx and MP5-BHxx renamed positioned images alongside raw UUID-named originals)](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1ih8P8CC9pSUq-uMhNLG_v1RkmsyjkrXc/view) (A 4-page compiled PDF (one CORE PHOTOGRAPH OF BOREHOLE page per hole with the full header table incl. easting/northing/surface RL/contractor/rig/logger) plus its source docx, the positioned images it was built from, and the 'Positioned' folder showing raw-to-renamed processing). Reconstructed from STS's own
> field records on Google Drive — completed forms, labelled photos and
> scans, catalogued in [[Field records catalogue]]. It shows what the
> records evidence, not necessarily the current approved procedure —
> confirm against the current STS form and procedure before treating it
> as the standard method.

**Outcome.** Raw field snaps of core boxes become a client-ready document with one page per borehole: a perspective-corrected ('positioned') core photo under a standard header giving job, location, survey coordinates, rig, logger and date, issued as Word plus PDF.

## Inputs

- Raw core box photos (phone/camera, often oblique, with the STS board and in-box depth labels visible)
- Borehole survey data: easting, northing, surface RL (mAHD)
- Drilling metadata: contractor, drill rig, logger initials, coring dates
- STS Word template with logo header and core-photograph layout

## Procedure

1. Select the best raw photo of each core box (all trays visible, board legible, minimal glare).
2. Perspective-correct and crop each photo so the core box fills the frame square-on with the depth numbers running down the left edge — the 'positioned' image.
3. Rename each positioned image to its zone/area and borehole ID (e.g. MP4-BH01, MP5-BH8) and save them in a 'Positioned' subfolder alongside the raw originals.
4. Insert one positioned image per page into the Word template under the title 'CORE PHOTOGRAPH OF BOREHOLE: <ID>'.
5. Complete the header table on every page: Job No, Location, Client on the left; Easting, Northing, Surface RL (mAHD) in the centre; Contractor, Drill Rig, Logger and Date on the right.
6. Repeat for every cored hole in the package, then export the compiled document to PDF and file both docx and pdf in the job's core-photos folder.

## Decision rules

- Keep raw, positioned and compiled versions as three separate layers; never overwrite raw photos with corrected ones.
- One borehole per page; where a hole needs several boxes, use additional pages under the same borehole title.
- Use surveyed coordinates and RL in the header, not phone GPS from the photo, since the deliverable is the coordinate of record.
- Date field may span a range (e.g. 19-20/03) when coring of a hole crossed days.

## Checks

- Borehole ID in the page title matches the ID readable on the photo board and in-box strip within the image.
- In-box depth labels visible in the positioned image are consistent with the stated hole depth and the borehole log.
- Easting/northing/RL in each header match the survey schedule for that hole.
- Every cored hole in the job appears exactly once; page count equals borehole count.

## Common errors

- Pairing the wrong photo with a borehole when several boxes were shot in one session (UUID/IMG filenames make mix-ups easy before renaming)
- Skipping the perspective correction so scale varies across the image and depth rows cannot be compared
- Leaving header coordinates blank or copying them from the previous page without updating
- Compiling from WhatsApp-recompressed copies instead of the original-resolution photos

## Caveats

- Reconstructed from STS field records — confirm against the current STS procedure before treating as the standard method
- The tool used for perspective correction is not evidenced (only its output); any image editor that squares and crops the box achieves the same result
- Whether the compilation is issued standalone or appended to the factual report is not evidenced here

## Standards cited

AS 1726 (geotechnical site investigations — reporting of core)

## Related

- [[Field records catalogue]]
- [[AS 1726 soil and rock description]]
- [[Reduced levels and datums]]
- [[Borehole log conventions]]
- [[Skills]]

notes.title: Complete a DCP and Perth penetrometer deep test field sheet (Form S26)
notes.body:
# Complete a DCP and Perth penetrometer deep test field sheet (Form S26)

> **Source:** [Google Drive — 2520E-G/Field Sheets/2427E-G.pdf (page 1)](https://drive.google.com/file/d/197Eg1nMVzS96OTO8ecyfFmeI2G55vbiY/view) (Completed S26 sheet with two DCP tests (P1 from 0.7m, P2 from 0.0m) in silty clay, blows per 100 mm recorded to ~1.5 m, header warning and footer codes visible). Reconstructed from STS's own
> field records on Google Drive — completed forms, labelled photos and
> scans, catalogued in [[Field records catalogue]]. It shows what the
> records evidence, not necessarily the current approved procedure —
> confirm against the current STS form and procedure before treating it
> as the standard method.

**Outcome.** A completed 'Dynamic Cone & Perth Penetrometer - Deep Test' worksheet recording penetration resistance in blows per 100 mm for up to three test locations, with soil description and refusal coding.

## Inputs

- Form S26 (Dynamic Cone & Perth Penetrometer - Deep Test, Date of Issue 10/07/25, Revision 2)
- DCP or Perth penetrometer apparatus with known apparatus number
- Test locations, start depths (from pre-drilled hole or surface)

## Procedure

1. Fill the header: Project, Client, Project No. / STS No. (e.g. 32422/2427E-G), Technician initials, Sheet _ of _.
2. Circle the test method on the printed line: AS 1289.6.3.2-DCP, AS1289.6.3.3-Perth, or RTA T161-DCP.
3. For each of the three test columns fill: Site No. (with start depth noted in brackets, e.g. 'P1 (from 0.7m)', 'P2 (0.0)'), Chainage if applicable, Start Depth (m), Soil Description (e.g. 'Silty CLAY, m-plasticity, brown, trace sand'), Moisture Condition (e.g. dry-moist).
4. Drive the penetrometer and record blows per 100 mm in the depth rows, which run 0.00-0.10 up to 5.90-6.00 m in 0.10 m increments.
5. Use the printed codes where full blows are not recorded: R = Refusal, D = Discontinued, S = Stone, * = Pre-Drilled Hole.
6. Record the Apparatus Number, and circle Y/N for 'Apparatus Function and drop height Checked'.
7. Date the sheet and have it signed off in Checked By.

## Decision rules

- NEVER combine DCP and Perth tests on the same work sheet — printed as a warning on the form header.
- When testing from the base of a pre-drilled or excavated hole, record the start depth against the Site No. and use the * code for the pre-drilled interval.
- Stop and code R (refusal), D (discontinued) or S (stone) rather than forcing counts.

## Checks

- Test method circled matches the apparatus used
- Apparatus function and drop height check circled Y before testing
- Blows recorded continuously from start depth with no unexplained gaps
- Sheet numbering completed when the job runs to multiple sheets

## Common errors

- Mixing DCP and Perth results on one sheet (explicitly banned on the form)
- Omitting the start depth for tests begun below surface
- Leaving the apparatus number or drop-height check blank

## Caveats

- Reconstructed from STS field records — confirm against the current STS procedure before treating as the standard method
- Based on one completed example sheet; handwriting of some blow counts is hard to read and values were not relied on

## Standards cited

AS 1289.6.3.2 (DCP) (printed on form), AS 1289.6.3.3 (Perth penetrometer) (printed on form), RTA T161 (DCP) (printed on form)

notes.title: Complete a Report of Pile Hole Inspection form (OP GEO pile hole inspection family)
notes.body:
# Complete a Report of Pile Hole Inspection form (OP GEO pile hole inspection family)

> **Source:** [Google Drive — Field Sheets (STS blank templates + reference)/OP GEO 015  Pile Hole inspection report[29920].pdf](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1fymMsLdU_RZ3wOnrki24rOmrtWmExOz7/view) (Blank EI-branded Report of Pile Hole Inspection: RL/depth/stratigraphy table with assessed strength, roughness (R1-R4 definitions printed) and base cleanness columns, and design-vs-actual parameter block; footer OP GEO 005 RevB March 2016). Reconstructed from STS's own
> field records on Google Drive — completed forms, labelled photos and
> scans, catalogued in [[Field records catalogue]]. It shows what the
> records evidence, not necessarily the current approved procedure —
> confirm against the current STS form and procedure before treating it
> as the standard method.

**Outcome.** A per-pile inspection record proving founding conditions - stratigraphy, socket strength, roughness class and base cleanness - against the design parameters.

## Inputs

- Blank Report of Pile Hole Inspection form (file titled OP GEO 015; sheet footer reads OP GEO 005 RevB, March 2016)
- Project no., client, date, inspector and reviewer names, pile number
- Approximate RL of ground surface (mAHD) and supplied BEL (bulk excavation level)
- Design parameters from the piling drawings (toe level, socket material, socket length, pile diameter)
- Observation of the drilled shaft (spoil, sidewall, base) during piling

## Procedure

1. Head the form with project no., project, location, client, date, inspected by / reviewed by, the pile number and approximate ground surface RL (mAHD).
2. Work down the main table row by row: for each depth interval record relative level (mAHD), depth (m) and the inferred stratigraphy and defect description observed from cuttings and the shaft wall.
3. For socket material rows, complete assessed strength, roughness and base cleanness columns.
4. Assign roughness using the printed R1-R4 classes: R1 straight smooth-sided socket with grooves/indentations under 1 mm at spacings over 200 mm; R2 grooves 1-4 mm deep and wider than 5 mm at 50-200 mm spacing; R3 grooves 4-10 mm deep at spacings up to 200 mm; R4 grooves or undulations deeper than 10 mm and wider than 10 mm at spacings up to 200 mm.
5. Assess base cleanness as the percentage of natural rock exposed at the shaft and base (definition printed on the form).
6. Fill the paired parameter block: design pile toe level, design socket material, design socket length and design pile diameter on one side; actual pile toe level (mAHD), actual socket material, actual socket length and hole diameter on the other.
7. Complete Comments/Recommendations including piling rig, pile type, shoring wall and supplied BEL, plus any rock-class parameters used.
8. Have the form reviewed (Reviewed: field in header) before issue.

## Decision rules

- Compare actual vs design side by side before the pile is poured - any shortfall in socket length, weaker-than-design socket material or undersized hole is raised for engineering direction, not just recorded.
- Roughness class comes from the printed groove-geometry definitions, not general impressions.
- Base cleanness below the project acceptance percentage means the base is re-cleaned and re-inspected before concrete.

## Checks

- Depth and RL columns are arithmetically consistent with the ground surface RL.
- Every pile has its own numbered form; pile no. matches the piling layout drawing.
- Both inspector and reviewer fields completed.

## Common errors

- Recording only the actual parameters and leaving the design side blank, which defeats the conformance comparison.
- Writing a strength adjective without basis while the socket is wet or obscured - note the limitation instead.
- Confusing hole diameter (actual) with design pile diameter.

## Caveats

- Reconstructed from STS field records — confirm against the current STS procedure before treating as the standard method
- Filename says OP GEO 015 but the printed footer says OP GEO 005 RevB (March 2016) - confirm the current form code and revision before use.

## Standards cited

AS 2159 (piling design and installation - founding verification)

## Related

- [[Field records catalogue]]
- [[Rock socket length]]
- [[AS 2159 piling]]
- [[Reduced levels and datums]]
- [[Skills]]

notes.title: Complete an STS Geotech Drilling Daily Record (drilling/coring time and production log)
notes.body:
# Complete an STS Geotech Drilling Daily Record (drilling/coring time and production log)

> **Source:** [Google Drive — Field Sheets (STS blank templates + reference)/STS Geotech Drilling Daily Record.pdf (with STS Geotech_Daily Log.pdf and OP GEO 003_RevD Geotech_Daily Log_EI.pdf as the companion daily-log family)](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1XG_2_8xY03HbjnuIyRsjtHoInLPYO7AJ/view) (Blank 2-page STS template: timed sections for service location, traffic control, drilling, breakdowns, coring runs I-X, final ground observations, field-work narrative and dual signatures). Reconstructed from STS's own
> field records on Google Drive — completed forms, labelled photos and
> scans, catalogued in [[Field records catalogue]]. It shows what the
> records evidence, not necessarily the current approved procedure —
> confirm against the current STS form and procedure before treating it
> as the standard method.

**Outcome.** A signed daily record of drilling and coring production for each borehole - set-up, run times, breakdowns and end-of-hole ground summary - that supports invoicing and later log preparation.

## Inputs

- STS Geotech Drilling Daily Record blank (paired with the STS Geotech Daily Log / OP GEO 003 RevD daily form family)
- BH number(s), date, watch or phone time
- Drilling contractor activity through the day (service location, traffic control, drilling, coring, breakdowns)
- Observed ground profile at completion of the hole

## Procedure

1. Head the sheet with BH no., date, and overall start/end time; the form is marked Confidential - Subject to Legal Professional Privilege, so treat it as a controlled project record.
2. Service location section: tick YES/NO for whether service locating was required and, if yes, record its start time, end time and total hours.
3. Traffic controls section: tick YES/NO for whether traffic control was required; record traffic set-up time, then start/end times and total hours.
4. Drilling works: record rig set-up time, then borehole drilling start time, end time and total hours.
5. Log every breakdown in the breakdown table - one row per event with BH no., start and end of the stoppage, total hours and the reason.
6. Coring works: record coring set-up time and coring start/end/total hours, then fill the core-run table (rows Core Run I to X) with start time, end time, total hours and comments for each run.
7. After completing the hole, fill the Final Observation section: topsoil/fill depths, natural soil depths, extremely weathered material depth, and a classification of bedrock including strength and weathering.
8. Use the continuation Field Work page to describe site conditions and stage of works (the page prompt also reminds you to take photographs).
9. Close out with field staff initials and signature, and obtain the client name and signature.

## Decision rules

- Every non-productive interval (service location, traffic setup, breakdowns) gets its own timed entry - do not fold standby into drilling hours.
- One breakdown row per event, each tied to a BH number, so downtime can be attributed per hole.
- Core runs are numbered sequentially (I, II, III...) - keep run numbering consistent with the core boxes and BH log.
- The bedrock classification must include both strength and weathering terms, not just a rock name.

## Checks

- Section subtotals (service location, traffic, drilling, coring) should reconcile with the overall start/end times for the day.
- Breakdown hours plus productive hours should account for the full shift.
- Both field staff and client signatures present before leaving site - the client signature validates chargeable hours.

## Common errors

- Leaving the YES/NO service-location and traffic boxes unticked, which makes it unclear whether the activity was not needed or just not recorded.
- Recording core-run times but forgetting total hours, forcing later back-calculation.
- Skipping the final observation block on the drilling record because the ground is 'already on the BH log' - the daily record is meant to stand alone.

## Caveats

- Reconstructed from STS field records — confirm against the current STS procedure before treating as the standard method
- The blank template carries no revision code on its face; the companion daily log exists in several revisions (OP GEO 003 RevD, STS Daily Log V1/V2), so check which issue is current.

## Standards cited

AS 1726 (soil/rock description for the bedrock classification block)

## Related

- [[AS 1726 soil and rock description]]
- [[Rock weathering classes]]
- [[Borehole log conventions]]
- [[Library - RMS and TfNSW specifications]]
- [[Soil description order]]
- [[Skills]]

# Complete an STS Geotechnical Daily Field Form

> **Source:** [Google Drive — 2520E-G/Field Sheets/2427E-G.pdf (pages 2-4)](https://drive.google.com/file/d/197Eg1nMVzS96OTO8ecyfFmeI2G55vbiY/view) (Two completed daily field forms from consecutive visits for a bored pier inspection job, both signed by field staff and the client representative). Reconstructed from STS's own
> field records on Google Drive — completed forms, labelled photos and
> scans, catalogued in [[Field records catalogue]]. It shows what the
> records evidence, not necessarily the current approved procedure —
> confirm against the current STS form and procedure before treating it
> as the standard method.

**Outcome.** A signed daily record of a field visit — tasks, weather, H&S observations and a narrative of the field work — countersigned by the client representative on the day.

## Inputs

- STS Geotechnical Daily Field Form (headed 'Confidential - Subject to Legal Professional Privilege', STS Geotechnics logo)
- Job details (project number/STS number, project name, client contact, site address)

## Procedure

1. Fill the header block: Project Number (e.g. 33520/2427E-G), Project Name, Client Contact, Site Address/Location, Sheet _ of _, Date, Time at Arrival, Time at Departure.
2. State the Tasks for the visit (examples: 'Perform the pier installation inspection / 2 DCPs', 'pier inspection to the weathered rock for footings').
3. Record Contractors present and Weather including recent rainfall and temperature (examples: '9° - 11°C', 'Cloudy, 12°C').
4. Note any Health & Safety / Environmental Observations on the ruled lines.
5. Write the Field Work narrative — the form prompts: describe site conditions, stage of works, take photographs. The examples record what was inspected, depths and materials encountered, what tests were performed, and the engineering conclusion reached on site (e.g. piers achieving allowable bearing capacity at depth, or additional excavation needed to reach the required rock class for a socket).
6. Close out with Field Staff Initials and Field Staff Signature, then obtain Client Name and Client Signature the same day.
7. One form per visit; multi-visit jobs accumulate one form per day in the job's Field Sheets bundle.

## Decision rules

- The narrative must state the on-site verdict, not just observations — the examples end with acceptance ('found suitable') or required action ('additional excavation needed for Class 3 rock for the 1.5m socket').
- Get the client signature before leaving site — both examples are countersigned.

## Checks

- Arrival and departure times filled
- Weather block completed
- Field staff and client signatures both present
- Tasks line matches what the narrative actually reports

## Common errors

- Leaving the Contractors or H&S lines blank rather than writing nil observations (blank on the examples — an ambiguity worth avoiding)
- Narrative describing work done without the resulting geotechnical decision
- Missing client countersignature

## Caveats

- Reconstructed from STS field records — confirm against the current STS procedure before treating as the standard method
- Parts of the handwritten narratives are hard to read; wording quoted above is the legible portion
- The form carries a legal privilege header — treat completed forms as confidential

## Standards cited

None cited in the source passage.

# Complete an STS plate load test worksheet (Form S112)

> **Source:** [Google Drive — Field Sheets/PLT1.jpg, PLT3.jpg, PLT5.jpg and Field Sheets (1)/PLT-1 (1).pdf](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1JtJkR_LZropCNOzh7PHahUJxa5iYkFl_/view) (Four completed S112 worksheets from two different jobs (132/138 McEvoy Street, Alexandria and 105-113 Hollinsworth Road, Marsden Park), all with the same header fields, load/unload/reload cycle and three dial gauge columns). Reconstructed from STS's own
> field records on Google Drive — completed forms, labelled photos and
> scans, catalogued in [[Field records catalogue]]. It shows what the
> records evidence, not necessarily the current approved procedure —
> confirm against the current STS form and procedure before treating it
> as the standard method.

**Outcome.** A completed 'Load Settlement - Time Relationship Worksheet (Plate Load Testing)' recording dial gauge settlements through a load / unload / reload cycle for one test location, ready for office reduction.

## Inputs

- Form S112 (Load Settlement - Time Relationship Worksheet, Date of Issue 01/10/19, Revision 1)
- Loading system with load readout in kN (and/or bar)
- Three (up to four) dial gauges on the plate
- Thermometer
- Test plate (records show 600 mm diameter, 25 mm thick)

## Procedure

1. Fill the header: Project, Project No. / STS No., Client, Technician (dual initials where two staff attend, e.g. KM/SN), Date Tested.
2. Circle the test method on the printed line: BS1377:Part 9 | ASTM D1196.
3. Record Soil Description (e.g. 'Gravelly Sand Gray' or the pavement material such as DGB20), Page number (circled; one page per test location, numbered through the job), Plate Diameter (mm), Plate Thickness (mm), Temp at Start, Temp at End.
4. Fill Static Load Details and Field Density (t/m3) if applicable, and Test Location (PLT1, PLT3, PLT5 ...).
5. Take the zero-load Initial reading on all dial gauges and note 'Initial reading' in Comments.
6. Load in increments, writing one row per increment with Load (kN)/(Bar) and Dial Gauge 1, 2 and 3 readings (records show the sequence 0, 2, 4, 13, 31, 50, 68, 87, 110 kN, extended to 150 and 180 kN on one job).
7. Unload in decrements recording the same columns (records show 87, 40, 17, 2 kN), leaving a blank row between load stages.
8. Reload through the increments again (4, 13, 31, 50, 68, 87 ... kN) recording all gauges.
9. Columns for Time, Elapsed Time (min), Temp., Ave Set. (mm) and Def. Rate (mm/min) are on the form for holds where readings must stabilise.
10. Complete the footer equipment traceability: Load Cell No., Dial Gauge No(s), Stop Watch No., Thermometer No.
11. If a reading is written in error, strike through and write the correct value above (visible on the records); never overwrite illegibly.

## Decision rules

- One sheet per test location; pages numbered consecutively across the job so PLT1 = page 1, PLT3 = page 3, etc.
- Leave a blank row between the loading, unloading and reloading stages so the cycle boundaries are unambiguous.
- Gauges may read in different senses (one record shows a gauge counting from 300.00 and another job recording negative values); record what the gauge shows and let the office reduce it.

## Checks

- Initial reading row present and flagged in Comments
- Every load increment row has all active dial gauges filled
- Unload readings recover consistently across gauges (records show recovery on all three gauges)
- Header temperatures at start and end both recorded
- Equipment numbers in the footer filled in

## Common errors

- Missing the strike-through convention and overwriting a misread value
- Not separating load/unload/reload stages, making the cycle hard to reduce
- Leaving footer instrument numbers blank (blank on some of the example sheets)
- Header STS number corrected after the fact — write the confirmed job number before starting

## Caveats

- Reconstructed from STS field records — confirm against the current STS procedure before treating as the standard method
- Time / Elapsed Time / Ave Set / Def Rate columns are blank on all four examples, so the hold-duration practice is not evidenced
- The printed method line reads 'BS1377:Part 0' on the scans — it is taken to mean Part 9 (plate loading), but confirm on the current form

## Standards cited

BS 1377: Part 9 (printed on form), ASTM D1196 (printed on form)

# Complete the Geotechnical Testing & Site Record Sheet for AS 3798 Level 1 supervision (Form S69)

> **Source:** [Google Drive — 02 LEVEL1 DAILY SITE REPORT/Level 1 Daily Sheet 25-02-026.pdf and 14-02-026.pdf; Site Record 2025/05.pdf](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1AQNJPCscDqx7zM48oiUR02vyrrJuyCBn/view) (Three completed S69 sheets across two years of the same Level 1 earthworks project, showing identical form structure and the per-area narrative practice). Reconstructed from STS's own
> field records on Google Drive — completed forms, labelled photos and
> scans, catalogued in [[Field records catalogue]]. It shows what the
> records evidence, not necessarily the current approved procedure —
> confirm against the current STS form and procedure before treating it
> as the standard method.

**Outcome.** A completed daily site record for Level 1 earthworks supervision — mandatory material-source questions answered, plant and testing logged, and a per-area narrative of placement, compaction, proof rolling and sampling.

## Inputs

- Form S69 'Geotechnical Testing & Site Record Sheet' (Date of Issue 01/10/19, Revision 1)
- Job details (project, STS number, client, contractor, foreman)
- Day's nuclear density test numbers and sample records
- Site plan for locating tests/samples (referenced by the form)

## Procedure

1. Fill the header: Project, Project No. / STS No. (e.g. 32913/1829E-L), Client, Technician initials, Test Method (written as 'AS3798 Level 1 Testing'), Date Tested, Contractor, Foreman, Time Arrived on Site, Time Left Site.
2. Answer the four printed mandatory questions: 1) Is fill material imported from off site? (Y/N, and where from); 2) Has a Validation Certificate been sighted for this material? (Y/N — if No, contact office and arrange for certificate); 3) Is there an Unexpected Findings Protocol required? (Y/N — if Yes, attach daily Unexpected Findings sheet); 4) Has an Unexpected Find occurred today? (Y/N).
3. List Equipment on Site with counts and types (e.g. '2x Excavator, 2x Pad Foot Roller, 1x Water Cart, 3x Dump Truck, 1x Smooth Drum Roller, 2x Grader').
4. Complete Testing / Sampling: Field Density Taken as a test-number range (e.g. '#224 to #241'), Field Density Retests and what they were for (or N/A), Contamination Samples Taken range; ensure all tests/samples are located on the attached plan (printed instruction).
5. Write Comments / Remarks as a narrative organised by work area (examples use headings MP4 AREA / MP6 AREA / MP5 AREA), covering: material placed and layer thickness/RL, moisture conditioning relative to OMC, compaction plant used, proof rolls and their outcome, soft spots found and the excavate-and-replace treatment with RLs, nuclear density testing done, and samples sent to the laboratory; also record salinity/groundwater observations where the management plan requires it.
6. Note the printed footer obligation: the Level 1 timesheet (Form A7) must be signed at the end of each day by the contractor/client site representative.

## Decision rules

- If imported fill arrives without a sighted validation certificate, the form directs: contact the office and arrange the certificate.
- If a proof roll finds a soft spot, the record shows the practice: define the area, excavate to competent material (record both RLs), backfill with approved material in compacted layers, then density test the replacement.
- Field density tests are logged as a continuous numbered range for the day so the gauge printout, sheet and plan reconcile.

## Checks

- All four mandatory questions answered every day
- Test number range on the sheet matches the number of density tests actually taken
- Every test/sample located on the attached plan
- Arrival/departure times filled
- Form A7 timesheet signed by the contractor/client representative before leaving

## Common errors

- Leaving mandatory questions uncircled (blank on some examples)
- Narrative missing layer thickness or RL, which the better examples always give
- Contractor/Foreman fields left blank
- Forgetting the end-of-day Form A7 signature

## Caveats

- Reconstructed from STS field records — confirm against the current STS procedure before treating as the standard method
- None of the three examples has the mandatory Y/N answers visibly circled in the extracted text — the questions are printed but completion practice could not be verified
- The attached test-location plans referenced by the form were not in the retrieved files

## Standards cited

AS 3798 (Level 1 testing, written in the Test Method field)

- [[Reduced levels and datums]]
- [[Library - salinity and sodic soils]]

notes.title: Compute a planar-failure factor of safety in RocPlane and verify by hand
notes.body:
# Compute a planar-failure factor of safety in RocPlane and verify by hand

> **Source:** [YouTube — RocPlane Tutorial: Slope Safety Factor for Planar Failure](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=EJ4-rpbmkD4&t=0s) (00:00-05:32). A YouTube lecture — learning
> material, not an approved design procedure. Equations and numbers were
> heard through auto-captions; read them off the video before use, and
> verify anything design-relevant against the standard and the project
> specification. Engineering conclusions need qualified review.

**Outcome.** A deterministic factor of safety for a rock block sliding on a single failure plane, cross-checked against a hand calculation

## Inputs

- Slope height (12 m in the example) measured on site
- Unit weight (22 kN/m3, entered as 0.022 MN/m3)
- Slope face angle measured with a geological compass (64 degrees in the example)
- Failure plane angle (42 degrees) from site measurement
- Upper face angle (zero in the example because the crest was a straight line; enter the measured low angle if one exists)
- Mohr-Coulomb strength of the failure plane: friction angle 33 degrees, cohesion 10 kPa entered as 0.01 MPa

## Procedure

1. Check Project Settings: metric units with stress in MPa, and deterministic analysis when single values are known rather than ranges
2. Enter the geometry in Input Data: slope height, slope face angle, failure plane angle, and upper face angle
3. Enter unit weight converted from kN/m3 to MN/m3
4. Select the Mohr-Coulomb strength model and enter friction angle and cohesion, converting cohesion from kPa to the MPa field
5. Compute and read the factor of safety (0.992 in the example)
6. Verify against the closed-form hand calculation for planar failure — the same example gives the identical 0.992 by hand

## Decision rules

- Deterministic analysis is appropriate when each parameter has a single known value; use probabilistic settings if you hold ranges for cohesion, friction angle or unit weight
- Set the upper face angle to zero when the slope profile above the crest is a straight continuation with no bench

## Checks

- Reproduce the software result with the hand formula at least once to confirm inputs are interpreted correctly
- Double-check the two unit conversions: kN/m3 to MN/m3 for unit weight, and kPa to MPa for cohesion

## Common errors

- Entering cohesion in kPa into an MPa field (a factor-of-1000 error)
- Leaving default geometry values (e.g. a default upper face angle) unchanged instead of the measured ones

## Caveats

- YouTube lecture — learning material, not an approved design procedure; verify against project specification and current standards
- Drainage and water pressure are not addressed in this example; the computed factor of safety assumes a dry plane unless water is added
- The hand-calculation formula is in a companion video — equation shown on screen, read from the video

## Standards cited

None cited in the source passage.

## Related

notes.title: Compute a wedge failure factor of safety in Swedge
notes.body:
# Compute a wedge failure factor of safety in Swedge

> **Source:** [YouTube — Swedge Tutorial: Factor of Safety for Wedge Failure](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=exQ2fECKPbQ&t=0s) (00:00-10:30). A YouTube lecture — learning
> material, not an approved design procedure. Equations and numbers were
> heard through auto-captions; read them off the video before use, and
> verify anything design-relevant against the standard and the project
> specification. Engineering conclusions need qualified review.

**Outcome.** A deterministic factor of safety for a rock wedge formed by two intersecting joints in a slope face, including sensitivity to water filling of the joints

## Inputs

- Slope face dip and dip direction (60 / 037 in the class example) and slope height (8 m)
- Upper face (crest) dip and dip direction (about 10 degrees at the same dip direction in the example)
- Rock density or unit weight (density 2.6 t/m3, entered as about 0.026 MN/m3)
- For each of the two wedge-forming joints: dip and dip direction (40/060 and 70/320 in the example), cohesion and friction angle (c = 0, phi = 35 degrees in the example), and a waviness assumption (zero for planar joints)

## Procedure

1. Set Project Settings to deterministic analysis when each parameter has a single value rather than a distribution
2. Enter slope data: dip, dip direction, height, and the upper face geometry
3. Enter the unit weight; note the software works in MN/m3 so density must be converted
4. Enter both joints' dip and dip direction, cohesion, friction angle, and waviness
5. Compute; the software forms the wedge, calculates the trend and plunge of the line of intersection of the two joints internally, and reports the factor of safety (1.11 in the example)
6. For water sensitivity, open Input Data > Water, enable joint water pressure, and set the percent-filled value; re-compute at increasing saturation (e.g. 20, 50, 100 percent)

## Decision rules

- The orientation of a line of intersection is described by trend and plunge, not dip and dip direction — the software computes it from the two joint planes
- For observed wedge failures, cohesion on the joints is typically taken as zero, leaving friction to resist sliding
- Report the factor of safety rounded (e.g. 1.1), never to four decimals — field measurement and assumption accuracy cannot support that precision, and over-precise reporting loses marks in the lecturer's classes
- A factor of safety below 1 is treated as unstable in this analysis framework
- Small changes in unit weight (0.026 vs 0.025 MN/m3) barely affect the result; joint orientations and shear strength dominate

## Checks

- Verify units on entry: density in t/m3 versus unit weight in MN/m3
- Run the percent-filled water sweep — safety factor falls slightly at modest saturation and drops sharply at full saturation, so check the design case includes a defensible water assumption

## Common errors

- Copying the factor of safety from the software with spurious decimal precision
- Describing the line of intersection with dip and dip direction
- Ignoring water: a wedge acceptable dry can fail at high joint saturation

## Caveats

- YouTube lecture — learning material, not an approved design procedure; verify against project specification and current standards
- Some orientation values in the auto-captions are ambiguous (e.g. joint dip vs dip direction phrasing) — read the exact input values from the video screen or description
- The percent-filled water model is a simplified joint pressure assumption; confirm the water pressure model required for your project

## Standards cited

None cited in the source passage.

## Related

- [[Library - RMS and TfNSW specifications]]
- [[Skills]]

notes.title: Compute the factor of safety of a planar rock slope failure with tension crack by hand
notes.body:
# Compute the factor of safety of a planar rock slope failure with tension crack by hand

> **Source:** [YouTube — Planar Failure of Rock Slopes — Full Stability Analysis](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=fYyTzq4rUPs&t=0s) (00:01-19:35). A YouTube lecture — learning
> material, not an approved design procedure. Equations and numbers were
> heard through auto-captions; read them off the video before use, and
> verify anything design-relevant against the standard and the project
> specification. Engineering conclusions need qualified review.

**Outcome.** A hand-calculated factor of safety for a planar failure surface behind a slope crest, including geometry-derived tension crack depth, failure plane length and block weight

## Inputs

- Slope height H and slope face angle
- Failure plane angle
- Rock mass unit weight, cohesion and friction angle (from site or laboratory investigation)
- Unit weight of water if pore pressures are considered
- Tension crack depth z (given, or estimated from geometry)
- Optional: seismic coefficient, anchor force and inclination

## Procedure

1. Estimate tension crack depth z from slope geometry using the published expression combining slope height with the cotangent of the face angle and the tangent of the failure plane angle (worked example: H = 12 m, face 60 degrees, plane 35 degrees gives z about 4.35 m)
2. Compute failure plane length A = (H - z) / sin(failure plane angle) (example: about 13.34 m); cohesion acts along this full length
3. Compute block weight per metre width from the published weight formula using unit weight, H, z/H ratio and the cotangents of the plane and face angles (example: about 1241.4 kN/m)
4. If water is present, compute the uplift force U on the failure plane from water unit weight, water depth in the crack, and plane length (example: about 284.6 kN/m for a fully filled crack) and the horizontal crack water force V from water unit weight times crack water depth squared over two (example: about 92.8 kN/m)
5. Assemble the factor of safety as resisting over driving: numerator is cohesion times A plus (normal component of weight, minus seismic normal reduction, minus U, minus V times sin of plane angle, plus anchor normal contribution) times tan(friction angle); denominator is the downslope weight component plus seismic driving term plus V times cos of plane angle minus anchor driving reduction
6. Evaluate for the load case at hand, setting absent terms to zero

## Decision rules

- Factor of safety above 1 indicates stability; below 1 indicates the block can fail
- Water in the tension crack acts twice: U reduces frictional resistance and V adds driving force — include both
- The tension crack depth need not be surveyed if face and plane angles are known; it can be estimated from geometry

## Checks

- Confirm all forces are expressed per metre width of slope so units are consistent (kN/m)
- Check that omitted effects (seismic, water, anchor) are explicitly zeroed rather than left in with stale values
- Compare the dry-slope result against software (RocPlane reproduces 1.54 for this example)

## Common errors

- Applying cohesion over the slope height instead of over the failure plane length A
- Dropping either U or V when water is present
- Sign errors on the seismic terms, which reduce the numerator and increase the denominator simultaneously

## Caveats

- YouTube lecture — learning material, not an approved design procedure; verify against project specification and current standards

A hand calculated factor of safety for a planar failure surface behind a slope crest, including geometry derived tension crack depth, failure plane length and block weight Inputs Slope height H and slope face angle Failure plane angle Rock mass unit weight, cohesion and friction angle (from site or laboratory investigation) Unit weight of water if pore pressures are considered Tension crack depth z (given, or estimated from geometry) Optional: seismic coefficient, anchor force and inclination Procedure 1. Estimate tension crack depth z from slope geometry using the published expression combining slope height with the cotangent of the face angle and the tangent of the failure plane angle (worked example: H = 12 m, face 60 degrees, plane 35 degrees gives z about 4.35 m) 2. Compute failure plane length A = (H z) / sin(failure plane angle) (example: about 13.34 m); cohesion acts along this full length 3. Compute block weight per metre width from the published weight formula using unit weight, H, z/H ratio and the cotangents of the plane and face angles (example: about 1241.4 kN/m) 4. notes.title: Compute the size-corrected point load strength index Is(50) from test data
notes.body:
# Compute the size-corrected point load strength index Is(50) from test data

> **Source:** [YouTube — Point Load Test Part 2: Data Analysis](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=FPrjUBPRHFM&t=87s) (01:27-06:01). A YouTube lecture — learning
> material, not an approved design procedure. Equations and numbers were
> heard through auto-captions; read them off the video before use, and
> verify anything design-relevant against the standard and the project
> specification. Engineering conclusions need qualified review.

**Outcome.** A normalised point load strength index Is(50) for each valid test, from peak load and sample dimensions, for both diametral and axial loading configurations

## Inputs

- Peak failure load P (kN) per test
- Sample dimensions: core diameter D for diametral tests; thickness D and width/diameter W for axial tests

## Procedure

1. Determine the equivalent diameter De: for a diametral test on core loaded perpendicular to the axis, De simply equals the core diameter (De = 51 mm in the example)
2. For an axial test, compute the loaded area A = W times D (51.6 x 39.4 = 2033 mm2 in the example), then De from the equivalent-area relation De = square root of (4A / pi), about 50.9 mm in the example
3. Compute the uncorrected point load strength: peak load times 1000 divided by De squared (the factor 1000 reconciles kN with mm units); this gave 1.23 and 0.26 (MPa) for the two rocks
4. Apply the size correction to normalise to a 50 mm reference diameter: multiply by (De/50) raised to the power 0.45, giving Is(50) values of 1.241 and 0.27 in the example
5. Report Is(50); it can then be correlated to unconfined compressive strength (covered in a companion video)

## Decision rules

- A markedly low Is(50) may reflect weathering or an invalid failure mode from the test rather than intrinsic strength — check the test video/record before reporting
- A spreadsheet with the formulas pre-built is the practical way to process multiple tests

## Checks

- De route matches the loading configuration (direct diameter for diametral, equivalent-area formula for axial)
- Units consistent: P in kN, dimensions in mm, with the factor of 1000 applied once
- Size correction applied after, not instead of, the uncorrected index calculation

## Common errors

- Using the core diameter as De for an axial test instead of the equivalent-area formula
- Dropping or double-applying the factor of 1000 in the mixed kN/mm units
- Skipping the (De/50)^0.45 normalisation, making results from different sample sizes incomparable

## Caveats

- YouTube lecture — learning material, not an approved design procedure; verify against project specification and current standards
- Some caption digits are unreliable (50.878 vs 50.78 for De; 0.26 vs 0.27 progression) — equation shown on screen — read from the video and recompute
- The Is(50)-to-UCS correlation factor is not given in this video

## Standards cited

None cited in the source passage.

notes.title: Compute traffic exposure ratings (average vehicle risk and percent decision sight distance) for rockfall rating
notes.body:
# Compute traffic exposure ratings (average vehicle risk and percent decision sight distance) for rockfall rating

> **Source:** [YouTube — How to Perform Rockfall Hazard Assessment — Step by Step](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1i5D-RdYsR0&t=923s) (15:23-21:36). A YouTube lecture — learning
> material, not an approved design procedure. Equations and numbers were
> heard through auto-captions; read them off the video before use, and
> verify anything design-relevant against the standard and the project
> specification. Engineering conclusions need qualified review.

**Outcome.** Two traffic-related inputs to the rockfall hazard rating: the average vehicle risk along the affected road length and the ratio of actual to decision sight distance

## Inputs

- Traffic volume (cars per hour, or cars per day divided by 24)
- Length of road section affected by rockfall, in kilometres
- Posted speed limit
- Actual sight distance measured on site (distance from which a driver first sees a small object on the road, accounting for road curvature)
- Decision sight distance table indexed by posted speed limit

## Procedure

1. Compute average vehicle risk as traffic volume per hour multiplied by affected road length in kilometres, divided by the posted speed limit, expressed as a percentage
2. If traffic is supplied in cars per day, convert to cars per hour before applying the formula
3. Look up the decision sight distance for the posted speed limit, interpolating between tabulated speeds where needed
4. Measure the actual sight distance by driving the section and noting the distance at which a small rock-sized object first becomes visible; curves reduce it
5. Compute percent decision sight distance as actual sight distance divided by decision sight distance, times 100
6. Convert both percentages to rating points from the table, interpolating between tabulated percentages where time allows

## Decision rules

- If computed average vehicle risk exceeds 100 percent, cap it at 100 percent (maximum points) for the rating
- Lower percent decision sight distance is worse; if close to a tabulated boundary and no time to interpolate, adopt the worse (higher-point) category
- Always use the posted speed limit, not observed traffic speed

## Checks

- Confirm the road length was converted to kilometres before use
- Confirm units of traffic volume (per hour vs per day) match the formula form being used

## Common errors

- Mixing cars-per-day with a cars-per-hour formula
- Using actual driving speeds instead of the posted limit
- Measuring sight distance on the straight-line assumption when the road is curved

## Caveats

- YouTube lecture — learning material, not an approved design procedure; verify against project specification and current standards
- Formulas and the decision-sight-distance table are shown on screen — read from the video; auto-captions garble the symbols
- Worked example values: 120 cars/hr, 0.6 km, 60 km/h limit gave 120 percent AVR (capped at 100); 72 m actual over 171 m decision distance gave about 42 percent

## Standards cited

None cited in the source passage.

notes.title: Conduct a landslide hazard analysis and build the site geotechnical model (AGS 2007)
notes.body:
# Conduct a landslide hazard analysis and build the site geotechnical model (AGS 2007)

> **Source:** `42_1_4_amend.pdf` (AGS Practice Note Guidelines for Landslide Risk Management 2007 (Australian Geomechanics Vol 42 No 1, March 2007), Sections 4-5, Appendices B and E), held in the local reference library — see
> [[Reference library]]. This note is a paraphrased working aid, not the
> document. Values, clauses and criteria must be read from the source before
> they are relied on, and engineering conclusions need qualified review.

**Outcome.** A documented geotechnical model with characterised landslide hazards, estimated annual probabilities and travel distances, forming the front half of a defensible Landslide Risk Management (LRM) report.

## Inputs

- Desk-study data: geological maps, aerial photos, prior reports, council landslide inventory, local knowledge
- Site survey plan (or tape-and-clinometer plan) with contours, features and services
- Preliminary development design or assumed development (an element at risk must exist)
- Subsurface data from exposures, test pits or boreholes to below potential failure surfaces; groundwater/rainfall response information

## Procedure

1. Define scope with client and regulator requirements; issue a reverse brief (Section 4).
2. Assemble and source-reference all desk-study data (Section 5.1).
3. Inspect the site and surrounds and field-map geomorphic features to scale, covering upslope, downslope and adjacent areas, using standard mapping symbols (Section 5.2.2, Appendix E).
4. Establish the subsurface profile; where pre-existing landslides are suspected, prefer test pits (to see shear planes) or boreholes with inclinometers (Section 5.2.3).
5. Assess groundwater levels and their response to trigger rainfall; qualitative estimates may suffice for low-risk jobs, monitored piezometers for higher-risk or drainage-design cases (Section 5.2.4).
6. Draw natural-scale cross-sections integrating all data to express the geotechnical model, its groundwater and its uncertainties (Section 5.2.5).
7. Identify and characterise each landslide type (classification, volume, location, mechanism, travel distance potential) using Appendix B terminology, considering slope-forming processes and rates (Sections 5.2.6-5.3).
8. Estimate annual probability P(H) for each landslide with a technique matched to study level: inventory/history, geomorphic reasoning (Varnes principle), rainfall-frequency correlation, event trees, or expert judgement 'degree of belief'; partition as P(trigger) x P(slide given trigger) across the trigger range where useful (Section 5.4).
9. Estimate travel distance and probability of spatial impact P(S:H) using site evidence and empirical methods (e.g. Khalili et al 1996 for intact rotational slides; Hunter and Fell 2002, Corominas 1996 for break-up slides/flows), calibrated locally (Section 5.4.3).

## Decision rules

- Choose the qualitative likelihood term FROM the estimated probability — never adopt a probability from a qualitative term (practitioners diverge by orders of magnitude, Section 5.4.2(a)).
- Investigation is adequate only when the model explains slope processes, landslide extent, triggers and process rates; otherwise investigate further (Section 5.2.8).
- Full probabilistic/simulation frequency modelling only for special cases with extensive calibration data; expert judgement is often the only viable option.
- Sanity-check assessed annual probabilities against implied cumulative probability over the design life and known area performance (Section 5.4.2(c)).

## Checks

- Cross-sections at natural scale (plus a natural-scale summary if exaggeration used).
- Hazards addressed above, below and adjacent to the site, not just within the lot.
- Frequency reasoning documented transparently, with sensitivity/uncertainty stated; expert-judgement accuracy typically half to two orders of magnitude.

## Common errors

- Skipping the site walkover/field mapping — mandatory for every assessment.
- A geotechnical model that ignores off-site landslides which could travel onto or regress into the site.
- Inferring more precision in frequency than the data supports, without a stated conservative bias.
- Ignoring altered triggers (development, drainage changes, climate change) when extrapolating from historical performance.

## Caveats

- Verify method details and referenced correlations against the full Practice Note and its Commentary before use; this summary omits the Commentary's worked examples.
- Check for later AGS updates or council-specific policies that modify requirements.

## Standards cited

AGS 2000 Landslide Risk Management Concepts and Guidelines (companion), AGS 2007a Landslide Zoning Guideline, AGS 2007d Commentary; AGS 2007e GeoGuides

## Related

- [[Borehole log conventions]]

notes.title: Conduct a scanline discontinuity survey of a rock face
notes.body:
# Conduct a scanline discontinuity survey of a rock face

> **Source:** [YouTube — How to Perform Fracture Discontinuity Survey of Rock Mass](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Pe1tcfjycQY&t=26s) (00:26-04:33). A YouTube lecture — learning
> material, not an approved design procedure. Equations and numbers were
> heard through auto-captions; read them off the video before use, and
> verify anything design-relevant against the standard and the project
> specification. Engineering conclusions need qualified review.

**Outcome.** A field record, per discontinuity along a scanline, of type, orientation, persistence, aperture/infill, roughness, and spacing/count — the inputs needed by rock mass classification systems

## Inputs

- Accessible rock wall or exposure
- Tape/rule for the scanline and for measuring persistence and aperture
- Compass-clinometer for dip and dip direction
- Survey sheet or spreadsheet with type options (fault, joint, cleavage, shear, foliation, bedding)

## Procedure

1. Establish a scanline (an imaginary measuring line) across the face and work systematically along it, e.g. left to right
2. For each discontinuity intersected, record its type (bedding plane, joint set, shear plane, fault, cleavage, foliation)
3. Measure and record dip and dip direction (compass-clinometer technique covered in a companion video)
4. Measure persistence — the trace length of the discontinuity (about 1 m for the demonstrated example)
5. Assess aperture: measure the opening of open joints (about 3 mm in the demo); record tightly closed joints as closed; record any infill material (e.g. clay or sand) when present
6. Assess surface roughness (measurement method covered in a companion video)
7. Measure the spacing between successive discontinuities along the scanline
8. Count the total number of discontinuities intersected by the line (nine in the demo) and use the count to estimate average spacing

## Decision rules

- Spacing and discontinuity count are the priority measurements: they feed classification systems and indicate rock mass strength
- Record infill material type whenever a joint is not clean — soil infill (clay, sand) changes behaviour

## Checks

- Every discontinuity crossing the scanline has an entry — none skipped
- Count along the line and measured spacings are mutually consistent

## Common errors

- Recording only orientations and neglecting persistence, aperture, and infill
- Measuring spacing between arbitrary joint pairs rather than successive intersections along the scanline

## Caveats

- YouTube lecture — learning material, not an approved design procedure; verify against project specification and current standards
- The demonstration uses a rock wall simulation; field surveys add access and safety considerations not covered here

## Standards cited

None cited in the source passage.

notes.title: Confirm select fill and bedding material conformity for pipes under R11
notes.body:
# Confirm select fill and bedding material conformity for pipes under R11

> **Source:** `r011.pdf` (Clauses 3.1-3.2, 4.4.1, 2.6; Annexure R11/L (Ed 5 Rev 2)), held in the local reference library — see
> [[Reference library]]. This note is a paraphrased working aid, not the
> document. Values, clauses and criteria must be read from the source before
> they are relied on, and engineering conclusions need qualified review.

**Outcome.** Bedding and support fill materials are demonstrated conforming, at the specified testing frequency, before placement around pipes and culverts.

## Inputs

- Material source and stockpile identification
- Particle size distribution and Plasticity Index test results
- Placement volumes per material type
- Drawings/AS 3725 support type requirements

## Procedure

1. Classify the material by zone: Type BH Select Fill for bed and haunch zones, Type SO Select Fill for side and overlay zones, and the clean crushed stone/gravel requirement for material adjacent to weepholes (Clauses 3.1-3.2).
2. Check Type BH against its grading envelope (referenced to AS 3725 / AS 1597.2 tables) and its Plasticity Index ceiling; check Type SO against its maximum particle dimension and PI band (Clause 3.1).
3. Confirm pipe support is the specified type (HS3 per AS 3725 and the RMS model drawing) and that flowable fill is used at pipe connections where required (Clause 4.4.1).
4. Verify testing frequency against Annexure R11/L: PSD and PI tests are required per fixed volume increments of material placed (different rates for BH vs SO zones), all prior to placement.
5. Obtain the supplier/contractor certificate of conformity before the material or manufactured product is incorporated (Clause 2.6 Hold Point).

## Decision rules

- Material failing grading or plasticity limits must not be placed in the nominated zone - reassign or reject.
- If testing frequency in Annexure R11/L has not been met for the volume placed, the lot lacks conformity evidence regardless of the results in hand.
- Weephole-adjacent material must meet the maximum particle size and the fines limit on the 9.5 mm sieve; ordinary select fill is not a substitute.

## Checks

- Test methods match those nominated (RMS T201 for grading, RMS T109 for plasticity)
- Sampling was done prior to placement, not retrospectively
- Certificates of conformity are on file as identified records

## Common errors

- Using one combined stockpile for BH and SO zones without testing to the stricter BH frequency
- Overlooking the flowable fill requirement at pipe connections
- Treating the Annexure R11/L frequencies as targets rather than minimums per volume placed or part thereof

## Caveats

- Verify the spec edition is current for the project before relying on values.
- Contract documents and project-specific annexures override the base specification.

## Standards cited
