notes.title: Fit Hoek-Brown intact-rock parameters (sigma-ci, mi, tensile strength) from triaxial test data
notes.body:
# Fit Hoek-Brown intact-rock parameters (sigma-ci, mi, tensile strength) from triaxial test data

> **Source:** [YouTube — Hoek-Brown Failure Criteria for Rock — Examples and Solutions](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=9sb4QWHgzGw&t=28s) (00:28-08:15). A YouTube lecture — learning
> material, not an approved design procedure. Equations and numbers were
> heard through auto-captions; read them off the video before use, and
> verify anything design-relevant against the standard and the project
> specification. Engineering conclusions need qualified review.

**Outcome.** Unconfined compressive strength, the material constant mi, and an estimated tensile strength for intact rock, obtained by linearising the intact-rock special case of the Hoek-Brown criterion against triaxial results

## Inputs

- Triaxial test results for several samples (six in the example): confining pressure sigma-3 and major principal stress sigma-1 at failure for each test
- Spreadsheet with linear trendline capability (or graph paper)

## Procedure

1. Use the intact-rock special case of the generalized Hoek-Brown criterion: set s = 1 and alpha = 0.5, and use mi in place of mb (intact samples have no discontinuities)
2. For each test compute (sigma-1 minus sigma-3) squared and plot it against sigma-3 at failure
3. Fit a straight line of best fit through the points and read its slope and intercept from the trendline equation
4. The intercept equals sigma-ci squared, so sigma-ci is the square root of the intercept (about 16.6 MPa in the example)
5. The slope equals mi times sigma-ci, so mi = slope divided by sigma-ci (about 31.2 in the example)
6. Estimate tensile strength from the criterion's tensile expression using mi, sigma-ci and s = 1; the result carries a negative sign by convention and was about 0.5 MPa in magnitude in the example

## Decision rules

- s = 1 and alpha = 0.5 apply only to intact rock (lab-scale samples or exposures without discontinuities); jointed rock masses need the generalized criterion with mb, s, alpha from rock mass characterisation
- Harder rock geology gives higher mi — mi varies with rock type
- Tensile strength from this fit is negative (tension); report magnitude with the sign convention stated

## Checks

- Intercept and slope are taken from the fit through all tests, not from any single test
- Back-substitute the fitted sigma-ci and mi into the criterion and confirm the test points are reasonably reproduced

## Common errors

- Plotting (sigma-1 minus sigma-3) unsquared, which destroys the linearisation
- Applying intact-rock constants (s = 1) to a jointed rock mass
- Dividing the slope by the intercept instead of by sigma-ci (the square root of the intercept) when computing mi

## Caveats

- YouTube lecture — learning material, not an approved design procedure; verify against project specification and current standards
- Auto-captions state the slope inconsistently (570 vs 517.78) and garble parts of the tensile-strength expression — equation shown on screen — read from the video
- The lecture does not discuss effective vs total stresses for the triaxial data; confirm the stress basis of your own test data before fitting

## Standards cited

None cited in the source passage.

## Related

notes.title: Forecast time to rock slope collapse from displacement monitoring data
notes.body:
# Forecast time to rock slope collapse from displacement monitoring data

> **Source:** [YouTube — Can We Predict Rock Slope Collapse? Using Monitoring Data](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=9Idq3XYHMZY&t=0s) (00:01-06:38). A YouTube lecture — learning
> material, not an approved design procedure. Equations and numbers were
> heard through auto-captions; read them off the video before use, and
> verify anything design-relevant against the standard and the project
> specification. Engineering conclusions need qualified review.

**Outcome.** An empirical estimate of the number of days until collapse of an accelerating rock slide, from the onset velocity of progressive movement

## Inputs

- Long-term displacement/velocity monitoring record
- Identified transition point from regressive (decelerating/steady) to progressive (accelerating) movement and the onset velocity v0 at that point
- Empirical constant K, estimated as the ratio between mid-record and initial velocities (previous studies suggest a magnitude around 7; the example used 7.25)
- Velocity-time chart with logarithmic velocity axis

## Procedure

1. Plot monitored velocity against time and locate the change in curve character marking the start of the progressive stage; record the onset velocity v0 (example: 0.01 m/day)
2. Estimate K from the monitoring record as the ratio of a mid-record velocity to the initial velocity (example magnitude about 7.25)
3. Compute the collapse velocity as K squared times the onset velocity (example: 7.25 squared times 0.01 gives about 0.53 m/day)
4. Enter the log-scale velocity axis of the monitoring chart at the collapse velocity and read across/down to the corresponding time (example: about 61 days from onset)
5. Use the forecast to plan monitoring intensification, access restrictions and next steps rather than as a precise date

## Decision rules

- Regressive-stage movement alone does not warrant collapse forecasting; the method applies once progressive acceleration is established
- Treat the forecast as an order-of-magnitude planning tool: the correlation is highly empirical and will not hold in all cases

## Checks

- Confirm the trend of the progressive stage is well established (near-linear on the chart) before extrapolating
- Read the log velocity axis carefully; small reading errors change the forecast substantially

## Common errors

- Picking v0 from an arbitrary point instead of the regressive-to-progressive transition
- Treating the empirical K as universal rather than checking it against the site's own monitoring ratio
- Reporting the forecast date as deterministic to stakeholders

## Caveats

- YouTube lecture — learning material, not an approved design procedure; verify against project specification and current standards
- Method is empirical, derived from a small number of open-pit case studies; the lecturer repeatedly warns it may not apply everywhere
- The exact form of the velocity formulas and the sign convention for K are shown on screen — read from the video; captions garble them

## Standards cited

None cited in the source passage.

notes.title: Inspect bored pile sockets for sidewall smear and base cleanliness before certifying design assumptions
notes.body:
# Inspect bored pile sockets for sidewall smear and base cleanliness before certifying design assumptions

> **Source:** `Bored Piles Socketed Into Shale And Sandstone by pells.pdf` (Walker & Pells, Australian Geomechanics Dec 1998, pp 31-33; Sections 3 (Inspection) and 6 (Pile construction and inspection)), held in the local reference library — see
> [[Reference library]]. This note is a paraphrased working aid, not the
> document. Values, clauses and criteria must be read from the source before
> they are relied on, and engineering conclusions need qualified review.

**Outcome.** A socket confirmed (or rejected) as meeting the cleanliness and roughness conditions that modern high-capacity side-shear and end-bearing design values assume.

## Inputs

- Socket diameter, depth and drilling method (dry, under water, under mud, hand excavation)
- Design assumptions on sidewall roughness class and base cleanliness
- Access method (descent by cage/ladder for >=600 mm diameter, downhole TV camera for smaller)
- Nearby cored borehole logs or proving holes in the socket base

## Procedure

1. Confirm rock quality at socket level matches the class assumed in design, using nearby cored boreholes or cored/percussion proving holes in the base.
2. Inspect sidewalls for crushed or smeared rock or soil; smear from auger drilling in moist weathered rock can reach roughly 20 mm thick and infills the grooves that generate side shear.
3. Inspect the base for debris (softened, broken or crushed rock), which alters load-deflection behaviour and increases working-load settlement.
4. If smear or debris is found, require cleaning (drilling or stirring under water, special sidewall-cleaning tools, hand or purpose-built bucket base cleaning) and re-inspect.
5. Record and report the inspection items required by the specification (the paper's Draft Specification Clause A6.2) and certify only that inspections were done and construction matches design assumptions.

## Decision rules

- Piles that cannot be inspected (method precludes descent or camera access) must not be designed with the high side-shear and end-bearing parameters of the referenced methods.
- Piles formed under drilling mud should not normally use parameters applicable to piles formed dry or under water.
- Piles under 600 mm diameter cannot be descended, so use a downhole TV camera.
- If the required cleanliness standard is uneconomic for the project, revert to conservative code-level capacities instead of invoking high design values.

## Checks

- Sidewall substantially free of crushed/smeared material; base debris within design limits.
- Rock class at founding level matches design assumption.
- NSW confined-space requirements (harness, breathing apparatus, crane licence for lowering personnel) satisfied for manned descent.

## Common errors

- Assuming flight-auger drilling in moist weathered shale or sandstone leaves clean walls; it usually does not.
- Relying on drag-pick buckets or augers for final base cleaning; they usually leave too much debris.
- Having the inspecting engineer engaged by the contractor rather than the principal, creating a conflict of interest.
- Treating statutory confined-space rules as a reason to skip inspection; they restrict but do not preclude descent.

## Caveats

- Guidance is based on Sydney-area geology; adapt with care elsewhere.
- This is a design reference, not a certification: all values and acceptance criteria must be verified against the source paper and reviewed by a qualified geotechnical engineer before use.

## Standards cited

NSW Occupational Health and Safety (Confined Spaces) Regulation 1990, Pells, Mostyn & Walker (1998) design parameters, Williams & Pells (1981); Rowe & Armitage (1989)

NSW confined space requirements (harness, breathing apparatus, crane licence for lowering personnel) satisfied for manned descent. Common errors Assuming flight auger drilling in moist weathered shale or sandstone leaves clean walls; it usually does not. Relying on drag pick buckets or augers for final base cleaning; they usually leave too much debris. Having the inspecting engineer engaged by the contractor rather than the principal, creating a conflict of interest. Treating statutory confined space rules as a reason to skip inspection; they restrict but do not preclude descent. Caveats Guidance is based on Sydney area geology; adapt with care elsewhere. This is a design reference, not a certification: all values and acceptance criteria must be verified against the source paper and reviewed by a qualified geotechnical engineer before use. notes.title: Interpret an AX01a printed plate bearing test record
notes.body:
# Interpret an AX01a printed plate bearing test record

> **Source:** `AX01 Sample Results with GPS.pdf` (Single sample record sheet (Record number 2)), held in the local reference library — see
> [[Reference library]]. This note is a paraphrased working aid, not the
> document. Values, clauses and criteria must be read from the source before
> they are relied on, and engineering conclusions need qualified review.

**Outcome.** The engineer can read a DIN 18134-300 test record, verify its metadata, and judge pass/fail against the nominal Ev2 and Ev2/Ev1 targets.

## Inputs

- AX01a test record (printout or Excel sheet)
- Project acceptance values for Ev2 and Ev2/Ev1

## Procedure

1. Verify the header: record and card numbers, start/end time, device number, plate diameter (300 mm), lever ratio, sensor details, and the GPS latitude/longitude confirming the test location.
2. Trace the tabulated stress/deflection pairs through first loading, unloading and second loading, and check they match the plotted curve.
3. Read the results block: maximum first-cycle stress s1max, Ev1, Ev2, Ev2/Ev1 and the Westergaard modulus.
4. Compare each actual value with its nominal target and rating - in the sample, Ev2 of 76.68 MN/m2 against a nominal 45 rates OK, while Ev2/Ev1 of 2.642 against a nominal 2.2 rates failed - and treat the test as non-conforming if any criterion fails.
5. Where the ratio fails but Ev2 comfortably exceeds the requirement, consider the concession (from the German framework) that higher ratios may be acceptable when Ev1 reaches 60% of the required Ev2, subject to the project specification.

## Decision rules

- Both the Ev2 floor and the Ev2/Ev1 ceiling must pass for compaction acceptance; a high Ev2 alone does not save a failed ratio.
- A failed ratio with adequate Ev2 typically signals further compaction of the layer is achievable.

## Checks

- Deflection at the end of unloading versus the first-cycle maximum gives the plastic (unrecovered) settlement.
- GPS coordinates match the intended test location.

## Common errors

- Reporting the test as passing because Ev2 rated OK while overlooking the failed Ev2/Ev1 rating.
- Ignoring header metadata, so records cannot be matched to test positions later.

## Caveats

- This document is a single example printout, not a procedure; the pass/fail concession comes from the companion calculations document, not this sheet.
- Nominal values (45 MN/m2, ratio 2.2) are the example's settings, not universal requirements.

## Standards cited

DIN 18134

notes.title: Interpret the rock-core section of a borehole log
notes.body:
# Interpret the rock-core section of a borehole log

> **Source:** [YouTube — How to Read and Understand Borehole Logs Part 2: Rock Core, Weathering, Strength, Discontinuity, RQD](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NMNzMLSO91w&t=0s) (00:00-05:15). A YouTube lecture — learning
> material, not an approved design procedure. Equations and numbers were
> heard through auto-captions; read them off the video before use, and
> verify anything design-relevant against the standard and the project
> specification. Engineering conclusions need qualified review.

**Outcome.** Correct reading of a real borehole log's rock columns — weathering grade, strength grade, fracture spacing, RQD, core recovery, and the per-depth discontinuity records — and recognition of where soil logging conventions stop and rock conventions begin

## Inputs

- A borehole log with rock core section (description, weathering, strength, fracture spacing, RQD, core recovery, discontinuity columns)
- The log's legend for graphic lithology patterns and symbols

## Procedure

1. Identify the soil-rock boundary: upper soil intervals (fill, clay, extremely weathered material behaving as soil) carry SPT results and sample marks but no weathering/strength/fracture-spacing entries, because those parameters only apply to rock
2. Read the weathering column symbols (EW, HW, MW, SW etc.) for each rock interval
3. Read the strength column grades (extremely low, very low, low, medium, high, very high, extremely high)
4. Read fracture spacing in metres as the distance between discontinuities visible in the core (e.g. 0.2-0.5 m spacing implying spacing mostly greater than 0.1 m)
5. Read RQD as a percentage — high values (e.g. 91%) indicate high-quality rock — and cross-check that wide fracture spacing is consistent with high RQD
6. Read core recovery; 100% is ideal, lower values mean core was lost to drilling issues, not necessarily poor rock
7. Read the discontinuity records: each entry gives depth (e.g. 3.30 m, 3.55 m, 3.71 m), type, inclination, roughness, aperture, and surface coating symbols
8. Use the legend at the bottom of the log to decode graphic lithology patterns rather than memorising them

## Decision rules

- Absence of weathering/strength/spacing data over an interval signals soil-type material, not missing data
- High RQD plus wide fracture spacing plus full recovery together indicate good quality rock mass; treat inconsistencies between them as a prompt to re-examine the log

## Checks

- Fracture spacing, RQD and core recovery tell a consistent story for each interval
- Every discontinuity record has a depth and a full symbol string

## Common errors

- Treating low core recovery as low rock quality when it may be a drilling/technical artefact
- Trying to memorise graphic log patterns instead of using the legend supplied with the log

## Caveats

- YouTube lecture — learning material, not an approved design procedure; verify against project specification and current standards
- Symbol conventions vary between logging houses; always defer to the specific log's legend

## Standards cited

None cited in the source passage.

## Related

- [[Rock weathering classes]]
- [[Borehole log conventions]]
- [[Skills]]

notes.title: Investigate ground for excavation adjacent to road
notes.body:
# Investigate ground for excavation adjacent to road

> **Source:** `gtd-2020-001.pdf` (Geotechnical investigations section (GTD 2020/001)), held in the local reference library — see
> [[Reference library]]. This note is a paraphrased working aid, not the
> document. Values, clauses and criteria must be read from the source before
> they are relied on, and engineering conclusions need qualified review.

**Outcome.** A geotechnical investigation scoped to the authority's minimums for retaining-wall design beside transport infrastructure.

## Inputs

- Wall alignment length and final excavation level
- Anticipated geology (soil/rock, defect-prone units)
- Access constraints for drilling

## Procedure

1. Plan boreholes along the wall alignment at the maximum spacing, drilled below final excavation level into competent material by the required margin.
2. Use cored drilling with triple-tube sampling in rock; do not rely on test pits.
3. Characterise soil/rock units and groundwater to build the geological model and design parameters.
4. In predominantly rock excavations, define adverse defect systems (joints, faults, intrusions, weak zones) that could affect the excavation or adjacent assets.
5. For deep rock excavations, geologically map the cut face at regular excavation increments and review results against design assumptions before excavating further.

## Decision rules

- At least one borehole per 30 m of wall length, taken at least 3 m into competent material below final excavation level (gtd-2020-001 geotechnical investigations section).
- Test-pit-only investigations are generally not acceptable (gtd-2020-001 geotechnical investigations section).
- Rock excavations deeper than 10 m require face mapping every 2 m of excavation by a qualified engineering geologist or geotechnical engineer, with design-conformance review before progressing (gtd-2020-001 geotechnical investigations section).

## Checks

- Groundwater conditions established, including accidental cases (e.g. main breaks, damming).
- Investigation depth measured below final excavation level, not existing surface.

## Common errors

- Terminating holes at excavation level instead of 3 m into competent material.
- Skipping staged face mapping in deep rock cuts.
- Treating refusal in fill or boulders as 'competent material'.

## Caveats

- Verify currency; project-specific authority requirements override.
- The 2012 predecessor stated similar but not identical requirements - use the current edition.

## Standards cited

AS 1726

## Related

- [[AS 1726 soil and rock description]]
- [[Groundwater observations]]
- [[Borehole log conventions]]
- [[Skills]]

notes.title: Keep and compile a signed STS Site Timesheet (Form A7) for the billing period
notes.body:
# Keep and compile a signed STS Site Timesheet (Form A7) for the billing period

> **Source:** [Google Drive — O4 DAILY SITE TIMESHEET/329131829E-L(30-01-2026 TO 25-02-2026).pdf](https://drive.google.com/file/d/12KpAqkhuM-P4jxjTQgzLAbLH_PooRHTG/view) (Signed monthly compilation of handwritten Form A7 Site Timesheet blocks for job 32913/1829E-L (Marsden Park works), with per-day signatures, travel-inclusive totals and a rain-cancellation annotation). Reconstructed from STS's own
> field records on Google Drive — completed forms, labelled photos and
> scans, catalogued in [[Field records catalogue]]. It shows what the
> records evidence, not necessarily the current approved procedure —
> confirm against the current STS form and procedure before treating it
> as the standard method.

**Outcome.** A daily-signed record of site hours (onsite and including travel) per technician and project, compiled into a signed package covering the invoice period.

## Inputs

- STS Geotechnics Site Timesheet blocks (Form A7, Revision 1, date of issue 01/10/19 printed in footer)
- Technician name, project no. and STS job no.
- Daily start/finish times and travel time
- Client or supervisor signature each day

## Procedure

1. Head each timesheet block with Name, Project No. and STS No. (the job/purchase reference, e.g. an E-L suffixed job code).
2. Each worked day, enter one row: date, time start, time finish, hours onsite, and total hours including travel.
3. Obtain a signature in the row's Signature column the same day - the signer varies by day (site representative), so the signature belongs to the day, not the sheet.
4. Annotate non-standard days directly under the affected row (e.g. a note that rain cancelled the work explaining short hours).
5. Total the hours in the Total row of each block and record any authorised overtime against AUTHORISED O/T.
6. At the end of the billing period, compile the sheets covering the period (e.g. 30-01 to 25-02) into a single scanned package named with job number and date range for invoicing.

## Decision rules

- Hours onsite and total hours are separate columns - travel is only ever added to the total column.
- A cancelled or rained-off day still gets a row with the hours actually incurred and a reason note.
- Overtime is only claimable if it appears against the authorised O/T field.

## Checks

- Every row signed; an unsigned day is a dispute risk at invoicing.
- Total hours minus hours onsite equals a plausible travel allowance for the site.
- Compiled package covers the full period with no missing dates that were actually worked.

## Common errors

- Batch-signing several days at once at week end, which weakens the record's evidentiary value.
- Writing 9.5 hrs onsite and forgetting to add travel in the total column, undercharging the day.
- Date slips across month boundaries (e.g. 30/01 written in a February block) - check sequence when compiling.

## Caveats

- Reconstructed from STS field records — confirm against the current STS procedure before treating as the standard method

## Standards cited

None cited in the source passage.

- [[Skills]]

notes.title: Label core boxes using the STS printed photo-board template
notes.body:
# Label core boxes using the STS printed photo-board template

> **Source:** [Google Drive — Field Sheets (STS blank templates + reference)/Core Box Label.pptx; Core Photos (MP4 compilation)/MP4-BH01.jpeg; Photos (Nov 2021 site photo dump)/IMG20211126131944.jpg](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1qEsHuXWIxTp9NDT1IswJ3xK-lWfp_dES/view) (The 9-slide pptx template (six-field table, 0.0-1.0 m scale bar at 0.1 m graduations, logo, QR code, office-address strip); a 2026 core photo showing the printed board filled in marker with colour chart, per-row depth numbers and 'Coring End at 19.98m'; a 2021 photo showing the legacy handwritten-strip/metre-block/tape-measure method). Reconstructed from STS's own
> field records on Google Drive — completed forms, labelled photos and
> scans, catalogued in [[Field records catalogue]]. It shows what the
> records evidence, not necessarily the current approved procedure —
> confirm against the current STS form and procedure before treating it
> as the standard method.

**Outcome.** Every core box is photographed behind a standard printed STS board identifying project, client, address, date, borehole and depth, with a 1 m graduated scale bar and colour reference, and with depth progress marked inside the box, so any core photo is self-identifying and dimensionally interpretable.

## Inputs

- Core Box Label.pptx template (STS branded, multiple layout variants)
- Printer / laminated board stock for the label
- Permanent marker for handwriting job details
- Core box with recovered core runs placed in depth order

## Procedure

1. Print the label board from the PowerPoint template; the slide carries a six-field table (PROJECT NO, CLIENT, ADDRESS on the left; DATE, BOREHOLE NO, DEPTH on the right), the STS Geotechnics logo, a QR code, and a full-width 1 m scale bar graduated at 0.1 m intervals from 0.0 m to 1.0 m.
2. Hand-fill the six fields in marker for the box being photographed: project number, client, site address, photo date, borehole ID, and the depth (total or box depth range).
3. Place the board across the top of the core box together with the colour/greyscale calibration chart so both appear in frame with the core.
4. Inside the box, mark depth progress on the tray dividers or spacer blocks (metre marks per row) and write the termination on the last row (e.g. 'Coring End at 19.98 m').
5. Keep a handwritten strip in the first tray repeating job number, address, borehole ID, date and run start depth as a backup identification independent of the board.
6. Photograph the box square-on from above with board, scale bar, colour chart and all trays fully in frame.

## Decision rules

- Choose the template slide variant that matches the box format being photographed; all variants keep the same six identification fields and 1 m scale bar.
- If a printed board is not available on site, fall back to the legacy manual method: handwritten strip along the box edge (job no, site, BH, date, initials, START depth), white spacer blocks at each metre, an END block at termination depth, and a tape measure laid along the core for scale.
- Depth field on the board records how deep the hole/box extends; the in-box end-of-coring note records the exact termination depth to two decimals.

## Checks

- All six board fields are legible in the final photo and agree with the borehole log for the same hole and date.
- Scale bar and colour chart are unobstructed so measurements and colour can be corrected from the image.
- In-box depth marks run consecutively with no missing metres, and the end-of-coring depth matches the logged termination depth.

## Common errors

- Leaving board fields blank or filling them after the photo, breaking the link between image and hole
- Cropping the scale bar or colour chart out of frame, making the photo unusable for measurement
- Depth on the board disagreeing with the handwritten in-box strip or the borehole log
- Photographing at an oblique angle so the scale bar cannot be used across the full box width

## Caveats

- Reconstructed from STS field records — confirm against the current STS procedure before treating as the standard method
- The core-box PHOTO practice (photographing with the STS photo board) was mined separately; this skill covers producing and completing the label board itself and marking depths inside the box
- Purpose of the QR code on the board is not evidenced in the records

## Standards cited

AS 1726 (geotechnical site investigations — core handling and logging context)

## Related

- [[Field records catalogue]]
- [[AS 1726 soil and rock description]]
- [[Borehole log conventions]]
- [[Skills]]

Common errors Leaving board fields blank or filling them after the photo, breaking the link between image and hole Cropping the scale bar or colour chart out of frame, making the photo unusable for measurement Depth on the board disagreeing with the handwritten in box strip or the borehole log Photographing at an oblique angle so the scale bar cannot be used across the full box width Caveats Reconstructed from STS field records — confirm against the current STS procedure before treating as the standard method The core box PHOTO practice (photographing with the STS photo board) was mined separately; this skill covers producing and completing the label board itself and marking depths inside the box Purpose of the QR code on the board is not evidenced in the records Standards cited AS 1726 (geotechnical site investigations — core handling and logging context) Related Field records catalogue AS 1726 soil and rock description Borehole log conventions Skills

notes.title: Log a borehole soil profile by hand on the OP GEO 007a/007b BH soil field log sheets
notes.body:
# Log a borehole soil profile by hand on the OP GEO 007a/007b BH soil field log sheets

> **Source:** [Google Drive — Field Sheets (STS blank templates + reference)/OP GEO 007a reva bh soil log 5m with grid line.pdf and OP GEO 007b RevB bh soil log 10m.pdf](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1bsF6f8Vw-FBtqaycQLnqRNj8qcCCy4Dw/view) (Blank EI Australia-branded BH soil field log sheets, 5 m gridded and 10 m variants, with printed description-order header and Logged/Checked sign-off). Reconstructed from STS's own
> field records on Google Drive — completed forms, labelled photos and
> scans, catalogued in [[Field records catalogue]]. It shows what the
> records evidence, not necessarily the current approved procedure —
> confirm against the current STS form and procedure before treating it
> as the standard method.

**Outcome.** A handwritten field borehole soil log with depth-referenced descriptions in the standard order, ready for checking and transcription into the final log.

## Inputs

- OP GEO 007a RevA (5 m sheet with 0.1 m grid lines) or OP GEO 007b RevB (10 m sheet) blank log
- Project, location, position, job no., client, contractor, drill rig, inclination (pre-printed -90 degrees for vertical holes)
- Drilling returns/spoil, samples and field tests as the hole advances
- EI Soil Logging Cheat Sheet as the wording reference

## Procedure

1. Fill the header: project, location, position, job no., client, contractor, drill rig and inclination; enter borehole ID after 'BOREHOLE: BH', sheet x of y, date started/completed.
2. Choose the sheet scale: the 5 m sheet (007a) has fine 0.1 m grid lines for detailed shallow logging; the 10 m sheet (007b) suits deeper holes at 1 m major divisions.
3. As the hole advances, record in the Drilling columns the method, penetration resistance and any water observations against depth.
4. Enter depth (m) and RL down the depth column; mark strata boundaries at their measured depths.
5. In the Sampling columns record each sample or field test (type and depth) and whether it was recovered.
6. Sketch the graphic log and assign a USCS symbol per stratum.
7. Write the material description in the printed order: secondary soil then PRIMARY SOIL; grain size/plasticity, colour, secondary constituents (with description), strength/density, moisture condition, then other remarks (this order is printed on the 007b header).
8. Complete the Moisture Condition and Consistency/Density columns per stratum, and use Structure and Additional Observations for zoning, cementation, fill indicators, seepage and similar notes.
9. Sign as 'Logged' with date, and have the log 'Checked' and dated by a second person.

## Decision rules

- Primary soil name in capitals with secondary constituents around it, exactly in the printed description order - do not free-form the description.
- Use the 5 m gridline sheet when strata changes or test intervals need better than 0.5 m resolution; switch to continuation sheets rather than crowding one sheet.
- If material becomes rock, move to the companion rock core log (OP GEO 008 series) rather than stretching soil terminology.
- The log must be read with the EI/STS accompanying standard notes (stated on the sheet footer) - terminology follows those notes.

## Checks

- Every stratum has all description elements (name, grain size/plasticity, colour, constituents, strength/density, moisture) - a missing element is a gap, not a default.
- Sample depths on the log agree with sample labels and the daily record.
- Logged and Checked signatures with dates are both present before the sheet is filed.

## Common errors

- Writing colour or moisture ahead of the primary name, breaking the standard description order.
- Leaving the Consistency/Density column blank when it is already embedded in the text description - the column is the scannable summary and must still be filled.
- Forgetting RL entries so the log cannot later be tied to reduced levels.

## Caveats

- Reconstructed from STS field records — confirm against the current STS procedure before treating as the standard method
- Templates are EI Australia-branded (used within STS practice); revision codes 007a RevA and 007b RevB should be checked for currency.

## Standards cited

AS 1726.1 (geotechnical site investigations - soil descriptions), USCS classification

- [[Soil description order]]

notes.title: Log rock core by hand on the OP GEO 008a/008b BH rock log sheets
notes.body:
# Log rock core by hand on the OP GEO 008a/008b BH rock log sheets

> **Source:** [Google Drive — Field Sheets (STS blank templates + reference)/OP GEO 008a RevA BH Rock log 5m.pdf and OP GEO 008b RevB BH Rock log 10m.pdf](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1gSvA4_vf799Y4kyiMl6--jAvKIJ9p3YA/view) (Blank EI-branded cored borehole log sheets with TCR/RQD columns, banded Is(50) inferred-strength scale and log-scale defect-spacing columns; coring observation practice from the EI logging guide sheet in the same folder). Reconstructed from STS's own
> field records on Google Drive — completed forms, labelled photos and
> scans, catalogued in [[Field records catalogue]]. It shows what the
> records evidence, not necessarily the current approved procedure —
> confirm against the current STS form and procedure before treating it
> as the standard method.

**Outcome.** A handwritten cored-borehole field log capturing core recovery, rock description, weathering, inferred strength and defect data against depth.

## Inputs

- OP GEO 008a RevA (5 m) or OP GEO 008b RevB (10 m) blank rock log sheet
- Header data as for the soil log (project, job no., contractor, drill rig, inclination)
- Core runs laid out in boxes with run markers
- Point load or field strength assessments per interval

## Procedure

1. Complete the same header block as the soil log (project, location, position, job no., client, contractor, drill rig, inclination, dates, sheet numbers).
2. For each core run record the Drilling columns: method, water observations, TCR (total core recovery) and RQD (SCR) against the run interval.
3. Mark depth and RL; draw the graphic log per lithology.
4. Describe rock in the standard order (ROCK NAME; grain size, colour, fabric/texture, inclusions or minor components, strength, weathering) in the Rock/Soil Material Description column.
5. Tick the Weathering column band (RS/XW/HW/DW/MW/SW/FR terms per the logging guide).
6. Mark inferred strength in the Is(50) MPa banded columns - the sheet prints bands from extremely low through extremely high keyed to point load index values (0.03, 0.1, 0.3, 1, 3, 10 MPa boundaries).
7. Record each defect in Defect Description & Additional Observations using the convention depth: type; angle, shape, roughness, coating, coating material (e.g. a bedding parting or joint entry), and plot Average Defect Spacing in the log-scaled mm columns (10 to 3000 mm).
8. During coring also note water return percentage and colour changes, and drilling rate changes per run - these flag weathering changes, clay-filled joints and core-loss zones.
9. Sign Logged and have Checked completed with dates.

## Decision rules

- TCR and RQD are recorded per run, not per lithology - keep run boundaries visible on the log.
- Strength is inferred in the field from pick/knife/hand behaviour and confirmed by Is(50) testing; tick the band, do not write a bare number without basis.
- Defects below the 100 mm size threshold use seam abbreviations, larger use zone abbreviations (per the EI logging guide convention).
- Sudden penetration-rate or water-return changes get an explicit note even if the core looks uniform.

## Checks

- TCR/RQD percentages consistent with what is actually in the core box (cross-check against core box photos).
- Every defect entry has depth, type and orientation at minimum.
- Weathering and strength ticks exist for the full cored depth with no unexplained gaps.

## Common errors

- Averaging defects mentally instead of using the average-defect-spacing columns, losing fracture-spacing data for design.
- Recording RQD without noting SCR basis where core is weak, overstating rock quality.
- Omitting water-return observations, which are hard to reconstruct after the shift.

## Caveats

- Reconstructed from STS field records — confirm against the current STS procedure before treating as the standard method
- No completed handwritten example of this rock log was found in the sampled folders, so column usage is inferred from the blank sheet plus the companion logging guide.

## Standards cited

AS 1726.1 (rock description, weathering and defect terminology), ISRM point load index Is(50)

- [[Rock weathering classes]]
- [[Rock strength classes]]
- [[Reduced levels and datums]]
- [[Borehole log conventions]]
- [[Skills]]

notes.title: Log rock core with defect groups
notes.body:
# Log rock core with defect groups

> **Source:** `guideline-geotechnical.pdf` (Section 4, Tables 4.1.1(a)-(b) and defect notes), held in the local reference library — see
> [[Reference library]]. This note is a paraphrased working aid, not the
> document. Values, clauses and criteria must be read from the source before
> they are relied on, and engineering conclusions need qualified review.

**Outcome.** Rock core logs capturing weathering, strength, RQD per rock-mass unit and grouped defect descriptions suitable for design and kinematic assessment.

## Inputs

- Clean rock core inspected wet in natural light, as soon as boxed
- Field strength tests, later point-load and UCS results
- Protractors for defect angle measurement
- Detailed core logging and defect forms

## Procedure

1. Describe rock in four ordered rows: NAME with map-unit symbol; weathering/alteration class followed by colour, grainsize, texture, fabric, representative strength and RQD per rock-mass unit; features/inclusions/minor components with mm scale; then defect sets.
2. Where rock is extremely weathered/altered to soil properties but retains rock fabric, log it as 'recovered as' followed by a full soil description.
3. Group defects by angle-of-incidence ranges to the plane normal to the core axis, listed by prevalence, each described as: type, angle, frequency per metre, roughness, shape (if observable at sufficient scale), aperture, infill; distinguish drilling-induced breaks and note healed defects.
4. Record per-run recovery, core loss and RQD on the drilling data form; build detailed weathering, intact-strength and defect-spacing histograms from the detailed logging form and reconcile them against RQD and test results.
5. Reconcile field strength estimates against later point-load/UCS results considering failure mode; complete a separate detailed defect log where kinematic analysis is needed.

## Decision rules

- Overlapping weathering terms (e.g. HW/MW) are not permitted for a unit; minor zones 0.1-1.0 m are detailed in the weathering column, and intervals under 100 mm go to the additional-data column (guideline sections 4.1.1-4.1.2).
- Aperture measured in mm; infill thicker than 1 mm described as a seam or vein with composition and thickness (guideline defect notes).
- Defect persistence can only be measured in the field, not from core (guideline defect notes).

## Checks

- Defect spacing histogram reconciles with RQD and the listed defect sets.
- Drilling-induced breaks excluded from defect statistics.
- 'Massive' only used where observed at greater than 1 m scale.

## Common errors

- Logging dry, dirty core and misjudging colour and weathering.
- Averaging weathering across a unit with a single hybrid term.
- Counting mechanical drilling breaks as natural defects, depressing RQD.

## Caveats

- TMR-specific presentation; verify the project's governing logging standard.
- Field strength estimates are provisional until laboratory confirmation.

## Standards cited

AS 1726:2017, TMR Form F:GEOT017, TMR Forms F:GEOT199/533

notes.title: Log soil strata to TMR convention
notes.body:
# Log soil strata to TMR convention

> **Source:** `guideline-geotechnical.pdf` (Sections 2-3, Tables 3.1.1(a)-(b) (TMR Geotechnical Logging Guideline, March 2019)), held in the local reference library — see
> [[Reference library]]. This note is a paraphrased working aid, not the
> document. Values, clauses and criteria must be read from the source before
> they are relied on, and engineering conclusions need qualified review.

**Outcome.** Borehole/test-pit soil descriptions in the standard row order and naming convention, ready for review and model building.

## Inputs

- Field observations of cuttings, disturbed and undisturbed samples
- Pocket penetrometer and simple field test results
- Laboratory PSD and plasticity results (for finalisation)
- The authority's terms-and-symbols reference form

## Procedure

1. Describe soils in six ordered rows: name with origin; colour/moisture/consistency; then primary, secondary and minor component particle characteristics (each with estimated percentage, grainsize, shape, grading or plasticity); then structure (zoning, defects, cementation with mm thicknesses).
2. Name composite soils as lower-case secondary prefix + UPPER-CASE primary + lower-case minor suffix, with origin in brackets (FILL/TOPSOIL upper case).
3. Describe colour in the moist state from the standard colour list, moisture as dry/moist/wet, and use consistency terms for cohesive and relative-density terms for non-cohesive soils.
4. Assign a preliminary group symbol in brackets from field tests; replace with the unbracketed final symbol once laboratory PSD/plasticity results are in.
5. Cross-check sample labels against the log and drilling data form; describe SPT samples before sealing, and pocket-penetrometer test tube ends before sealing undisturbed samples.

## Decision rules

- All descriptions must follow AS 1726:2017 and the authority's terms-and-symbols form; field logging is completed in the field wherever physically possible (guideline sections 1.1, 2.2.2).
- Final soil names/classifications are set by laboratory results, not field impressions (guideline section 3.1).

## Checks

- Groundwater strike depth and time recorded; piezometer readings dated on final logs.
- Geologist present in the field for all investigation stages.
- Component percentages sum sensibly and match the assigned name hierarchy.

## Common errors

- Writing descriptors out of the prescribed row order, breaking downstream data capture.
- Using consistency terms on sands or density terms on clays.
- Finalising group symbols without laboratory confirmation.

## Caveats

- Queensland TMR document - conventions differ in detail from other agencies; verify currency and any project-specified logging standard.
- Licensed no-derivatives; follow, don't adapt, the convention on TMR work.

## Standards cited

AS 1726:2017, TMR Form F:GEOT017, TMR Forms F:GEOT026/199/533

## Related

- [[AS 1726 soil and rock description]]
- [[Borehole log conventions]]
- [[Library - RMS and TfNSW specifications]]
- [[Soil description order]]
- [[Skills]]

notes.title: Look up standard geotechnical logging terms, symbols and classification tables (TMR GEOT 017/10)
notes.body:
# Look up standard geotechnical logging terms, symbols and classification tables (TMR GEOT 017/10)

> **Source:** `Terms-Symbols-GEOT017_10 (1).pdf` (Queensland TMR Form F:GEOT 017/10 (2019), Parts 1 and 2), held in the local reference library — see
> [[Reference library]]. This note is a paraphrased working aid, not the
> document. Values, clauses and criteria must be read from the source before
> they are relied on, and engineering conclusions need qualified review.

**Outcome.** Fast, consistent AS 1726:2017-aligned terminology for logging soil and rock — particle size fractions, accessory-component wording, plasticity, consistency/density, moisture, rock strength/weathering, defect descriptions, and standard symbols/abbreviations.

## Inputs

- A logging or report-review task needing standard descriptive terms
- The TMR form: Part 1 Geotechnical Terms and Tables, Part 2 Geotechnical Symbols and Abbreviations

## Procedure

1. Identify whether the item is a soil description, rock description, defect description or a symbol/abbreviation question.
2. For soils, use the Part 1 tables (after AS 1726:2017): particle size fractions and subdivisions, accessory-component thresholds (trace / with / prefixed adjective by fines or coarse percentage), organic content classes, peat decomposition, carbonate reaction terms, and plasticity terms tied to liquid limit ranges.
3. For rock and defects, use the corresponding Part 1 tables for strength, weathering and defect terminology.
4. For log symbols and abbreviations (e.g. Bo, Co, cGr, fSa), use Part 2.
5. Cite the specific table (each is cross-referenced to its AS 1726:2017 table number) in reports.

## Decision rules

notes.title: Maintain, calibrate and troubleshoot the AX 01a plate bearing tester
notes.body:
# Maintain, calibrate and troubleshoot the AX 01a plate bearing tester

> **Source:** `BedAnlAx01a_engl V40a.pdf` (Chapters 10-15 and 19, pp. 19-23), held in the local reference library — see
> [[Reference library]]. This note is a paraphrased working aid, not the
> document. Values, clauses and criteria must be read from the source before
> they are relied on, and engineering conclusions need qualified review.

**Outcome.** The engineer can keep the device within its calibration and safety regime and diagnose common hydraulic faults in the field.

## Inputs

- AX 01a system and its calibration certificate
- Manufacturer-supplied hydraulic oil
- Access to Anix GmbH or authorised specialists for repairs

## Procedure

1. Before every use, inspect the measuring device, cables, load cell, displacement transducer, connectors, pump, hose, cylinder and measuring bridge; never assemble or use a damaged system (pp. 5, 20).
2. Recalibrate once per year and after any repair, per the DIN 18134 requirement cited in the manual (p. 19).
3. Change hydraulic oil at least yearly using only the manufacturer's oil; plan hose replacement at six-year intervals under normal use (including at most two years' storage), per German accident-prevention rules (p. 19).
4. Store only in dry rooms, keep the battery charged (2 h charge; operating range 0 to +38 deg C), and never expose the system to heavy rain - it is only splash-proof (pp. 4, 19-20).
5. Diagnose hydraulic faults from the symptom table: e.g. a cylinder that will not advance points to an open release valve, loose coupler, low oil, pump fault, overload or leaking seals; advance in spurts indicates air in the system; failure to hold load indicates pump fault, leaking connection, wrong setup or leaking seals (p. 23).
6. Respect hydraulic safety limits: 700 bar maximum, never exceed component ratings, never handle pressurised hoses, keep clear of hydraulically supported loads (pp. 21-22).

## Decision rules

- Any visible damage means do not test - the manual treats this as a potentially fatal hazard.
- Repairs only by Anix or Anix-authorised staff; non-genuine parts void safe operation.

## Checks

- Calibration date on the device Info screen is within the last year.
- Force zero is checked (and reset unloaded if drifted, e.g. from temperature) before testing (p. 13).

## Common errors

- Zeroing the force sensor while it is still loaded.
- Using non-manufacturer oil or lubricants.
- Ignoring temperature limits or leaving the battery flat in storage.

## Caveats

- The calibration clause cites the 2001 edition of DIN 18134 even though the manual's procedures follow the 2012 edition.
- Hose-replacement interval derives from German statutory insurance rules; local WHS rules may differ.

## Standards cited

DIN 18134:2001-09

notes.title: Manage hold and witness points through R11 drainage construction
notes.body:
# Manage hold and witness points through R11 drainage construction

> **Source:** `r011.pdf` (Annexure R11/C; Clauses 2.4.1, 2.6, 4.1.1, 4.2.1, 4.3.3, 4.7.2, 4.10 (Ed 5 Rev 2)), held in the local reference library — see
> [[Reference library]]. This note is a paraphrased working aid, not the
> document. Values, clauses and criteria must be read from the source before
> they are relied on, and engineering conclusions need qualified review.

**Outcome.** No drainage work proceeds past a required inspection gate without release, avoiding rework and nonconformances.

## Inputs

- Annexure R11/C schedule of hold and witness points
- Construction program for drainage works
- Submission documents (certificates, set-out notices, survey reports)

## Procedure

1. Map the R11/C1 schedule onto the program: holds at supply of load-bearing precast members and large water-retaining structures (2.4.1), incorporation of any manufactured drainage product without a certificate of conformity (2.6), set-out notification (4.1.1), inability to achieve minimum open-drain grade (4.2.1), replacement of inadequate foundation material (4.3.3), and heavy plant crossing pipes/culverts (4.10).
2. Map witness points: excavation for pipes and other drainage structures (4.3) and construction of drainage structures other than pipes/box culverts (4.7.2), with the required advance notice periods.
3. For inadequate foundation material, notify the Principal when suspect material is found in the base or trench sides, excavate only to the extent directed, and hold before replacing so the excavation can be inspected (Clause 4.3.3).
4. For construction traffic over culverts, submit the certified protective measures design before any heavy plant crossing (Clause 4.10).
5. Keep the identified records listed in R11/C2 (product drawings, certificates of conformity, CCTV reports) in the quality records.

## Decision rules

- Work that would alter a held process before release is nonconforming even if the end product later tests conforming.
- Previously submitted precast documentation can be re-certified rather than re-submitted only within the currency window stated in Clause 2.4.1.
- If the Principal directs further excavation of inadequate foundation material, the hold remains until re-inspection.

## Checks

- Notice periods met (e.g. 7 days for precast supply documents and certificates of conformity)
- Release evidence recorded against each hold point before dependent work started
- Surveys before/after removal of inadequate material captured for quantity measurement

## Common errors

- Backfilling an inadequate-foundation excavation before the Principal inspects it
- Running haul routes over installed culverts without the protective measures hold point released
- Treating witness points as optional notifications and giving insufficient notice

## Caveats

- Verify the spec edition is current for the project before relying on values.
- Contract documents may add or modify hold points; the contract governs.

## Standards cited

RMS Q, RMS G2, RMS R44

notes.title: Manage over-wet earth fill using NR44 placement strategies
notes.body:
# Manage over-wet earth fill using NR44 placement strategies

> **Source:** `nr44 Earthworks Specification.pdf` (Guide commentary to Clause 7.2 (moisture) and Clause 7.4.1 (NR44 Ed 2 Rev 0)), held in the local reference library — see
> [[Reference library]]. This note is a paraphrased working aid, not the
> document. Values, clauses and criteria must be read from the source before
> they are relied on, and engineering conclusions need qualified review.

**Outcome.** Over-optimum-moisture material is placed or treated without compromising embankment stability or pavement support, minimising drying downtime.

## Inputs

- Moisture content results vs the project A5 range
- Material type (permeability, expansiveness)
- Embankment geometry and available placement zones (deep fill core, medians, flat batters)
- Season/climate outlook and available drying areas

## Procedure

1. Recognise early that drying over-wet clays is slow in winter/wet seasons and that large drying areas rarely exist at project start; if wet heavy clays in cuttings are known pre-tender, push for specified (and paid) stabilisation instead of relying on drying.
2. Where over-optimum cutting material must be used, consider placement deep in high fills with geotechnical branch concurrence - compaction is achievable but the specified moisture may not be, and compaction-induced pore pressures will cause heave under plant.
3. Pace the work: wait (typically overnight) for pore pressures to dissipate before the next layer; avoid stacking layers in quick succession on wet clays.
4. Check for problematic heave by proof rolling with a fully loaded item of plant and watching for surface movement - minor movement at depth is normally tolerable for the finished pavement.
5. Use zoned construction (wet material in the fill core where future moisture change is small) rather than full-width placement of over-wet expansive clay; alternatively place over-wet material in wide medians or very flat batters clear of the carriageway deflection zone.
6. Stay alert to apparently stable layers destabilising after rain or when wet material is placed on them.

## Decision rules

- Full-width over-wet expansive clay placement risks embankment instability - zone it or relocate it.
- If heave under loaded plant is severe or persists, stop and allow further dissipation or re-treat; do not bury the problem under the next layer.
- The specification still governs conformity: deviations (using material outside the moisture range) need Principal/geotechnical concurrence, not just site judgement.

## Checks

- Pore-pressure/heave observations logged layer by layer
- Placement zones for wet material clear of pavement deflection influence
- Contract cost allocation understood - drying, lime treatment and rehandling sit with the contractor unless specified otherwise

## Common errors

- Programming earthworks assuming quick drying in cool/wet months
- Placing successive wet layers before pore pressures dissipate, then failing proof rolling
- Treating minor deep-seated movement under proof rolling as automatic rejection

## Caveats

- NR44 is guidance on intent, not a contract document; R44 and the contract govern acceptance.
- Based on R44 Ed 4 Rev 1 - cross-check clause numbers against the project's R44 edition.

## Standards cited

RMS R44, RMS 3211 (lime), RMS T198

## Related

- [[Skills]]

notes.title: Manage salinity in subdivision and single-lot development design
notes.body:
# Manage salinity in subdivision and single-lot development design

> **Source:** `INDUSTRY_GUIDE_T56_Residential_Slabs_and_Footings_in_Saline_Environments.pdf` (Section 5 (Site Management, pp. 7-9)), held in the local reference library — see
> [[Reference library]]. This note is a paraphrased working aid, not the
> document. Values, clauses and criteria must be read from the source before
> they are relied on, and engineering conclusions need qualified review.

**Outcome.** Development-scale measures (drainage, earthworks, landscaping, water management) that keep groundwater and salt away from structures and avoid creating new salinity.

## Inputs

- Site investigation results (existing/potential salinity, recharge-discharge model, watertable depth)
- Development layout options (levels, cut/fill, retaining walls, drainage corridors)
- Landscape/irrigation plans and water sources (grey water, stormwater reuse)

## Procedure

1. For subdivisions: track salt loading when groundwater is intercepted (cut and fill, retaining walls, service trenches divert salt to receiving waters); consider deliberate interception to control watertable height, leach salts, or divert to evaporation basins sized for typical rain events.
2. Set block levels with positive falls to the street so runoff leaves and ponding/waterlogging (recharge) is prevented; use street stormwater or subsoil drains, deepened if needed, to hold the watertable down in flat, low-lying areas.
3. Prefer 'slabscaping' (terraced level blocks formed during subdivision) on sloping ground: it enables slab-on-ground without individual cut/fill and gives estate-wide drainage control.
4. When filling low-lying areas with non-saline material, install a drained drainage layer beneath the fill to stop groundwater rising through it; treat capping layers over saline soil cautiously — they can suppress evaporation, let groundwater rise to the fill underside, and capillary action in clayey capping can lift salt back toward the surface.
5. For single lots: design cut/fill knowing it may expose saline material (upgrade concrete durability accordingly); keep strip footings' greater embedment depth in mind; put membranes behind concrete retaining walls plus proper drainage; place membranes under external paving on saline soils; grade ground so water cannot pond; plant deep-rooted and salt-tolerant vegetation to limit recharge.
6. At the whole-site scale, minimise infiltration and disturbance: water-sensitive design that infiltrates stormwater, unsealed detention ponds, over-irrigation, septic/rubble pits and removal of deep-rooted vegetation all push the watertable up; replace soils in original order after excavation and design utility trenches so they do not become saline groundwater conduits.

## Decision rules

- If an existing salinity problem is identified, design every element for it and aim the subdivision design at improving conditions over time (tree planting, drainage that lowers groundwater and leaches salt).
- If only potential hazard exists, either demonstrate no future problem or build basic durability measures into concrete elements now — guarantees over a 50-year design life are hard to sustain.
- Estate filling over saline areas may be false economy if capillary rise can still deliver salts; putting the money into building design/materials can be more cost-effective.
- Match management to the process zone: recharge areas need infiltration control; discharge/shallow-watertable areas need drainage, salt-proof materials and possibly pier-and-beam construction.

## Checks

- Drainage layers beneath fill are actually drained (not just present).
- Capping-layer proposals assessed for long-term capillary bypass, not just short-term covering.
- Sediment and erosion control plans account for saline and sodic soils.
- Monitoring (piezometers) persists through construction into occupation.

## Common errors

- Detention basins and water features left unlined in recharge areas, feeding the watertable.
- Trench backfill creating preferential saline flow paths to structures.
- Assuming short-term impact assessments hold over the 50-year design life of housing.
- Exposing sodic/saline subsoil in cut without erosion or durability response.

## Caveats

- Classification and aggressivity calls must be verified against the source document and the project spec.
- Management-option lists merged from booklet3siteinvestigationsforurbansalinity (2).pdf Phase 4 (pp. 15-17), which is the secondary source (recharge/discharge/shallow-watertable option sets, pier-and-beam advantages).
- Evaporation basin and drainage designs are concept-level here — hydraulic design requires separate analysis.

## Standards cited

Western Sydney Salinity Code of Practice (WSROC 2003), AS 2870 (drainage falls near footings), Managing Urban Stormwater: Soils and Construction (NSW Blue Book)

## Related

- [[AS 2870 residential site classification]]
- [[Groundwater observations]]
- [[Borehole log conventions]]

- [[Library - RMS and TfNSW specifications]]
- [[Skills]]

notes.title: Mark up field density test locations on the project drawing set
notes.body:
# Mark up field density test locations on the project drawing set

> **Source:** [Google Drive — Field Density Test Locations Drawings/flomar_250819_071947.pdf](https://drive.google.com/file/d/10GjmsTKAub4YsIbRzo5KodVminNcTL9V/view) (Scanned stormwater-drainage overall plan (Marsden Park/Flomar package) hand-annotated with circled density test numbers across lots, sheet-boundary marks, and adhesive notes grouping batter tests and test-number ranges). Reconstructed from STS's own
> field records on Google Drive — completed forms, labelled photos and
> scans, catalogued in [[Field records catalogue]]. It shows what the
> records evidence, not necessarily the current approved procedure —
> confirm against the current STS form and procedure before treating it
> as the standard method.

**Outcome.** A scanned, annotated project drawing showing every nuclear-gauge density test number at its true location, linking test reports to the works area.

## Inputs

- Current civil/earthworks drawing for the area (e.g. the stormwater drainage overall plan shop drawing used on the Flomar/Marsden Park package)
- Density test numbers as issued in the day's test sequence
- Pen and adhesive notes; scanner or scan app

## Procedure

1. Print or carry the relevant project drawing (a shop drawing or overall plan that shows lot/building outlines and sheet boundaries).
2. At each nuclear density test, write the test number on the drawing at the tested location and circle it so numbers stay legible among linework.
3. Where many tests belong to one element (a batter, a building pad), group the numbers on an adhesive note stuck on that area of the drawing, stating the element and orientation (e.g. batter tests on the northern side) and the run of test numbers or number range.
4. Respect the drawing's sheet split (Sheet 1/2/3 boundaries marked on the plan) so each test falls on the sheet where the work is detailed.
5. Scan the marked-up drawing at day end (filename with job/date) and file it with the density test records so each report number can be located on plan.

## Decision rules

- Every test number on the day's gauge record must appear exactly once on the drawing - the drawing is the location index for the test reports.
- Use number ranges on notes only for genuinely contiguous sequences; isolated tests get individually placed circles.
- If the works area spans drawing sheets, mark the sheet boundary and continue on the correct sheet rather than crowding one plan.

## Checks

- Count of circled/listed numbers equals count of tests reported for the day/area.
- Sticky-note groups state which element they cover, not just numbers.
- Scan legibility check - circled numbers over dense linework are the first thing lost in a poor scan.

## Common errors

- Recording test locations only as chainages in a notebook with no plan markup, making later disputes about coverage hard to resolve.
- Placing a note listing many tests without anchoring which face/side of the element it refers to.
- Scanning at low resolution so handwritten numbers on the plan become unreadable.

## Caveats

- Reconstructed from STS field records — confirm against the current STS procedure before treating as the standard method

## Standards cited

AS 1289.5.8.1 (nuclear gauge field density), AS 3798 (earthworks testing frequency/coverage context)

notes.title: Measure ground and building vibration correctly
notes.body:
# Measure ground and building vibration correctly

> **Source:** `vibrationguide0643.pdf` (Sections 4.2-4.5), held in the local reference library — see
> [[Reference library]]. This note is a paraphrased working aid, not the
> document. Values, clauses and criteria must be read from the source before
> they are relied on, and engineering conclusions need qualified review.

**Outcome.** Vibration measurements whose transducer mounting, dynamic range and location make them valid for assessment against criteria.

## Inputs

- Triaxial accelerometers or geophones with conditioning and recording system
- Access constraints (indoor vs outdoor measurement)
- Surface types at measurement points (rock/concrete, firm soil, soft ground, floors)

## Procedure

1. Measure where the vibration affects people (inside buildings) where practical; otherwise measure externally and convert with a justified, ideally test-derived, transfer function; meeting criteria in external ground is an acceptable screen for meeting them indoors, subject to resonance caution.
2. Mount transducers per the accelerometer-mounting standard: rigid, light mountings; three uniaxial transducers on a rigidly fixed metal cube in preference to brackets; bolts/epoxy on rock, asphalt or concrete.
3. On soils, use a stiff star-stake driven through loose surface material (projecting only a few mm), burial to about three times the unit dimension in soft ground, or a well-bedded surface plate; keep clear of structures and large trees to avoid feedback.
4. Verify instrumentation performance and dynamic range, and correct or reject data with inadequate signal-to-noise margin over background.
5. Avoid measuring on soft floor coverings; if unavoidable, run comparative mass/coupling checks.

## Decision rules

- Transducer plus monitoring unit mass must not exceed 10% of the building element's mass (vibrationguide0643 Section 4.4).
- Never use double-sided foam tape for mounting (Section 4.4).
- Signal-to-noise ratio generally at least 5 dB; between 5 and 10 dB the measured value must be corrected downward and the method reported; dynamic range 40 dB adequate, 50 dB preferred (Section 4.3).
- In multi-storey buildings, external-source vibration tends to reduce with height, but floor/wall resonance can amplify indoor values - assess case-by-case (Sections 4.2, 2.2).

## Checks

- Transducer orientation per manufacturer, aligned to source direction where relevant.
- Instrumentation meets the referenced BS performance requirements.
- Background vibration defined and quantified.

## Common errors

- Foam-tape or magnet mounting on rough surfaces giving high-frequency artefacts.
- Heavy geophones loading light building elements.
- Measuring on carpet and reporting distorted spectra.

## Caveats

- Guideline is from 2006; instrument standards have since been revised - verify current editions.
- Consent conditions may prescribe different measurement locations or descriptors and override.

## Standards cited

AS 2775-2004, BS 6841-1987, BS 7482 Parts 1 and 3

notes.title: Measure soil salinity by EC1:5 and classify it using field texture
notes.body:
# Measure soil salinity by EC1:5 and classify it using field texture

> **Source:** `Salinity and textural classification.pdf` (pp. 1-3 (procedure, multiplier table, salinity rating table)), held in the local reference library — see
> [[Reference library]]. This note is a paraphrased working aid, not the
> document. Values, clauses and criteria must be read from the source before
> they are relied on, and engineering conclusions need qualified review.

**Outcome.** A repeatable field/lab workflow converting a 1:5 soil:water EC reading into an ECe value and salinity class via texture-based multipliers.

## Inputs

- Air/oven-dried soil crushed and sieved to pass 425 um (enough for ~100 g+ of fines)
- Distilled water, clean jars, 5 mL teaspoon measure, 25 mL syringe
- Calibrated EC meter with buffer solution
- Texture assessment kit (hand, water bottle) and the texture/ribbon reference table

## Procedure

1. Dry the sample, crush with mortar and pestle (or compaction mould and hammer for hard clays) and sieve to minus 425 um.
2. Place one level teaspoon (5 mL) of dried, sieved soil in a clean jar; add 25 mL distilled water (1:5 soil:water by volume); agitate and stand for 30 minutes.
3. Calibrate the EC meter against buffer solution, then measure and record EC1:5 for each jar.
4. Texture the same soil by bolus: wet ~25 g in the palm until it just fails to stick, form a bolus, then press a ribbon between thumb and forefinger; classify from ribbon length and feel (e.g. sands give minimal ribbon, light clay ~50-75 mm, medium/heavy clay ~75 mm or more) per the AS 1547 texture table.
5. Convert: ECe = EC1:5 x texture multiplier — 17 for sands/loamy/clayey sands, 14 for sandy loams, 10 for loams, 9 for clay loams/light clays group, 8 for light medium clay, 7 for medium clay, 6 for heavy clay.
6. Assign the salinity class from ECe in dS/m: non-saline <2, slightly saline 2-4, moderately saline 4-8, then the two upper classes to >16 (see caveat on class naming).
7. Optionally estimate permeability (m/day) from the textural class using the AS 1547-derived table if needed for effluent/drainage design.

## Decision rules

- Always keep EC1:5, ECe and ECw distinct in records; only ECe (texture-corrected) feeds the salinity class.
- Clay-dominated soils are hardest to texture — add water slowly and re-add soil if over-wetted before judging ribbon length.
- If texture is uncertain across a class boundary, report the ECe range for both multipliers rather than a single value.

## Checks

- EC meter calibrated against buffer before each batch.
- Enough dried fines prepared (the procedure sheet targets at least ~108 g of -425 um material).
- Jars cleaned/drained between samples to avoid carryover.
- Multiplier used is recorded next to each result.

## Common errors

- Reporting raw EC1:5 as the soil salinity (understates true salinity several-fold, most severely in sandy soils).
- Texturing a different subsample than the one tested for EC.
- Skipping the 30-minute stand time, giving unstable readings.
- Using tap water instead of distilled water.

## Caveats

- Classification and aggressivity calls must be verified against the source document and the project spec.
- This is a rough OCR of a workshop procedure sheet: its rating table reads 'Highly Saline 8 to 15.99, Very Saline >16', which swaps the class names relative to booklet3siteinvestigationsforurbansalinity (2).pdf and INDUSTRY_GUIDE_T56 (both: Very Saline 8-16, Highly Saline >16) — treat the class names above 8 dS/m as unreliable in this sheet and defer to the Richards convention.
- Multiplier tables in the merged sources agree closely but not identically (e.g. sands 17 here and in T56 vs a smudged '17'/'1710' OCR artifact in booklet3); confirm against a clean copy before contractual use.
- Same skill also taught in booklet3siteinvestigationsforurbansalinity (2).pdf Appendix 1 and INDUSTRY_GUIDE_T56_Residential_Slabs_and_Footings_in_Saline_Environments.pdf Section 3.5-3.6 (both recorded here as secondary sources).

## Standards cited

AS 1547 (texture Table A1 and effluent permeability values, as cited in the procedure), Richards (1954) USDA Handbook 60 (ECe class basis)

## Related

- [[Library - salinity and sodic soils]]
- [[Library - RMS and TfNSW specifications]]
- [[Soil description order]]
- [[Skills]]

notes.title: Operate, maintain and repair a working platform through its service life
notes.body:
# Operate, maintain and repair a working platform through its service life

> **Source:** `Working Platforms for tracked plant.pdf` (Chapter 5 (Operation, maintenance and repair); Sections 1.3, 1.6), held in the local reference library — see
> [[Reference library]]. This note is a paraphrased working aid, not the
> document. Values, clauses and criteria must be read from the source before
> they are relied on, and engineering conclusions need qualified review.

**Outcome.** A platform that keeps performing to its design over the works duration, with controlled usage, monitored condition, prompt reinstatement of excavations, and clear responsibility for upkeep.

## Inputs

- Design statement: permitted plant, designated working areas, acceptable minimum thickness, design life
- Contractual allocation of maintenance/repair responsibility (principal contractor holds overall site safety responsibility under CDM)
- Monitoring arrangements: regular visual assessment of platform, plant behaviour and drainage

## Procedure

1. Keep the platform under day-to-day control of competent site staff; ensure contractual arrangements cover inspection, control and maintenance for the whole working life.
2. Restrict use to the plant and areas the platform was designed for; manage conflicts where the platform doubles as a haul road (concrete trucks, service cranes may need strengthened routes).
3. Monitor regularly: visual assessment of performance, drainage, contamination (mud, bentonite, spoil) and rutting; simple thickness checks with profile boards; give special attention to ramps and heavily trafficked routes.
4. Maintain a reasonably level, well-drained surface; prevent water flowing across the platform; use suitably graded stable material similar to the installation spec for maintenance.
5. Permit any activity that breaches the platform (e.g. excavation through it) only under competent supervision, and reinstate to the original specification.
6. Backfill all empty bores with self-compacting granular material; take particular care backfilling around guide walls.
7. Repair damage promptly, reinstating to the required specification; increase local thickness above minimum where performance problems demand.

## Decision rules

- Most rig instability incidents trace to maintenance/repair failures rather than design or installation defects — treat deterioration signals as safety-critical, not cosmetic.
- Rig bouncing when travelling is not covered by design calculations; it must be prevented operationally, with specialist advice if it persists.
- If the plant list, loading or usage changes from what was designed for, refer back to the platform designer before allowing it.

## Checks

- Regular documented inspections; deteriorating areas detected before they become hazards.
- All excavations through the platform logged and reinstated to spec; empty pile bores backfilled.
- Platform edges, exclusion zones and unfinished areas clearly marked and physically controlled.

## Common errors

- Assuming the original design protects against a platform later trafficked by heavier plant or used as an unplanned haul road.
- Leaving bores or service trenches through the platform unreinstated or poorly backfilled — the classic localised failure that overturns rigs.
- Letting surface water pond or flow across the platform, softening the subgrade.
- Unclear responsibility between subcontractors so nobody owns maintenance.

## Caveats

- OCR noise present — verify details against the original BR 470.
- Responsibility framework is UK CDM-based; translate to the applicable local safety legislation.

## Standards cited

BRE BR 470 (2004), CDM Regulations (UK), CIRIA C703 (crane stability on site)

## Related

- [[Library - RMS and TfNSW specifications]]
- [[Skills]]

notes.title: Perform point load tests with sample-geometry screening and failure-mode vetting
notes.body:
# Perform point load tests with sample-geometry screening and failure-mode vetting

> **Source:** [YouTube — Point Load Test: How to Break Rock in One Minute — Experimental procedure](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=miKpYQ-VeUs&t=1s) (00:01-10:16). A YouTube lecture — learning
> material, not an approved design procedure. Equations and numbers were
> heard through auto-captions; read them off the video before use, and
> verify anything design-relevant against the standard and the project
> specification. Engineering conclusions need qualified review.

**Outcome.** Valid peak failure loads from point load tests on rock core, with unsuitable samples and invalid failure modes screened out

## Inputs

- Rock core samples or lump/disk samples of the same rock type (at least three, preferably four or five)
- Point load apparatus with force readout
- Calipers or rule for measuring diameter, length, width and thickness
- Safety glasses

## Procedure

1. For a diametral test on core: measure diameter D and length L, and confirm L is greater than half the diameter before accepting the sample (D about 51 mm and L about 32 mm passed in the demo)
2. For an axial/disk test: measure thickness D and width W and check D against the standard's geometric limits relative to W (a 20 mm thick disk on a 50 mm core failed the check and was rejected)
3. Wear safety glasses, seat the sample between the two conical platens
4. Increase the load slowly until the sample breaks and record the peak force in kN (3.2 kN for the first sandstone core)
5. Record the measured dimensions alongside the peak force in the test spreadsheet
6. Inspect the failure surface after every break: the failure must pass through the sample between the platens, not spall off a side or corner
7. Repeat on further samples of the same rock type until at least three valid results exist

## Decision rules

- Reject a test where failure ran along a pre-existing crack or broke only at the sample edge (seen with a weathered sample that failed at 0.265 kN); weathered samples are prone to this
- One or two samples is never enough — a minimum of three tests per rock type, more if material is available
- Re-measure the sample thickness before a retest — the relevant dimension changes after a partial break (39.4 mm on the re-test in the demo)

## Checks

- Geometry check passed and recorded before loading
- Failure plane inspected and judged valid before the force reading is kept
- Peak force and dimensions written down immediately per test

## Common errors

- Writing down every peak force without looking at how the sample actually failed
- Testing disks that are too thin relative to their width
- Drawing conclusions from a single test on a variable, weathered rock

## Caveats

- YouTube lecture — learning material, not an approved design procedure; verify against project specification and current standards
- The lecturer refers to 'the standard' for sample geometry limits without naming it; the axial-test thickness-to-width limits are garbled in auto-captions — equation shown on screen — read from the video
- Low anomalous results from weathered samples may still be recorded for information but should be flagged, not pooled blindly with valid results

## Standards cited

None cited in the source passage.

## Related

- [[Rock weathering classes]]
- [[Rock strength classes]]
- [[Skills]]
