notes.title: Photograph a shrink-swell sample with depth labelling
notes.body:
# Photograph a shrink-swell sample with depth labelling

> **Source:** [Google Drive — Shrink Swell photo/BH1 0.7-1.0m.jpg](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1g3tBM2nLEioR04xqmowsK0xW6Pa840Ru/view) (Tray photo of an undisturbed sample with handwritten card '31380/8008D-L / S1, BH1 0.7-1.0m / S/swell'). Reconstructed from STS's own
> field records on Google Drive — completed forms, labelled photos and
> scans, catalogued in [[Field records catalogue]]. It shows what the
> records evidence, not necessarily the current approved procedure —
> confirm against the current STS form and procedure before treating it
> as the standard method.

**Outcome.** A photographic record tying an undisturbed sample to its job number, borehole, depth interval and the laboratory test it is allocated to, before it leaves the field/sample store.

## Inputs

- Undisturbed tube sample (extruded core segment and/or capped tube ends)
- Card or paper label and pen
- Tray to contain the sample and label in one frame

## Procedure

1. Write a card with three lines: job number / STS number (e.g. 31380/8008D-L), sample and location with depth interval (e.g. 'S1, BH1 0.7-1.0m'), and the allocated test written as 'S/swell' for shrink-swell.
2. Place the sample components (extruded core, tube ring, capped end) and the card together in a clean tray.
3. Photograph from directly above with the card legible and the sample condition visible.
4. Name the image file with the borehole and depth interval exactly as on the card (file is 'BH1 0.7-1.0m.jpg').
5. File in the Shrink Swell photo folder.

## Decision rules

- The filename must repeat the label (BH + depth interval) so the photo can be found without opening it.
- Photograph before any trimming/testing so the as-received condition (roots, moisture, layering visible in the record) is documented.

## Checks

- Card text legible in the photo: job/STS number, sample ID, BH, depth interval, test allocation.
- Depth interval on card, filename and the borehole log all agree.

## Common errors

- Photographing the sample without the identification card in frame
- Filename not matching the labelled depth interval, breaking traceability

## Caveats

- Reconstructed from STS field records — confirm against the current STS procedure before treating as the standard method
- Based on a single example photo; the card line order may vary

notes.body:
# Photograph a site or test location with a time-GPS overlay

> **Source:** [Google Drive — 2520E-G/Site Photos/TimePhoto_20260624_100529.jpg and TimePhoto_20260624_100527.jpg](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1Bkw9QTMHd-nWJuagplD0iUCpn0H83uZu/view) (Two consecutive overlay-stamped photos of a bulk excavation with piling rig and pier reinforcement cages; overlay carries date-time, bearing, full address, altitude, speed, compass rose and map inset). Reconstructed from STS's own
> field records on Google Drive — completed forms, labelled photos and
> scans, catalogued in [[Field records catalogue]]. It shows what the
> records evidence, not necessarily the current approved procedure —
> confirm against the current STS form and procedure before treating it
> as the standard method.

**Outcome.** A dated, geolocated, orientation-stamped site photograph that can stand as evidence of site conditions at a specific moment (e.g. bulk excavation level, pier cage delivery, piling rig on site).

## Inputs

- Phone with a timestamp-camera app (records show a 'TimePhoto'-style overlay)
- GPS/location services enabled
- Clear line of sight to the works being recorded

## Procedure

1. Open the timestamp camera app so the overlay is active before shooting (overlay in the records shows: date and time to the second, compass bearing in degrees plus cardinal direction, street address, suburb, LGA, state, altitude, speed, a compass rose, and a Google map inset with a location pin).
2. Stand at a vantage point that captures the works, plant and site boundary fencing in one frame.
3. Frame so the overlay text does not cover the subject of interest.
4. Take successive shots from the same standpoint at different bearings to cover the area (records show consecutive frames 2 seconds apart at 236° SW and 270° W of the same excavation).
5. Keep the app's default filename (TimePhoto_YYYYMMDD_HHMMSS.jpg) so files sort chronologically.
6. File the photos in the job's Site Photos folder under the STS project number (e.g. 2520E-G/Site Photos).

## Decision rules

- If the shot is evidentiary (levels, founding conditions, plant on site, progress claims), use the overlay app rather than the plain phone camera — plain PXL_ camera shots also exist in the same folder but carry no visible metadata.
- Change bearing, not standpoint, between consecutive shots so the compass stamp documents what direction each frame faces.

## Checks

- Overlay shows the correct site address and a plausible altitude before leaving the vantage point.
- Timestamp matches the works being recorded (the stamp is burned into the pixels and cannot be corrected later).
- Whole area of interest is inside the frame — excavation face, plant, and fencing visible in the examples.

## Common errors

- Using the plain camera app so the photo has no visible time/location stamp
- Overlay text obscuring the feature the photo is meant to prove
- GPS not settled, stamping a stale address or altitude

## Caveats

- Reconstructed from STS field records — confirm against the current STS procedure before treating as the standard method
- The specific app is not named in the records; the overlay format matches the 'TimePhoto' filename prefix
- Two other photos in the same folder (PXL_ prefix) could not be retrieved, so the split between overlay and plain photos is inferred from filenames only

## Standards cited

None cited in the source passage.

## Related

- [[Skills]]

notes.title: Photograph and label a core box
notes.body:
# Photograph and label a core box

> **Source:** [Google Drive — Core Photo/IMG_0798.jpg, MP4-BH01.jpeg, IMG_0797.JPG](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1uarZXf5Idpz_yF858Z0Nu-2bJBYIJdvo/view) (Three core box photos, two boreholes on the same job: BH-4 (0-20.5m, end of core 20.44m) and BH20 (coring 9.5-19.98m); all show the STS board, colour chart, scale bar, metre tags and annotated spacer blocks). Reconstructed from STS's own
> field records on Google Drive — completed forms, labelled photos and
> scans, catalogued in [[Field records catalogue]]. It shows what the
> records evidence, not necessarily the current approved procedure —
> confirm against the current STS form and procedure before treating it
> as the standard method.

**Outcome.** A single composite photograph per core box that identifies the project, borehole and depth range, gives a true metric scale and colour reference, and lets every core run be located by depth.

## Inputs

- STS-branded core photo board (green/white board with QR code, colour reference patches and greyscale, 0.0m-1.0m checkered scale bar)
- Whiteboard marker for the board fields
- White spacer blocks and marker for in-box annotations
- Metre-number tags for each core row
- Core box with 1 m split trays

## Procedure

1. Fill in the board fields in marker: PROJECT NO. (office no./STS job no., e.g. 32904/2014E-G), CLIENT, ADDRESS, DATE, BOREHOLE NO., DEPTH (depth range covered, e.g. 0-20.5m or 19.8m).
2. Lay the board across the top of the core box so its 0.0-1.0m scale bar sits parallel to the core rows.
3. Tag the left end of each row with its starting depth in metres (rows in the records are tagged 5, 6, 7 ... 20).
4. Where coring does not start at surface, write the start on a white spacer at the first run (record shows '32904/2014E-G / 105 Hollinsworth rd / BH-20 / Marsden Park / 19/03/2026 / coring started from 9.5m').
5. Mark the end of the hole on a white spacer block placed in the tray at the finish point (records show 'END OF CORE - 20.44m' and 'Coring End at 19.98m').
6. Photograph square-on from above in daylight with the whole box, the board, the colour chart and every row tag in frame.
7. Name/file the photo by borehole (records use MP4-BH01.jpeg and IMG_ sequence numbers in the Core Photo folder).

## Decision rules

- One composite photo covers a whole box; deeper holes need one photo per box with the board DEPTH field updated to that box's range.
- Depth tags are written on the tray divider at the start of each 1 m run, so any stone in the photo can be depth-located against the board's scale bar.

## Checks

- Board fields legible in the photo and consistent with the drill log (project no., BH no., date, depth range).
- Colour chart and greyscale visible for later colour correction.
- End-of-core depth written in the box matches the driller's final depth.
- Every metre tag readable — the OCR of one record recovered all tags 0.0m-1.0m and 5-20 plus 'END OF CORE- 20.44m', which is the standard to aim for.

## Common errors

- Photographing at an angle so the scale bar cannot be used for measurement
- Board depth range not updated between boxes of the same hole
- Missing start-of-coring annotation when the hole is augered before coring

## Caveats

- Reconstructed from STS field records — confirm against the current STS procedure before treating as the standard method
- IMG_0797.JPG exceeded the retrieval size limit and was read via OCR text only; its board fields matched the described layout

## Standards cited

None cited in the source passage.

## Related

- [[Field records catalogue]]
- [[Borehole log conventions]]
- [[Skills]]

notes.title: Plan a phased site investigation for urban salinity
notes.body:
# Plan a phased site investigation for urban salinity

> **Source:** `booklet3siteinvestigationsforurbansalinity (2).pdf` (Whole booklet, esp. pp. 3-7 (phases, Table 1) and pp. 15-17 (Phase 4)), held in the local reference library — see
> [[Reference library]]. This note is a paraphrased working aid, not the
> document. Values, clauses and criteria must be read from the source before
> they are relied on, and engineering conclusions need qualified review.

**Outcome.** A staged investigation (desktop review through to management plan) scaled to the development type, that identifies salt stores, water movement and the two-way impacts between the development and salinity processes.

## Inputs

- Proposed development type, layout and mapping scale (1:25 000 down to 1:1 000)
- Existing information: geological maps, soil landscape maps, urban capability maps, climate data, land use history, SALIS soil profiles, groundwater bore database records
- Initial site walk observations (salinity indicators, field EC readings of dams/creeks)
- Budget context (cost of testing vs value of the asset)

## Procedure

1. Phase 1: run a desktop review of the site and vicinity (geology, soils, groundwater, climate, land use history) and walk the site recording indicators such as bare scalds, surface salt crystals, puffy or black-stained soil, indicator vegetation, tree dieback and stained foundations; take field EC1:5 screening readings where salinity is suspected.
2. Map geomorphic landform units (crests, side slopes, foot slopes) since landform controls where salt outbreaks and accumulations are likely; note structural controls such as dykes and rock bars.
3. Phase 2: design and execute a detailed investigation — describe soil profiles per landform unit (arranged as transects for a 3D picture), dig test pits/backhoe pits, install piezometers where groundwater understanding is missing.
4. Phase 3: laboratory-analyse selected representative profiles and present results against standards and reference documents.
5. Phase 4: interpret current and likely future conditions, address cumulative impacts, and select management options (e.g. minimise infiltration, retain deep-rooted vegetation, salt-tolerant landscaping, drainage, material selection), then set up monitoring (retain piezometers through and after construction).

## Decision rules

- Set sample numbers from the mapping scale and land use intensity using the booklet's Table 1 (p. 6): denser sampling for larger-scale mapping and more intensive uses (e.g. roughly 6-18 initial observations per km2 at 1:25 000 open space, up to 50-100 per ha at 1:1 000 highly intensive construction).
- Use fewer samples when landscape/soil variability is low, local knowledge is good, or the land use will not mobilise salt (no irrigation, effluent disposal or clearing); use more when the opposite holds.
- Weigh sampling cost against asset value (the booklet's example: minimal testing for a small shed vs testing to justify sulphate-resistant cement for a house).
- Consider EMI (electromagnetic induction) survey with a few validation soil tests as an alternative to dense grid sampling.
- If Phase 1 shows little salt/groundwater hazard or well-understood processes, reduce Phase 2 scope.

## Checks

- At least one soil profile per landform unit, with profiles arranged in transects across the site.
- Field observations reconcile with lab results (a mapped salt scald should return high lab salinity; if not, suspect labelling or reporting errors).
- Groundwater interpretation distinguishes local, intermediate and regional systems and recharge vs discharge behaviour before management options are chosen.
- Piezometers are located where they can survive construction for ongoing monitoring.

## Common errors

- Treating a single water-body EC reading (ECw) as representative of soil salinity — surface water EC varies enormously in the short term and cannot be used to infer soil salinity.
- Assuming low soil-salinity results mean no future problem: small salt stores can be mobilised and concentrated by the development, and saline groundwater can rise from off-site causes.
- Applying one prescriptive test list to every site instead of tailoring the program to site processes.
- Ignoring cumulative impacts of many small developments.

## Caveats

- Classification and aggressivity calls must be verified against the source document and the project specification before use.
- The booklet dates from 2002 (costs, agency names and AS 2159-1995 references are dated; the appendix itself redirects to AS 2159-2009, now further superseded).
- Sampling densities in Table 1 are recommendations, not statutory minimums; council/consent authority requirements govern.
- Complementary context in booklet5new.pdf (Introduction to Urban Salinity) and INDUSTRY_GUIDE_T56_Residential_Slabs_and_Footings_in_Saline_Environments.pdf Section 3.

## Standards cited

AS 2159-2009 Piling - Design and Installation (durability, Section 6), AS 3600 Supp 1-1994 Concrete Structures Commentary Section C4, Managing Urban Stormwater: Soils and Construction (NSW 'Blue Book', 1998), McDonald et al (1990) Australian Soil and Land Survey Field Handbook

## Related

- [[AS 2159 piling]]
- [[Groundwater observations]]
- [[Library - salinity and sodic soils]]
- [[Skills]]

notes.title: Plan and interpret a seismic geophysical survey for site investigation
notes.body:
# Plan and interpret a seismic geophysical survey for site investigation

> **Source:** [YouTube — Seismic Geophysics Methods in Geotechnical Investigations](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=c0B-XU8NESY&t=0s) (00:01-07:15). A YouTube lecture — learning
> material, not an approved design procedure. Equations and numbers were
> heard through auto-captions; read them off the video before use, and
> verify anything design-relevant against the standard and the project
> specification. Engineering conclusions need qualified review.

**Outcome.** A cost-effective picture of subsurface layer boundaries over a large area from seismic wave velocities, correctly caveated and tied to borehole control

## Inputs

- Geophone array (spacing typically about 1 to 1.5 m) and a recording device
- An energy source to initiate elastic waves: a large hammer, or a small blast for large rock areas
- At least one borehole log in the survey area for ground-truthing
- An experienced analyst for the velocity data

## Procedure

1. Lay out geophones at roughly 1-1.5 m spacing across the area of interest
2. Initiate elastic waves with the hammer or small blast and record arrival times at each geophone
3. Analyse the recordings to produce a velocity-versus-depth profile; this is the hardest step because of wave noise, and should be done by someone with long experience
4. Interpolate between velocity values to pick boundaries between strata, understanding these picks are assumptions, not observations
5. Assign geology to each velocity layer only by matching against borehole logs from the same area — velocity alone (e.g. 1650 m/s) says nothing about what the material actually is
6. Optionally estimate rock strength from published velocity-strength correlations and the low/medium/high strength rock classification

## Decision rules

- Choose seismic methods when the area is large and budget matters: cheaper than boreholes, SPT or lab programmes, and covers area rather than points
- Never interpret geology from velocities without borehole confirmation; the combination of seismic coverage plus borehole control is presented as the best approach
- Expect the top metre or two to be soil, and treat near-surface velocities with extra caution

## Checks

- Confirm layer boundary picks against borehole logs before reporting
- Sanity-check velocity-derived strength classes against samples taken from the borehole

## Common errors

- Treating interpolated boundaries as measured contacts
- Assigning rock type from velocity alone with no borehole sample
- Underestimating the data-processing effort — noisy records need experienced interpretation

## Caveats

- YouTube lecture — learning material, not an approved design procedure; verify against project specification and current standards
- The transcript's description of the velocity-strength correlation direction is garbled (it reads as low velocity giving high strength at one point and the opposite shortly after) — read the correlation chart from the video before using it
- No penetration or sampling means the method cannot stand alone for design

## Standards cited

None cited in the source passage.

- [[Soil description order]]
- [[Skills]]

Optionally estimate rock strength from published velocity strength correlations and the low/medium/high strength rock classification Decision rules Choose seismic methods when the area is large and budget matters: cheaper than boreholes, SPT or lab programmes, and covers area rather than points Never interpret geology from velocities without borehole confirmation; the combination of seismic coverage plus borehole control is presented as the best approach Expect the top metre or two to be soil, and treat near surface velocities with extra caution Checks Confirm layer boundary picks against borehole logs before reporting Sanity check velocity derived strength classes against samples taken from the borehole Common errors Treating interpolated boundaries as measured contacts Assigning rock type from velocity alone with no borehole sample Underestimating the data processing effort — noisy records need experienced interpretation Caveats YouTube lecture — learning material, not an approved design procedure; verify against project specification and current standards The transcript's description of the velocity strength correlation direction is garbled (it reads as low velocity giving high strength at one point and the opposite shortly after) — read the correlation chart from the video before using it No penetration or sampling means the method cannot stand alone for design Standards cited None cited in the source passage. Related Borehole log conventions Soil description order Skills

# Plan excavation support next to transport infrastructure

> **Source:** `gtd-2020-001.pdf` (Design standards, loads, ground support, ground movement and submission sections (GTD 2020/001, 2 July 2020)), held in the local reference library — see
> [[Reference library]]. This note is a paraphrased working aid, not the
> document. Values, clauses and criteria must be read from the source before
> they are relied on, and engineering conclusions need qualified review.

**Outcome.** A retaining-structure design basis for a development excavation adjacent to state roads that will obtain TfNSW concurrence.

## Inputs

- Excavation depth and proximity to road/rail assets
- Geotechnical model from compliant investigation
- Groundwater regime (short-term, long-term, accidental) and any dewatering proposal
- Asset sensitivity advice from the authority

## Procedure

1. Design retaining structures to the listed Australian Standards with TfNSW documents taking precedence, for a permanent design life of at least 100 years, including short- and long-term effects and the unplanned-excavation stability case from the bridge foundations code.
2. Apply bridge-code load combinations with the minimum serviceability traffic UDL on the most adverse road position plus the minimum non-traffic surcharge UDL.
3. Screen the support scheme against the prohibited types for permanent retention.
4. Predict staged vertical and horizontal wall/ground movements graphically at critical sections over the full influence zone (demolition, wall installation, excavation, drawdown, consolidation).
5. Agree permissible movements with the authority before final design; make drainage relieving water pressure accessible for inspection/maintenance; include a dewatering management plan where needed.
6. Compile the submission: design documentation with geotechnical report, drawings showing assets/instrumentation/sequence, specifications, and dilapidation survey where sensitive assets are at risk; resubmit any design amendment before implementing it.

## Decision rules

- Not acceptable as permanent retention: steel sheet piles below the water table, and wall toes founded on unsupported rock ledges of quality inferior to medium-strength rock (Class III in the Sydney sandstone/shale classification) or with adverse defects (gtd-2020-001 ground support section).
- Minimum serviceability UDLs: 20 kPa traffic plus 10 kPa other surcharge (gtd-2020-001 design loads section).
- Serviceability horizontal wall movement for non-sensitive assets limited to the least of 0.5% of excavated height, 30 mm, or the wall's structural serviceability limit (gtd-2020-001 ground movement section).
- Where TfNSW and standard documents conflict, the TfNSW document governs (gtd-2020-001 design standards section).

## Checks

- Unplanned excavation case (AS 5100.3 Section 13.3.1) explicitly included in stability design.
- Utilities in the influence zone identified and their owners' movement tolerances addressed.
- Both temporary and permanent structures covered in the design report.

## Common errors

- Designing to building-code surcharge instead of the bridge-code traffic UDL.
- Finalising the design before agreeing movement limits with the authority.
- Proposing sheet piles below groundwater as permanent works.

## Caveats

- Verify currency (stated review date has passed); supersedes GTD 2012/001.
- Permissible movements are case-by-case; authority direction and DA conditions override.

## Standards cited

AS 5100, AS 5100.3, AS 1170, AS 1726, AS 2159, Pells et al 1998 classification

## Related

- [[AS 1726 soil and rock description]]
- [[AS 2159 piling]]
- [[Rock weathering classes]]
- [[Weathered siltstone]]
- [[Rock strength classes]]
- [[Groundwater observations]]

notes.body:
# Plot and manage discontinuity data in Dips

> **Source:** [YouTube — Plotting Great Circles and Poles of Discontinuities using Dips](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=HENt9tbWF78&t=0s) (00:00-06:03). A YouTube lecture — learning
> material, not an approved design procedure. Equations and numbers were
> heard through auto-captions; read them off the video before use, and
> verify anything design-relevant against the standard and the project
> specification. Engineering conclusions need qualified review.

**Outcome.** A correctly configured Dips file with discontinuity orientations plotted as poles or great circles, extra attribute columns, and summary charts, ready for kinematic analysis

## Inputs

- Discontinuity orientation measurements from site investigation (dip and dip direction, or another format such as trend or strike)
- Optional attribute data per discontinuity: spacing, length, type, shape, surface roughness

## Procedure

1. Start a new file; the input grid is a spreadsheet-like table with dip and dip direction columns
2. In Analysis > Project Settings, confirm the global orientation format matches your data (dip / dip direction rather than trend or strike); set a project title and comments if wanted
3. Enter orientation rows (e.g. 45/010, a near-vertical 89/235, a near-horizontal 02/180)
4. Click the pole (vector) plot button to draw the stereonet: near-vertical planes plot far from the centre, near-horizontal planes near it
5. To display planes instead, open plot options and tick the great-circles box; each measurement then appears as a great circle
6. Add extra columns by right-clicking to the right of the dip direction column (e.g. spacing, surface), and paste data from Word or Excel if it exists elsewhere
7. Use Analysis > Chart on any attribute column (e.g. surface) to summarise categories such as which roughness class dominates the data set

## Decision rules

- Set the orientation format before entering data — mixing formats silently corrupts every subsequent analysis
- Use pole plots for large data sets (hundreds of points) and great circles when a few individual planes need to be seen

## Checks

- Spot-check the plot: a near-vertical entry must fall near the perimeter side away from the centre and a near-horizontal one near the centre (for poles this relationship is the reverse of great circles)
- Open a library tutorial file to compare structure when unsure how attribute columns should look

## Common errors

- Entering trend/plunge or strike data while the project is set to dip / dip direction
- Confusing the pole and great-circle representations when visually checking the plot

## Caveats

- YouTube lecture — learning material, not an approved design procedure; verify against project specification and current standards

## Standards cited

None cited in the source passage.

notes.title: Plot discontinuity great circles and poles on a stereonet by hand
notes.body:
# Plot discontinuity great circles and poles on a stereonet by hand

> **Source:** [YouTube — How To Draw Stereonet: Great Circles, Dip and Dip Direction](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tg9PUGweZkY&t=31s) (00:31-08:36). A YouTube lecture — learning
> material, not an approved design procedure. Equations and numbers were
> heard through auto-captions; read them off the video before use, and
> verify anything design-relevant against the standard and the project
> specification. Engineering conclusions need qualified review.

**Outcome.** Hand-drawn great circles (and poles) on tracing paper representing measured dip / dip-direction pairs from a field discontinuity survey

## Inputs

- Dip and dip-direction measurements for each joint set (three-digit number is dip direction, two-digit is dip; e.g. 78/255 and 35/040)
- Printed equal-angle stereonet
- Tracing paper (baking paper works) and a pencil

## Procedure

1. Lay tracing paper over the stereonet and trace the outer circumference in pencil
2. Mark north (0), east (90), south (180) and west (270) on the tracing so the original orientation can always be recovered after rotations
3. For each joint: find the dip-direction value on the perimeter graduations and mark that point on the tracing
4. Rotate the tracing paper until the marked dip-direction point lies on the east-west line — the only straight line on the net, which is what allows dip to be counted and a great circle traced
5. Count the dip angle inward from the perimeter along the east-west line: the perimeter is 0 degrees, the centre is 90 degrees, and each grid line on the net represents 2 degrees
6. At the counted dip position, trace the great circle of the net visible through the tracing paper (interpolate between adjacent printed circles for odd dip values)
7. Rotate the tracing paper back to its original position; the traced arc is the great circle for that discontinuity
8. To plot the pole instead: with the dip-direction point still aligned on the east-west line, count the dip angle from the centre of the net toward the opposite side (90 degrees from the plane) and mark a single point; label it (e.g. P2) and rotate back

## Decision rules

- Three digits in an orientation pair always denote dip direction; the remaining value is dip
- Use a pole (one point) instead of a great circle when a compact representation of many joints is needed

## Checks

- Verify the tracing returned to the original orientation using the marked cardinal points before reading results
- Verify the dip count started at 0 on the perimeter, not at the centre (for great circles); the pole count runs from the centre

## Common errors

- Counting dip from the centre outward when drawing a great circle (that count is only for poles)
- Forgetting to mark the original north, so the tracing cannot be restored after rotation
- Tracing the great circle without first aligning the dip-direction mark with the east-west line

## Caveats

- YouTube lecture — learning material, not an approved design procedure; verify against project specification and current standards
- Software now does this faster; the manual method is for understanding the underlying construction
- Auto-captions garble some counted numbers (e.g. '170' for what should be 270 on the west mark); read graduations from the video

## Standards cited

None cited in the source passage.

## Related

- [[Skills]]

notes.body:
# Prepare equipment and field records before a plate load test

> **Source:** `050-Setup Proceedure for PLT Draft 4 Feb 2024.pdf` (Sections A-C, pp. 1-2), held in the local reference library — see
> [[Reference library]]. This note is a paraphrased working aid, not the
> document. Values, clauses and criteria must be read from the source before
> they are relied on, and engineering conclusions need qualified review.

**Outcome.** The engineer can mobilise to site with a complete, serviceable PLT kit and a datasheet that captures all identifying information before loading begins.

## Inputs

- AX01a PLT kit in its blue transport cases
- PPE and safety signage
- Hand tools: trowel, spatula, brush, hand level
- Fine to medium grained bedding sand
- Mobile phone with the test app installed
- Blank field datasheets

## Procedure

1. Visually inspect all equipment for damage before use, paying particular attention to the hydraulic hoses.
2. Check the electronic box battery and recharge it if the charge level has fallen below 50%.
3. Assemble the field kit: PPE and signs, the PLT cases, hand tools, bedding sand, phone with app, and datasheets.
4. Before testing, fill in the datasheet header: test pit number, site name and the civil works the test supports, names of field staff, GPS coordinates, and any other fields the sheet requires.

## Decision rules

- Recharge whenever battery charge is under 50% (p. 1).
- Do not proceed to site with damaged equipment, especially damaged hydraulic hoses.

## Checks

- All items on the equipment list are packed before leaving.
- Every header field on the datasheet is completed before the test starts.

## Common errors

- Starting a test with an undercharged electronic box.
- Leaving datasheet identification fields (pit number, GPS, staff names) to be filled in afterwards from memory.

## Caveats

- The procedure is a draft (Rev 0.0) with several steps and photos marked 'to be determined' or 'to be obtained during training', so it is incomplete in places.
- The document does not state which test standard the datasheet or app follows.

## Standards cited

None cited in the source passage.

notes.title: Present and interpret urban salinity investigation results
notes.body:
# Present and interpret urban salinity investigation results

> **Source:** `booklet3siteinvestigationsforurbansalinity (2).pdf` (Phase 3, pp. 12-14; Appendix 1 pp. 19-21 (units and conversions)), held in the local reference library — see
> [[Reference library]]. This note is a paraphrased working aid, not the
> document. Values, clauses and criteria must be read from the source before
> they are relied on, and engineering conclusions need qualified review.

**Outcome.** Results reported with unambiguous units, spatial context (maps, transects, depth profiles) and a process interpretation (recharge vs discharge, through-flow, corrosion risk) that supports management decisions.

## Inputs

- Field and laboratory results with test methods and units
- Site map base (topography, drainage, vegetation)
- Soil profile descriptions per landform unit

## Procedure

1. Tabulate all results with units and any conversion factors explicitly stated (EC vs ECe, dS/m vs mS/m etc.).
2. Prepare a site map showing soil/landform units, drainage lines, all observation and sample locations, legend, scale and north; consider a second map of constraint/management zones.
3. Plot profile transects across the site to build a three-dimensional picture of soil and salt distribution.
4. Graph EC against depth for each profile and read the shape: EC decreasing with depth suggests a discharge site; steady low EC suggests recharge; a high-EC zone at depth can mark a seasonal watertable or low-permeability layer (typical salt-profile shapes after Qld DNR 1997).
5. Cross-check results against field observations (visible scalds should test salty) and against permeability/sodicity/dispersibility interpretations to explain where water and salt concentrate.
6. Convert units where needed using the booklet's Appendix 1: dS/m = mS/cm = mmho/cm; dS/m x 100 = mS/m; dS/m x 1000 = uS/cm (EC units); dS/m x 640 ~ ppm/mg/L total dissolved salts (average factor; varies by salt species from ~400 for MgCl2 to ~970 for NaHCO3); EC1:5 (dS/m) x 0.34 ~ % total soluble salts.

## Decision rules

- If salinity is reported as EC1:5 without texture conversion, results understate ECe by about x14 (sandy loam) to x6 (heavy clay) — always state which quantity is reported.
- dS/m expressed in mS/m is 100x larger numerically; misread scale factors are the classic reporting failure.
- Where the EC-depth profile conflicts with the landform interpretation (e.g. recharge-shaped profile on a mapped discharge site), revisit sampling or the conceptual model before selecting management.

## Checks

- Every table states units and conversion factors used.
- Field-observed salinity outbreaks reconcile with lab data; discrepancies trigger a labelling/reporting audit.
- Interpretation distinguishes ECw (water measurements — snapshot only) from soil ECe.

## Common errors

- Mixing dS/m, mS/m and uS/cm in one report without flags.
- Using the 640 ppm-per-dS/m average without noting it varies with salt species.
- Inferring soil salinity from creek/dam ECw readings.
- Reporting only tables without maps/transects, so the spatial pattern that drives management is lost.

## Caveats

- Classification and aggressivity calls must be verified against the source document and the project spec.
- Conversion factors (texture multipliers, the 640 factor) are averages with acknowledged spread — cite them with the source page rather than treating them as exact.
- Salt-profile shape interpretation is indicative, not diagnostic; corroborate with piezometer data.

## Standards cited

Rayment & Higginson (1992) Australian Laboratory Handbook of Soil and Water Chemical Methods (dS/m convention), Richards (1954) USDA Handbook 60 (ECe salinity classes)

## Related

- [[Library - salinity and sodic soils]]
- [[Library - RMS and TfNSW specifications]]
- [[Skills]]

notes.title: Prove pavement process with trial section
notes.body:
# Prove pavement process with trial section

> **Source:** `dc_r071.pdf` (Clause 6.3 and Annexure R71/C), held in the local reference library — see
> [[Reference library]]. This note is a paraphrased working aid, not the
> document. Values, clauses and criteria must be read from the source before
> they are relied on, and engineering conclusions need qualified review.

**Outcome.** A trial pavement section demonstrating that materials, plant and methods achieve specified compaction, thickness and levels before full production is released.

## Inputs

- Agreed trial location
- Same materials, equipment and methods documented in the Project Quality Plan
- Test regime for compaction, thickness, level and surface requirements

## Procedure

1. Notify the authority ahead of the trial (witness point) and construct a trial section of the specified length range at the proposed lot width.
2. Test the trial against all conformity requirements and submit the results; general pavement construction is a hold point released only on conforming trial results.
3. If the trial fails, propose a disposition (possibly modified equipment/methods) and expect a further trial before release.
4. Repeat the trial whenever plant, equipment, method, materials, mix or rate of work changes, or after nonconforming work.

## Decision rules

- Trial length must be between 100 m and 200 m for the proposed lot width (dc_r071 Clause 6.3).
- Witness point notification at least 3 working days before trial construction (dc_r071 Clause 6.3).

- Trial results cover compaction, course thickness, levels and specified pavement properties, not just density.
- Nonconforming trial sections dispositioned through the nonconformity process.

## Common errors

- Starting production lots before hold point release on the trial.
- Quietly substituting plant after the trial without re-trialling.

notes.title: Rate rockfall hazard for a slope inventory using a point-based rating system
notes.body:
# Rate rockfall hazard for a slope inventory using a point-based rating system

> **Source:** [YouTube — How to Perform Rockfall Hazard Assessment — Step by Step](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1i5D-RdYsR0&t=0s) (00:00-14:55). A YouTube lecture — learning
> material, not an approved design procedure. Equations and numbers were
> heard through auto-captions; read them off the video before use, and
> verify anything design-relevant against the standard and the project
> specification. Engineering conclusions need qualified review.

**Outcome.** A summed hazard rating for each inspected slope that ranks it for remediation priority and sets the re-inspection or mitigation response

## Inputs

- Inventory of slopes with rockfall potential from regular site surveys
- Slope height
- Ditch/catchment condition and effectiveness
- Roadway width
- Geologic character: discontinuity orientation, persistence, joint surface friction, presence of clay infill (or, if unavailable, degree of erosion)
- Typical block size or potential rockfall volume
- Climate: precipitation and freezing periods
- Rockfall history at the site
- Traffic data and speed limit for the exposure ratings (see companion skill)

## Procedure

1. Inspect every slope in the inventory area that could produce rockfall in the near future
2. Score each factor from the rating table, where points escalate steeply between categories (low points = benign, high points = adverse)
3. For slope height beyond the table maximum, extrapolate the height-points trend but cap at the maximum allowed points
4. Judge ditch effectiveness from field evidence: loose rock retained in the catchment with a clear road indicates an effective ditch (low points); limited or no catchment scores high points
5. Score geologic character from discontinuity orientation and joint friction; if that information cannot be obtained, score the erosion category instead
6. Estimate average block size by walking the ditch and slope; if block sizes vary widely, estimate the potential rockfall volume instead
7. Score climate higher where precipitation is high and where freeze periods drive water-ice cycling in joints
8. Score history from observed frequency of past falls (few falls = low points, many or constant falls = high points)
9. Add the traffic exposure ratings (average vehicle risk and percent decision sight distance)
10. Sum all factor points to obtain the slope rating

## Decision rules

- Total below about 300 points: low priority, re-inspect on the normal cycle
- Total of about 500 points or more: act immediately with remedial works
- Totals between the thresholds: apply preventive measures if budget allows, otherwise increase monitoring/inspection frequency
- When a description sits between two category scores, use engineering judgment and document the reasoning

## Checks

- Confirm every factor received a score and that extrapolated scores respect the table caps
- Cross-check subjective scores (geology, history, ditch) against the written site description
- Verify the same rating system and category boundaries are used consistently across the whole inventory so rankings are comparable

## Common errors

- Treating the rating as objective; several categories (geologic character, history, ditch effectiveness) are judgment calls and should be justified
- Ignoring absence of clay-infill information: infill presence is the key difference between adjacent geology categories
- Failing to re-inspect slopes near the action threshold more frequently

## Caveats

- YouTube lecture — learning material, not an approved design procedure; verify against project specification and current standards
- Exact point values (3/9/27/81 style scales) and thresholds are read from the lecturer's table — read the table from the video before use
- Lecturer stresses the scoring is partly subjective and improves with field experience

## Standards cited

Rockfall Hazard Rating System as used in North America (named by lecturer as the source of the rating table; adapt to the local system in your jurisdiction)

- [[Skills]]

notes.title: Read dip and dip direction from stereonet great circles and poles
notes.body:
# Read dip and dip direction from stereonet great circles and poles

> **Source:** [YouTube — Stereonet Quiz — Reading Stereonet Data, Great Circles, Poles, Dips](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=naR9iWZjdW0&t=0s) (00:01-11:05). A YouTube lecture — learning
> material, not an approved design procedure. Equations and numbers were
> heard through auto-captions; read them off the video before use, and
> verify anything design-relevant against the standard and the project
> specification. Engineering conclusions need qualified review.

**Outcome.** Correct interpretation of discontinuity dip magnitude and dip direction from either great-circle or pole representations on a stereonet

## Inputs

- A stereonet plot showing discontinuities as great circles, poles, or both
- The compass frame of the net: north at top is 0 degrees, east 90, south 180, west 270

## Procedure

1. For dip magnitude with great circles: dip is 90 degrees at the centre of the net and 0 at the perimeter, so the great circle passing closest to the centre represents the steepest plane, and the one furthest from the centre the shallowest
2. For dip magnitude with poles: the rule inverts because a pole plots 90 degrees away from its great circle — the pole furthest from the centre represents the steepest plane, and a pole near the centre a near-horizontal plane
3. For dip direction with a great circle: construct the line perpendicular to the chord joining the great circle's ends, passing through the circle's crest, and extend it to the perimeter; the azimuth where it meets the perimeter is the dip direction
4. For dip direction with a pole: draw a line from the pole through the centre of the net and extend to the far perimeter; the azimuth at the crossing point is the dip direction

## Decision rules

- Great circle near centre = steep; pole near centre = shallow — always state which representation you are reading before applying the closeness rule
- Two poles at the same azimuth but different radii represent planes with the same dip direction but different dips

## Checks

- Convert between representations as a self-check: the pole and its great circle must give the same dip and dip direction
- Confirm the answer against the perimeter azimuth graduations (0/90/180/270)

## Common errors

- Applying the great-circle closeness rule to poles, concluding a pole near the centre is a steep plane
- Reading dip direction from the pole's own azimuth instead of projecting the line through the centre to the opposite side of the net

## Caveats

- YouTube lecture — learning material, not an approved design procedure; verify against project specification and current standards
- Some quoted azimuth numbers in the auto-captions are garbled (e.g. a value read as both 230 and 330 degrees in the same exercise) — read exact values from the video frames

## Standards cited

None cited in the source passage.

notes.title: Recognise urban salinity indicators in the field
notes.body:
# Recognise urban salinity indicators in the field

> **Source:** `booklet5new.pdf` ('Salinity Indicators' section, pp. 3-5 of Introduction to Urban Salinity), held in the local reference library — see
> [[Reference library]]. This note is a paraphrased working aid, not the
> document. Values, clauses and criteria must be read from the source before
> they are relied on, and engineering conclusions need qualified review.

**Outcome.** Rapid, low-cost identification of sites where salinity is present or emerging, triggering targeted testing rather than assumption.

## Inputs

- Site walkover access (buildings, roads, drainage features, vegetation)
- Optional field EC meter for screening
- Knowledge of local salt-tolerant species

## Procedure

1. Scan vegetation for indicator signals: dieback, yellowing/defoliation, stunted growth, community shift toward salt-tolerant species (e.g. cumbungi, sea barley grass, annual beard grass, couch, salt sandspurrey, Juncus reeds).
2. Scan buildings for indicators: white efflorescence staining, a 'tide mark' showing capillary rise height on walls, mortar and brick fretting grain-by-grain, blistering paint/render, rapid metal corrosion, damage concentrated below the damp-proof course.
3. Scan ground and infrastructure: bare scalded patches, surface salt crystals, puffy dry or greasy wet soil, black staining, unexplained seepage, roads rutting or potholing faster than traffic would explain, damage near stormwater/detention structures.
4. Treat indicators as hypotheses: confirm with soil/water testing (e.g. field EC1:5 screening then lab tests) before attributing damage to salinity, since moisture, poor materials or other causes can mimic the symptoms.
5. Note the water source implicated (groundwater rise, leaking pipes/pools, overwatering, blocked gutters) because management differs by source.

## Decision rules

- Presence of salt-tolerant plants alone does not prove active salinity — they may simply be planted or opportunistic; use them to justify testing, not conclusions.
- A tide mark plus efflorescence points to rising damp carrying salts; damage from the top of walls down points to falling damp (gutters/roof) instead.
- Damage confined below the DPC line indicates the DPC is working; damage above it suggests bridging or failure.

## Checks

- Each suspected indicator has a follow-up test or inspection recorded.
- Alternative causes (plumbing leaks, condensation, poor drainage) explicitly considered.
- Observations photographed and located for the site map.

## Common errors

- Diagnosing salinity from a single indicator without testing.
- Missing the distinction between the salt source and the water source mobilising it.
- Expecting obvious white salt crystals — at most salty sites they are rare; subtler indicators dominate.

## Caveats

- Classification and aggressivity calls need verification against the source documents and project spec; indicator observation is screening only.
- Merged sources: booklet3siteinvestigationsforurbansalinity (2).pdf p. 5 (outbreak indicators list) and INDUSTRY_GUIDE_T56_Residential_Slabs_and_Footings_in_Saline_Environments.pdf Section 3.4 (inspection of existing buildings) teach the same skill.
- Species lists are NSW-oriented; verify local indicator flora.

## Standards cited

LGSI companion booklets: 'Indicators of Urban Salinity' (DLWC 2002), 'Salinity Indicator Plants' (DIPNR 2005)

## Related

- [[Groundwater observations]]
- [[Library - salinity and sodic soils]]
- [[Library - RMS and TfNSW specifications]]
- [[Skills]]

notes.title: Record nuclear gauge daily standard counts (Form K38)
notes.body:
# Record nuclear gauge daily standard counts (Form K38)

> **Source:** [Google Drive — Field standard count/density reading_250818_075031.pdf](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1pB4ZoKaKkoaESFDHjKBiJD0rZ0Q8AeWu/view) (15 pages of completed K38 sheets for gauge 1449 (Humboldt, PS 0.64) with daily rows of density counts ~3130-3160 and moisture counts ~455-520, computed means, PL values, upper/lower limits and Y/N ticks). Reconstructed from STS's own
> field records on Google Drive — completed forms, labelled photos and
> scans, catalogued in [[Field records catalogue]]. It shows what the
> records evidence, not necessarily the current approved procedure —
> confirm against the current STS form and procedure before treating it
> as the standard method.

**Outcome.** A daily standard count check for a nuclear density gauge, verifying density and moisture counts fall within control limits before field density testing, combined with the gauge's remote storage record.

## Inputs

- Form K38 'Daily Standard Count Check & Remote Storage Record Sheet' (Date of Issue 01/10/19, Revision 1) — one sheet per gauge
- Nuclear density gauge with its gauge number and type (examples: gauge no. 1449, type Humboldt)
- The gauge's (PS) Prescale Value (0.64 on the examples)
- Previous four standard count readings for the running means

## Procedure

1. Head the sheet with Nuclear Gauge No., Type, and (PS) Prescale Value.
2. Each working day take the standard counts and complete one row: Date Checked, Checked By (initials), Standard Density Count.
3. Compute and record the density control values in the printed columns: (DS) Mean of Last 4 Readings; PL = √(DS/PS); Upper Limit DS + 2(PL); Lower Limit DS − 2(PL).
4. Tick/cross the 'Density Count within Limits (Y/N)' column by comparing today's count against the limits.
5. Repeat for moisture: Standard Moisture Count; (MS) Mean of Last 4 Readings; PL = √(MS/PS); Upper and Lower Limits from MS and PL; tick 'Moisture Count within Limits (Y/N)'.
6. Complete the storage-security fields on the sheet: circle storage location Vehicle/Garage, Vehicle Rego No., Base Storage Address, and 'Vehicle Equipped With Locked Alarm System: Y/N'.
7. File the sheets per gauge; the record set runs as a continuous multi-page daily log (15 pages in the example, with site annotations such as the depot address added by hand).

## Decision rules

- Limits are derived from the mean of the last four readings, so the running mean must be carried forward every day.
- A count outside its limits fails the daily check — the Y/N column exists to force that comparison before the gauge is used for field density testing.
- One sheet (and one running mean) per gauge — gauge number and prescale value are fixed in the sheet header.

## Checks

- Today's density and moisture counts each marked within limits
- Mean-of-last-4 recalculated, not copied
- Checked By initials present on every row
- Storage location, vehicle rego and alarm fields completed for source security

## Common errors

- Carrying yesterday's limits without updating the 4-reading mean
- Recording the count but skipping the within-limits Y/N decision
- Leaving the remote-storage/security section blank

## Caveats

- Reconstructed from STS field records — confirm against the current STS procedure before treating as the standard method
- The printed limit-formula text is small and partly unclear on the scans; the recorded numbers are consistent with limits of mean ± 2×PL for density, but verify the printed formulas (including the moisture limit multiplier) on a clean copy of Form K38
- The recorded PL values (~7.0 for DS ≈ 3140) match √(DS/PS) only with a scaling convention; confirm the intended calculation with the office before computing limits from scratch

## Standards cited

None cited in the source passage.

## Related

- [[Field records catalogue]]
- [[Borehole log conventions]]
- [[Skills]]

notes.title: Record Wenner resistivity readings from the AEMC tester onto the stored-measurements datasheet
notes.body:
# Record Wenner resistivity readings from the AEMC tester onto the stored-measurements datasheet

> **Source:** [Google Drive — Field Resistivity Test/Datasheet - blank - FRM-StoredMeasurements.pdf and Layout - Wenner.pptx](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1lJBBzVVjTwowr9KA4ZNKpb3KONAbRUT5/view) (Blank AEMC (Chauvin Arnoux) stored-measurements table (Date/Test #/Operator/Test Site/Results/Comments, Rev01 08/20) plus a one-slide Wenner four-terminal layout diagram with 100 m spacings). Reconstructed from STS's own
> field records on Google Drive — completed forms, labelled photos and
> scans, catalogued in [[Field records catalogue]]. It shows what the
> records evidence, not necessarily the current approved procedure —
> confirm against the current STS form and procedure before treating it
> as the standard method.

**Outcome.** A paper backup of every stored soil-resistivity measurement, tied to test number, operator and site, matching the tester's internal memory.

## Inputs

- AEMC FRM-StoredMeasurements blank datasheet (Rev01 - 08/20, 3 pages of table)
- Wenner electrode layout diagram (four terminals E(X), ES(Xv), S(Y), H(Z) set out at equal spacings along the traverse, e.g. 100 m a-spacings across a 300 m line with 50/150 m position markers)
- AEMC ground resistance tester with stored test numbers
- The already-documented AEMC Wenner resistivity SOP for the test procedure itself

## Procedure

1. Set out the four-electrode Wenner array per the layout diagram: electrodes in a straight line at equal spacing a, connected to the tester terminals in order E(X), ES(Xv), S(Y), H(Z); keep the geometry consistent when the array is walked along or the spacing changed.
2. Run the measurement per the SOP and let the instrument store the result under its test number.
3. Immediately transcribe each stored reading to the datasheet: date, test # (the instrument's stored-measurement number), operator, test site (traverse/station and spacing), results (reading with units) and comments (conditions, electrode contact issues, re-tests).
4. Use the comments column to flag any reading taken with degraded contact or nearby buried metal so the office interpretation can weight it.
5. Reconcile the sheet against the instrument memory before leaving site - every stored test number should appear once.

## Decision rules

- The instrument memory is not the record - the datasheet is the auditable record; transcribe on site, not back at the office.
- One row per stored measurement, including repeats - do not overwrite a bad reading, add the retest as a new row with a comment.
- Record the a-spacing with each result (in Test Site or Comments) since resistivity interpretation depends on it.

## Checks

- Row count equals stored-measurement count on the tester.
- Units stated in the Results column (ohm or ohm-m) - a bare number is ambiguous between resistance and computed resistivity.
- Operator and date filled on every page, since pages can separate.

## Common errors

- Recording only the computed resistivity and losing the raw resistance/test number linkage to the instrument memory.
- Omitting spacing changes mid-traverse, making depth interpretation impossible.
- Leaving transcription to end of day and losing readings when memory positions are reused.

## Caveats

- Reconstructed from STS field records — confirm against the current STS procedure before treating as the standard method
- The datasheet is a vendor form, not STS-coded; the test procedure itself is covered by the separately documented AEMC Wenner SOP.

AS/IEEE ground-resistance practice per the AEMC instrument documentation (Wenner four-point method)

notes.title: Reduce a plate load test in the STS PLATE LOAD TEST workbook and issue the report sheet
notes.body:
# Reduce a plate load test in the STS PLATE LOAD TEST workbook and issue the report sheet

> **Source:** [Google Drive — PLT calc/PLATE LOAD TEST-PLT1.xls and PLATE LOAD TEST-PLT1.pdf](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1ns4DfJN7rotCLuaqDm1RAFz54N9CVPVS/view) (Office-side calculation workbook (Input Data blue-cell entry, Bar-to-kN calibration tab, auto EV1/Ks report sheet) and its issued PDF for a Marsden Park compacted-DGB pad test; field side is the already-documented S112 worksheet). Reconstructed from STS's own
> field records on Google Drive — completed forms, labelled photos and
> scans, catalogued in [[Field records catalogue]]. It shows what the
> records evidence, not necessarily the current approved procedure —
> confirm against the current STS form and procedure before treating it
> as the standard method.

**Outcome.** A checked pressure-settlement curve with computed EV1 loading modulus and Ks(PLATE) subgrade reaction, issued as a one-page STS report per test location.

## Inputs

- Completed S112 field worksheet (Load Settlement - Time Relationship Worksheet) from site
- STS PLATE LOAD TEST-PLTx.xls workbook (sheets: Input Data, Report, Calibration Chart)
- Jack/load-cell calibration (the Calibration Chart tab converts gauge Bar to PSI/kN/pound-force using the ram effective area)
- Project header data: project no., client, report no., test method (e.g. ASTM D1195/D1195M), test and report dates

## Procedure

1. Open the workbook and work only in the blue entry cells of the Input Data sheet (instruction printed at the top).
2. Enter the header block: project, client, address, test location (PLT number), test method, project no., report no., report date, test date, signatory initials.
3. Enter test specifications: moisture conditions, weather, type of soil, wet unit weight (or '-'), plate diameter (cm; plate area auto-computes), and duration per pressure increment (min).
4. Transcribe the field readings by load stage - preload, first loading stage, unloading stage, second load cycle - entering gauge pressure in Bar and the three dial gauge readings (mm) per step; the sheet converts Bar to PSI and MPa via the calibration chart and averages the gauges into average settlement.
5. Let the EV1 calculation block fit its polynomial (a2/a1/a0 coefficients) to the loading branch; the Report sheet computes EV1 loading (MPa) and Ks(PLATE) (MN/m3).
6. Review the Report sheet: pressure-settlement chart with loading, unloading and reload branches, stepped pressure/settlement table, test specifications and the computed moduli.
7. Enter technician and report initials, obtain the approved signatory's signature, then print/export the Report sheet to PDF named PLATE LOAD TEST-PLTx and file it beside the source xls.

## Decision rules

- Stage structure in the workbook must mirror the field sheet exactly (preload, loading, unloading, reload) - do not merge stages to smooth the curve.
- If a dial gauge is unused, leave its column empty rather than entering zeros, so the average uses only real gauges.
- The reported modulus is EV1 from the loading branch; unload/reload data stays on the curve for interpretation but is not the headline value.
- Report only after an approved signatory reviews and signs - technician initials alone do not issue the report.

## Checks

- Average settlement column reproduces the field sheet averages (transcription check per step).
- Plate area equals pi/4 x diameter squared for the entered plate.
- Curve shape sensible: monotonic settlement on loading, partial recovery on unloading; investigate reversals before issuing.
- Report no., project no. and test date match the field worksheet and job records.

## Common errors

- Typing pressures in MPa into the Bar column - the calibration conversion then inflates results by orders of magnitude.
- Overwriting formula cells outside the blue input cells, silently breaking EV1.
- Issuing the PDF with a stale report date because the header was copied from a previous PLT file.

## Caveats

- Reconstructed from STS field records — confirm against the current STS procedure before treating as the standard method
- The EV1 polynomial fit and Ks derivation are embedded workbook formulas; verify the workbook version and jack calibration are current before reuse on a new job.

## Standards cited

ASTM D1195/D1195M (repetitive static plate load test), BS 1377:Part 9 / ASTM D1196 (alternative methods circled on the field sheet)

## Related

- [[Field records catalogue]]
- [[Library - plate load testing]]
- [[Skills]]

notes.title: Run a basic circular slip-surface slope stability analysis in Slide2 (Quick Start)
notes.body:
# Run a basic circular slip-surface slope stability analysis in Slide2 (Quick Start)

> **Source:** `Tutorial_01_Quick_Start.pdf` (Slide 2018 Tutorial Manual, Tutorial 01 (whole tutorial)), held in the local reference library — see
> [[Reference library]]. This note is a paraphrased working aid, not the
> document. Values, clauses and criteria must be read from the source before
> they are relied on, and engineering conclusions need qualified review.

**Outcome.** A computed factor of safety and critical circular slip surface for a homogeneous dry slope, using a Grid Search, with results interpreted and a second scenario compared.

## Inputs

- Slope geometry as external boundary vertex coordinates
- Material properties: unit weight, Mohr-Coulomb cohesion and phi
- Choice of limit-equilibrium methods (defaults: Bishop Simplified and Janbu)

## Procedure

1. Set Project Settings (Analysis > Project Settings): stress units, scenarios, analysis methods.
2. Add the External Boundary (Boundaries > Add External Boundary), entering vertices and closing with 'c'; upper segments represent the slope face, lateral/lower extents are arbitrary but generous.
3. Set Surface Options search method (Grid Search here; Auto Refine is the default alternative) and create a slip-centre grid via Surfaces > Auto Grid.
4. Understand Slope Limits: they filter surfaces (entry/exit must fall within them) and control circle generation with the Radius Increment; customise via Define Limits if the search needs focusing.
5. Define material properties (Properties > Define Materials); the first/default material auto-assigns for single-material models.
6. Save, Compute, then Interpret: read the Global Minimum FS per analysis method from the toolbar drop-list; view Minimum Surfaces, All Surfaces and safety-factor contours on the grid; use Filter Surfaces, Data Tips and Info Viewer for detail.
7. Optionally duplicate the scenario in the Document Viewer, switch search method (e.g. Auto Refine), recompute and tile views to compare.

## Decision rules

- Treat 'Global Minimum' with caution — it is only the minimum among surfaces actually searched; grid location, spacing, Radius Increment and Slope Limits all change the answer.
- The critical surface can differ between analysis methods; check each method separately.
- Use All Surfaces display to spot under-searched areas or clusters suggesting a focused re-search.

## Checks

- Search coverage adequate (contours and surface cloud reviewed), not just the single reported FS.
- Results consistent across at least two search methods before relying on the minimum FS.

## Common errors

- Accepting the first Grid Search minimum without varying search parameters — lower-FS surfaces may exist.
- External boundary drawn too tight, clipping potential failure surfaces.
- Comparing FS values between methods/scenarios without confirming they refer to the same slip surface.

## Caveats

- One of a 31-tutorial Slide2 series held locally; only five tutorials (01, 05, 07, 08, 28) are indexed here.
- Menus/values refer to Slide 2018; verify against the installed Slide2 version before following click-paths.

## Standards cited

Rocscience Slide2 Help system (analysis method assumptions)

notes.title: Run a deterministic planar-failure analysis in RocPlane and cross-validate hand calculations
notes.body:
# Run a deterministic planar-failure analysis in RocPlane and cross-validate hand calculations

> **Source:** [YouTube — Planar Rock Slope Failure — RocPlane Tutorial](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Uoi1iKNBqow&t=0s) (00:02-09:47). A YouTube lecture — learning
> material, not an approved design procedure. Equations and numbers were
> heard through auto-captions; read them off the video before use, and
> verify anything design-relevant against the standard and the project
> specification. Engineering conclusions need qualified review.

**Outcome.** A software factor of safety for a planar rock slope failure under dry, wet, seismic and anchored cases that matches independent hand calculation

## Inputs

- Slope height, slope face angle, failure plane angle, upper face angle
- Rock unit weight, Mohr-Coulomb cohesion and friction angle
- Tension crack location (distance from crest) or geometry
- Water fill percentage, seismic coefficient, bolt force and plunge as required

## Procedure

1. Set project units (e.g. kPa) in Analysis > Project Settings to match the cohesion units
2. Enter geometry in Input Data: slope height, face angle, failure plane angle, unit weight, zero upper face if none (example: 12 m, 60, 35, 26 kN/m3)
3. Use the 2D view to confirm the textbook geometry, driving and normal force layout
4. Add the tension crack, either at a specified distance from the crest (the software back-calculates crack length) or by direct geometry
5. Enter Mohr-Coulomb strength (example: 37 degrees, 25 kPa) and read the factor of safety (1.54 dry)
6. Add water: select plane water pressure with peak pressure at the tension crack base and set percent filled (100 percent gave 1.07; software reports U and V forces to compare with hand values)
7. Add seismic load in the Forces tab: coefficient 0.08, direction horizontal as the worst case (gave 0.92)
8. Add support in 3D view: place a bolt, set plunge angle and bolt force via bolt properties (400 kN at 35 degree plunge raised the factor of safety to about 1.4)
9. Compare wedge weight, failure plane length, U and V against hand-calculated values

## Decision rules

- Horizontal seismic direction is the worst case for this geometry
- Decreasing the bolt plunge angle increases stability for this setup — vary plunge and force to reach the target factor of safety
- Peak pressure at tension crack base with 100 percent fill represents the worst-case water assumption

## Checks

- Wedge weight, failure plane length, tension crack length, U and V reported by the software should reproduce hand-calculated values (1241 kN/m, 13.3 m, 4.35 m, 284.5, 92.7 in the example)
- Each added adverse effect should lower the factor of safety; each support should raise it

## Common errors

- Leaving default units inconsistent with the cohesion entered
- Forgetting to zero the upper face when the real slope has none
- Reading the factor of safety before re-running after a property change

## Caveats

- YouTube lecture — learning material, not an approved design procedure; verify against project specification and current standards
- Water is modelled as pressure distributions selected in the software, not as a phreatic surface; assumptions beyond percent fill are not stated

## Standards cited

None cited in the source passage.

## Related

- [[Skills]]

notes.title: Run a DIN 18134 plate load test on the AX 01a
notes.body:
# Run a DIN 18134 plate load test on the AX 01a

> **Source:** `BedAnlAx01a_engl V40a.pdf` (Chapter 3, pp. 7-8), held in the local reference library — see
> [[Reference library]]. This note is a paraphrased working aid, not the
> document. Values, clauses and criteria must be read from the source before
> they are relied on, and engineering conclusions need qualified review.

**Outcome.** The engineer can execute the full two-cycle DIN 18134 loading sequence on the AX 01a electronic box and obtain Ev1, Ev2 and their ratio on site.

## Inputs

- Fully set up AX 01a (plate, cylinder against reaction load, deflection beam, sensors plugged in with correct colour coding)
- SD card inserted if results must be saved
- Hand pump and load stage table for the plate in use

## Procedure

1. Insert the SD card before starting - without it results can only be printed and are lost at switch-off (p. 7).
2. Hold ON/OFF for at least a second to power up, then press OK to start a test.
3. At the Adjust prompt, bring the displacement transducer to roughly 0 mm with the tripod screws and press OK; the settlement reading auto-zeros. If the displayed stress is not zero, run the reset-force-to-zero function first.
4. Apply the preload of 0.01 MN/m2 (display 10 kN/m2), hold 30 s, press OK; settlement zeros again.
5. For a 300 mm plate, pump to each first-cycle stage in turn - 0.08, 0.16, 0.25, 0.33, 0.42, 0.50 MN/m2 - holding each for 60 s and pressing OK to store it (table, p. 7).
6. Unload in stages 0.25, 0.125, then back to about 0.01 MN/m2, each held 60 s and stored, using the pump vent to lower the load.
7. Run the second loading cycle to the penultimate stage only: 0.08, 0.16, 0.25, 0.33, 0.42 MN/m2, 60 s each.
8. Store the final 0.42 MN/m2 reading with OK before pressing MENU to finish and save; the display then shows Ev1, Ev2 and Ev2/Ev1, which can be printed or shown as a graph.

## Decision rules

- Holding ON/OFF for about 2 s aborts the test with nothing stored - use only to abandon a test.
- If the sequence is not completed, the device cannot compute Ev1/Ev2 and will show no moduli (p. 8).

## Checks

- Force reading is zero before preload; settlement auto-zeroed at Adjust and preload steps.
- Watch the tilt of the hydraulic cylinder and extension throughout loading (p. 7).
- Results screen shows record number, date/time, Ev1, Ev2 and the ratio.

## Common errors

- Pressing MENU before storing the last 0.42 MN/m2 point, losing the test result.
- Forgetting the SD card and losing data at power-off.
- Starting with a non-zero force reading instead of resetting it.

## Caveats

- The stage table shown is for the 300 mm plate; other plate diameters use different loads (see the Anix loading-stage sheet).
- The manual is a partial translation of a German original, so some wording is terse; one table entry ('0420') is an obvious OCR/typo for 0.420 MN/m2.

## Standards cited

DIN 18134:2012-04

## Related

- [[Library - plate load testing]]
- [[Skills]]

> document. Values, clauses and criteria must be read from the source before
> they are relied on, and engineering conclusions need qualified review.

**Outcome.** A steady-state FE seepage solution (phreatic surface, pore pressure/total head contours, flow vectors) whose pore pressures feed directly into the limit-equilibrium slope stability run, including optional matric suction strength above the water table.

## Inputs

- Slope geometry (single model serves both seepage and stability)
- Total head or other hydraulic boundary conditions along the external boundary, with vertices placed where head values change
- Saturated permeability Ks per material (plus unsaturated permeability model if needed)
- Optional unsaturated shear strength angle phi-b

## Procedure

1. Set Project Settings > Groundwater > Groundwater Method = Steady State FEA (this deletes any water pressure grid/water table in the scenario and enables Groundwater analysis mode).
2. In Slope Stability mode, edit boundaries as needed — add vertices where the phreatic surface meets the slope face and model edges so head boundary conditions land on the right segments (boundaries cannot be edited in Groundwater mode).
3. Switch to Groundwater mode; Discretize and Mesh (defaults: 3-noded triangles, ~1500 elements) and customise only if needed.
4. Set Boundary Conditions: assign Total Head values to the wetted boundary segments; the slope surface defaults to an Unknown (P=0 or Q=0) condition and remaining edges to zero nodal flow. Slide auto-creates ponded water wherever total head exceeds boundary elevation.
5. Define hydraulic properties (Ks) per material.
6. Compute (groundwater) and Interpret (groundwater) FIRST: check pressure head contours, the P=0 line (FE water table), flow vectors perpendicular-to-head-contour behaviour, iso-lines, and queries before trusting the stability run.
7. Return to Slope Stability mode and Compute — the stability engine automatically consumes the FE pore pressures; interpret FS results alongside groundwater contours.
8. Optionally set a non-zero unsaturated shear strength angle so matric suction (negative pore pressure above the water table) adds strength psi.tan(phi-b); rerun and compare FS.

## Decision rules

- Always compute and review the groundwater solution separately before the stability analysis, even though Slide will chain them automatically.
- Negative pressure heads above the water table are matric suction; they affect strength only if phi-b > 0.
- Since phi-b is rarely well known, run a sensitivity study varying it between zero and the material friction angle before relying on suction for stability.
- When comparing runs (e.g. against a pressure-grid model), verify via slip-centre coordinates/radius that the same critical surface is being compared.

## Checks

- FE water table position plausible against known groundwater levels (it is the P=0 iso-line).
- Ponded water auto-created where intended by the head boundary conditions.
- Iso-line and query checks confirm the pressure field (e.g. pond-bottom pressure head equals pond depth).

## Common errors

- Missing boundary vertices at phreatic-surface intersections so head boundary conditions smear across wrong segments.
- Skipping groundwater Interpret and feeding a bad seepage solution into the stability run.
- Attributing small FS differences between pore-pressure sources to error rather than interpolation-method differences.
- Relying on matric suction for a passing FS without sensitivity analysis on phi-b.

## Caveats

- Sample of a 31-tutorial local Slide2 series; steady-state only — transient seepage is covered in later tutorials.
- Slide 2018 menus; verify against installed version.

## Standards cited

Rocscience Slide2 Groundwater Verification Manual, Giam & Donald (1989) ACADS slope program review (source of the tutorial model)

notes.title: Run a flexural-toppling kinematic analysis in Dips
notes.body:
# Run a flexural-toppling kinematic analysis in Dips

> **Source:** [YouTube — Kinematic Analysis of Toppling in Rock Mass](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=swYSosPn4Mk&t=0s) (00:00-10:35). A YouTube lecture — learning
> material, not an approved design procedure. Equations and numbers were
> heard through auto-captions; read them off the video before use, and
> verify anything design-relevant against the standard and the project
> specification. Engineering conclusions need qualified review.

**Outcome.** A screening verdict on toppling risk for a rock cut, from the percentage of poles falling in the critical zone defined by the slip limit and lateral limits

## Inputs

- Pole plot of discontinuity data from site investigation (about 300 poles in the example)
- Slope face dip and dip direction (45 / 135 in the example)
- Friction angle of the dominant joints (35 degrees in the example)
- Lateral limits about the slope dip direction (plus/minus 30 degrees, attributed by the lecturer to Goodman)

## Procedure

1. Load the data and confirm dip / dip direction format (not trend/plunge)
2. Add a plane for the slope face using its dip and dip direction
3. Add the slip limit plane: same dip direction as the slope, with dip equal to slope dip minus friction angle (45 - 35 = 10 in the example); poles beyond this limit represent steeply inclined planes that can contribute to toppling
4. Add a cone defining the lateral limits: the cone trend is derived from the slope dip direction rotated 90 degrees, plunge 0, with an included angle covering plus/minus 30 degrees about the slope dip direction — exact cone entries shown on screen, read from the video
5. The critical zone is where steep poles fall within the lateral limits opposite the slope face; count poles in the zone and divide by the total to get a percentage
6. Shortcut: Analysis > Kinematic Analysis > Toppling, enter slope dip, dip direction, friction angle and lateral limits; the software shades the critical flexural toppling zone and reports count, total and percentage

## Decision rules

- A critical-pole percentage above about 6 percent raises a red flag and warrants a more thorough toppling investigation (the example returned 20 of 303 poles = 6.6 percent, flagged as a concern)
- Toppling candidates are discontinuities dipping steeply into the slope, roughly parallel to the slope face within the lateral limits

## Checks

- Cross-check the manual plane-and-cone construction against the built-in kinematic analysis output
- Verify the friction angle entered matches the investigation value (the lecturer initially mistyped 30 for 35)

## Common errors

- Computing the slip limit with the wrong sign (it is slope dip minus friction angle)
- Leaving the project in trend/plunge format while entering dip / dip direction values
- Manually counting poles when the software reports the percentage directly

## Caveats

- YouTube lecture — learning material, not an approved design procedure; verify against project specification and current standards
- The cone trend arithmetic in the auto-captions is garbled (135 plus 90 stated as 125) — equation shown on screen, read from the video
- The plus/minus 30 degree lateral limit and ~6 percent threshold are lecture rules of thumb; confirm against your project's adopted criteria

## Standards cited

None cited in the source passage.
