notes.title: Run a Monte Carlo probabilistic planar-failure analysis in RocPlane
notes.body:
# Run a Monte Carlo probabilistic planar-failure analysis in RocPlane

> **Source:** [YouTube — Probabilistic Rock Slope Stability Analysis — Planar Failure](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=CVW_7MVQD2g&t=0s) (00:02-11:12). A YouTube lecture — learning
> material, not an approved design procedure. Equations and numbers were
> heard through auto-captions; read them off the video before use, and
> verify anything design-relevant against the standard and the project
> specification. Engineering conclusions need qualified review.

**Outcome.** A probability of failure and factor-of-safety distribution for a planar rock slope that reflects the measured scatter in strength and water conditions

## Inputs

- Deterministic baseline model (geometry, unit weight, strength, tension crack, water, seismic)
- Statistical distributions for uncertain inputs: cohesion, friction angle, failure plane angle, tension crack water fill — means, standard deviations and relative min/max from site or laboratory test scatter
- Number of Monte Carlo samples (example: 10,000)

## Procedure

1. Tick Probabilistic in Project Settings and set units; choose Monte Carlo sampling with the sample count
2. Keep well-known deterministic inputs fixed (slope height, face angle) and assign distributions only to genuinely uncertain parameters
3. Assign normal distributions with realistic spread: example used failure plane angle 35 plus/minus 5 degrees, cohesion mean 25 kPa with standard deviation 2 and relative min/max 5, friction angle 37 with standard deviation 2 and plus/minus 2
4. Base the spreads on the distribution of laboratory results (e.g. 10-20 tested samples), not arbitrary numbers
5. Run and read the probability of failure; inspect the factor-of-safety histogram and the cumulative probability curve (read the cumulative value at factor of safety 1 — it should equal the reported probability of failure)
6. Add water as a distributed variable: set mean percent fill of the tension crack with relative min/max reflecting seasonal variation (example: mean 50 plus/minus 25 gave zero failure probability; mean 80 with bounds 20 gave 26 percent; fixed 100 percent gave 96 percent)
7. Adjust relative min/max so the absolute maximum fill cannot exceed 100 percent — the software rejects it otherwise

## Decision rules

- Vary only parameters with real measured uncertainty; fixing well-surveyed geometry keeps the result interpretable
- Water fill percentage dominates the failure probability in this problem — invest site investigation effort there
- Interpret probability of failure together with the FS histogram, not alone

## Checks

- Cumulative probability read at factor of safety = 1 must match the reported probability of failure
- Relative min/max plus the mean must stay within physical bounds (0-100 percent for water fill)
- Zero probability of failure should correspond to a histogram entirely above factor of safety 1

## Common errors

- Setting relative min/max that push the water fill above 100 percent
- Using single deterministic values for cohesion and friction when the lab data show a range
- Confusing relative min/max (offsets from the mean) with absolute bounds

## Caveats

- YouTube lecture — learning material, not an approved design procedure; verify against project specification and current standards
- Distribution parameters in the example are illustrative; project values must come from actual test statistics

## Standards cited

None cited in the source passage.

## Related

- [[Skills]]

notes.title: Run a planar-failure kinematic analysis in Dips
notes.body:
# Run a planar-failure kinematic analysis in Dips

> **Source:** [YouTube — Planar Failure in Rock Mass — Kinematic Analysis using Discontinuity Planes](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JIbr6XgPANQ&t=0s) (00:01-07:15). A YouTube lecture — learning
> material, not an approved design procedure. Equations and numbers were
> heard through auto-captions; read them off the video before use, and
> verify anything design-relevant against the standard and the project
> specification. Engineering conclusions need qualified review.

**Outcome.** A screening verdict on whether a jointed rock cut is at risk of planar sliding, based on the percentage of discontinuity poles that both daylight and exceed the friction angle

## Inputs

- Pole plot of discontinuity dip / dip direction data from site investigation (about 300 poles in the example)
- Slope face dip and dip direction (45 / 135 in the example road cut)
- Friction angle on the discontinuities (35 degrees in the example)

## Procedure

1. Load the discontinuity data and confirm the orientation format is dip / dip direction
2. Add the slope face as a plane and generate its daylight envelope; only poles inside the envelope represent planes that daylight (come out at the slope face) and can slide
3. Add a friction cone drawn from the centre of the net (cone at trend 0, plunge 90) with the cone angle equal to the friction angle; poles outside this cone represent planes dipping more steeply than the friction angle
4. The critical region is the overlap: poles inside the daylight envelope and outside the friction cone
5. Count the critical poles and express them as a percentage of the total pole count
6. Shortcut: Analysis > Kinematic Analysis > Planar Sliding (no limits), enter slope dip, dip direction and friction angle; the software shades the critical zone and reports the count and percentage automatically

## Decision rules

- Both conditions must hold for planar failure: the plane daylights, and its dip exceeds the friction angle
- If the critical percentage is below about 6 percent, planar failure is not considered a significant risk for the rock mass; in the example 1 pole out of 303 (under 1 percent) meant no planar failure concern
- Steeply dipping discontinuities that do not daylight are not planar-failure candidates but may still pose a toppling risk

## Checks

- Verify the manual envelope-plus-cone construction against the software's built-in kinematic analysis result
- Check the input dialog echoes the intended slope dip, dip direction and friction angle before accepting results

## Common errors

- Counting all steep poles as critical without applying the daylight condition
- Entering trend/plunge data when the project is set to dip / dip direction, or vice versa

## Caveats

- YouTube lecture — learning material, not an approved design procedure; verify against project specification and current standards
- The ~6 percent screening threshold is presented as a rule of thumb in the lecture; confirm the criterion adopted for your project
- Kinematic analysis screens geometry only — it says nothing about factor of safety, water pressure or block size

## Standards cited

None cited in the source passage.

notes.title: Run a plate load test to Norwegian standard SVV 15.328 on the AX 01a
notes.body:
# Run a plate load test to Norwegian standard SVV 15.328 on the AX 01a

> **Source:** `BedAnlAx01a_engl V40a.pdf` (Chapter 4, pp. 9-10), held in the local reference library — see
> [[Reference library]]. This note is a paraphrased working aid, not the
> document. Values, clauses and criteria must be read from the source before
> they are relied on, and engineering conclusions need qualified review.

**Outcome.** The engineer can switch the AX 01a to the SVV 15.328 procedure, hold stages to a settlement-rate criterion instead of fixed times, and read E1/E2 from the printout.

## Inputs

- AX 01a set up as for any test, with the norm setting changed to SVV 15.328
- Hand pump and the SVV stage table for the 300 mm plate

## Procedure

1. Set up the system as usual, switch on and press OK to begin; adjust the displacement sensor manually to within about -2 to +2 mm and confirm.
2. Apply a preload of 0.02 MN/m2 for several seconds and confirm; displacement auto-zeros.
3. Load the first cycle through 0.05, 0.18, 0.30, 0.42, 0.50, 0.60 MN/m2, holding each stage until the settlement rate falls below the 0.02 mm criterion; the box auto-stores after 60 s and underlines the reading if settlement is still moving more than 0.02 mm, then press OK to store (p. 9).
4. Unload to zero and repeat the same stages for the second cycle.
5. Press MENU to finish, OK to browse result pages, PRINT for the sheet.
6. Read E1, computed from readings at 30% and 70% of maximum load (180 and 420 kN/m2), and E2, from 30% and 100% (180 and 600 kN/m2); alternate E2 values for lower stages are also listed.
7. Select the governing E2 using the Norwegian guidance: take the second-cycle settlement between 180 kN/m2 and the highest stage where the curve is still approximately straight (p. 9).

## Decision rules

- Use SVV mode when the project specifies Norwegian road-administration testing; stage holds are settlement-rate governed, unlike DIN's fixed 60 s.
- Pick the alternate E2 for a lower stage when the upper part of the second-cycle curve departs from straight.

## Checks

- No underlined readings should be stored - underlining flags settlement still exceeding 0.02 mm since the last reading.
- Printout lists E1, E2 and alternate E2 values for review.

## Common errors

- Storing a stage while settlement is still creeping (underlined display).
- Applying DIN hold times instead of the settlement-rate criterion.

## Caveats

- The source's table writes the criterion as <=0.02 mm/s while the text says lower than 0.02 mm/min - an internal inconsistency (likely OCR/translation); the cited Norwegian manual should be checked for the authoritative rate.
- Stages listed are for the 300 mm plate only.

## Standards cited

SVV 15.328

## Related

- [[Skills]]

notes.title: Run a probabilistic slope stability analysis in Slide2
notes.body:
# Run a probabilistic slope stability analysis in Slide2

> **Source:** `Tutorial_08_Probabilistic_Analysis.pdf` (Slide 2018 Tutorial Manual, Tutorial 8 (whole tutorial; Eqns 1-3 for PF and RI)), held in the local reference library — see
> [[Reference library]]. This note is a paraphrased working aid, not the
> document. Values, clauses and criteria must be read from the source before
> they are relied on, and engineering conclusions need qualified review.

**Outcome.** Probability of failure, mean FS and reliability index for the critical slip surface, with input random variables (cohesion, phi, unit weight) defined statistically and convergence verified.

## Inputs

- A working deterministic Slide2 model
- Statistical distributions for chosen input parameters: mean, standard deviation, relative min/max (Normal used in the tutorial)
- Sampling settings (defaults: Latin Hypercube, 1000 samples, Analysis Type = Global Minimum)
- Optional cohesion-phi correlation coefficient (tutorial default -0.5)

## Procedure

1. Enable Probabilistic Analysis in Project Settings > Statistics.
2. Define random variables via Statistics > Materials using the Add wizard: pick properties (cohesion, phi, unit weight), choose distributions, then enter standard deviation and RELATIVE min/max for each.
3. Compute — the deterministic analysis runs first, then the probabilistic re-computation of the Global Minimum surface N times with sampled inputs.
4. Interpret: read FS(mean), PF (fraction of samples with FS < 1) and RI beside the slip centre; the Info Viewer lists the best-fit FS distribution indicating whether Normal or Lognormal RI applies.
5. Explore Histogram plots (highlight FS < 1 subset), Cumulative plots (Sampler at FS = 1 reads PF directly) and Scatter plots (input vs FS relationships, correlation coefficient, regression line).
6. Check a Convergence Plot of PF/mean FS; if not stabilised, increase the number of samples and rerun.
7. Optionally apply a negative cohesion-phi correlation in Material Statistics > Correlation and recompute — realistic correlation typically reduces PF for this model.

## Decision rules

- Set relative min/max at least ~3 standard deviations for Normal variables so the distribution is not truncated.
- A reliability index of at least ~3 is the commonly recommended minimum assurance of safe design (tutorial guidance).
- Use the RI (Normal vs Lognormal) matching the best-fit FS distribution reported in Info Viewer.
- Latin Hypercube gives Monte-Carlo-comparable results with far fewer samples; use Monte Carlo only deliberately.
- Analysis Type = Global Minimum probabilistically analyses only the deterministic critical surface — the probabilistic critical surface may differ (Overall Slope option exists for that).

## Checks

- Convergence plot flat at the final PF/mean FS values; else increase samples.
- Sampled statistics approach input statistics as sample count grows.
- Pseudo-random vs random seed setting understood — pseudo-random gives reproducible results.

## Common errors

- Entering absolute instead of relative min/max values for distributions.
- Ignoring cohesion-phi correlation, generating unrealistic parameter combinations and overstating PF.
- Quoting PF from an unconverged run with too few samples.
- Assuming PF from the deterministic global minimum surface covers the whole slope's failure probability.

## Caveats

- Sample of a 31-tutorial local Slide2 series (spatial variability is Tutorials 33-34).
- Slide 2018 menus; verify against installed version.

## Standards cited

Rocscience Slide2 Help, Probabilistic Analysis section

notes.title: Run a seismic slope stability analysis in Slide2 (pseudo-static, critical kc and Newmark displacement)
notes.body:
# Run a seismic slope stability analysis in Slide2 (pseudo-static, critical kc and Newmark displacement)

> **Source:** `Tutorial_28_Seismic_Analysis.pdf` (Slide 2018 Tutorial Manual, Tutorial 28 (Models 1-4)), held in the local reference library — see
> [[Reference library]]. This note is a paraphrased working aid, not the
> document. Values, clauses and criteria must be read from the source before
> they are relied on, and engineering conclusions need qualified review.

**Outcome.** Seismic performance of a slope expressed three ways in one multi-scenario model: pseudo-static FS under a chosen seismic coefficient, the critical seismic coefficient ky giving FS = 1 per surface, and Newmark permanent displacement from a real earthquake record.

## Inputs

- A computed static slope model (multi-material model in the tutorial)
- Design horizontal (and optionally vertical) pseudo-static seismic coefficient
- A seismic acceleration-time record for Newmark analysis: manual entry, imported .ssr/Slammer file, or a built-in example record (tutorial uses Mammoth Lakes-1 1980 CVK-090, PGA 0.416 g)

## Procedure

1. Run the static baseline scenario and note the critical surface FS.
2. Duplicate the scenario, then apply Loading > Seismic Load with the horizontal seismic coefficient (positive in the failure direction); compute and compare FS against the static case — seismic loading destabilises the slope (tutorial: 1.374 to 0.992 at k = 0.15).
3. For critical-coefficient analysis: duplicate the static scenario, enable Project Settings > Seismic > Advanced Seismic Analysis with 'Compute Ky for all failure surfaces', compute, and read ky at the critical surface; use Data > Filter Surfaces to display all surfaces with ky below the design coefficient.
4. For Newmark displacement: duplicate the ky scenario, open Newmark Analysis Options, define the seismic record (example records show PGA/PGV summaries and an acceleration-time plot), choose analysis type (Rigid / Coupled / Decoupled) and which accelerations drive displacement (tutorial: Rigid, maximum positive/negative), compute, and read the critical Newmark displacement in Interpret.
5. Tile scenario views vertically with synchronised zoom/pan to compare all four models.

## Decision rules

- Pseudo-static FS < 1 does not itself mean failure — the ky and Newmark analyses quantify how much shaking is needed and how far the mass would move.
- Many surfaces with ky below the design coefficient corroborates a pseudo-static FS near or below 1 at that coefficient.
- Duplicated scenarios share only geometry/master-scenario changes automatically; other setting changes stay per-scenario unless scenarios are linked.

## Checks

- Seismic coefficient sign/direction matches the failure direction.
- Advanced Seismic Analysis checkbox enabled before expecting ky or Newmark output.
- Chosen seismic record's PGA/PGV appropriate to the site hazard; record source documented (Slide's Newmark engine is based on USGS SLAMMER).

## Common errors

- Applying the seismic load in the wrong scenario (forgetting which scenario is selected before editing).
- Running Newmark without 'Compute Ky for all failure surfaces', so displacements cannot be computed.
- Reading only the pseudo-static FS and skipping the displacement check, over- or under-calling marginal slopes.

## Caveats

- Sample of a 31-tutorial local Slide2 series; tutorial FS/ky values are model-specific illustrations, not benchmarks.
- Selection of design seismic coefficient is a code/site-hazard decision outside this tutorial (e.g. AS 1170.4 context in Australia).

## Standards cited

USGS SLAMMER (Jibson et al. 2013, USGS Techniques and Methods 12-B1), Rocscience Slide2 Help, Seismic Analysis section

## Related

notes.title: Run a slope stability analysis with a pore water pressure grid in Slide2
notes.body:
# Run a slope stability analysis with a pore water pressure grid in Slide2

> **Source:** `Tutorial_05_Water_Pressure_Grid.pdf` (Slide 2018 Tutorial Manual, Tutorial 5 (whole tutorial)), held in the local reference library — see
> [[Reference library]]. This note is a paraphrased working aid, not the
> document. Values, clauses and criteria must be read from the source before
> they are relied on, and engineering conclusions need qualified review.

**Outcome.** A factor of safety for a slope whose pore pressures are interpolated from a discrete grid of total head (or pressure head / pore pressure) values, with ponded water modelled by a water table.

## Inputs

- Grid of X, Y, value points (total head, pressure head or pore pressure) from a flownet, field measurements or numerical seepage analysis — importable as .pwp or .dxf
- Slope geometry and material properties
- Water table polyline where ponded water exists above the slope

## Procedure

1. Set Project Settings > Groundwater > Groundwater Method to the appropriate Grid option (Total Head here); the default interpolation is Modified Chugh.
2. Add the external boundary, then add the water pressure grid (Boundaries > Water Pressure Grid), importing the .pwp file rather than typing points.
3. Display grid values or use the Property Viewer to preview the interpolated pore pressure field and sanity-check the import.
4. Add a Water Table above the external boundary to create ponded water — a pressure grid CANNOT create ponded water; it only supplies internal pore pressures, not the weight and hydrostatic forces of standing water.
5. Define material properties and ensure the Grid toggle is ON in the material's water parameters (OFF forces zero pore pressure for that material).
6. Compute and Interpret; compare Global Minimum surfaces across methods (they can differ), and use Add Query / Graph Query to plot pore pressure along the critical slip surface (values are interpolated at each slice base midpoint).

## Decision rules

- Points above the water table are assigned zero pore pressure even if grid interpolation says otherwise — useful protection when the grid is sparse.
- Choose grid type (total head vs pressure head vs pore pressure) in Project Settings to match the data source.
- Use a seepage analysis instead (Tutorial 07 workflow) when no measured grid or flownet exists.

## Checks

- Grid covers the zone slip surfaces will sample; sparse coverage produces interpolation artefacts.
- Ponded water hatch appears where expected after adding the water table.
- Queried pore pressure profile along the critical surface looks physically reasonable.

## Common errors

- Expecting the pressure grid to model ponded water loads — it does not; omit the water table and the pond's weight/hydrostatic force is lost.
- Leaving the material's grid toggle OFF, silently zeroing pore pressures.
- Assuming the Bishop and Janbu global minima are the same surface when graphing comparisons.

## Caveats

- Sample of a 31-tutorial local Slide2 series; version-specific menus (Slide 2018).

## Standards cited

Rocscience Slide2 Help (interpolation methods)

## Related

- [[Groundwater observations]]
- [[Skills]]

notes.title: Run an on-site plate bearing test with time-settlement acceptance criteria
notes.body:
# Run an on-site plate bearing test with time-settlement acceptance criteria

> **Source:** `1-s2.0-S2214509521003521-main.pdf` (Sections 3.3-3.4, p. 3; results Section 4, pp. 6-8), held in the local reference library — see
> [[Reference library]]. This note is a paraphrased working aid, not the
> document. Values, clauses and criteria must be read from the source before
> they are relied on, and engineering conclusions need qualified review.

**Outcome.** The engineer can execute an ASTM D 1194-style plate bearing test on compacted fill, recording settlement over time and knowing when a load stage is complete.

## Inputs

- 30 cm diameter steel bearing plate and loading/reaction system
- Compacted layer with water content controlled to within plus/minus 2% of optimum
- Settlement gauges and a timer

## Procedure

1. Compact and verify the layer, then seat the 30 cm plate on the surface to be tested (Section 3.3, p. 3).
2. Apply the load and record settlement at 0.5, 1, 2, 4, 8, 15, 30 and 60 minutes.
3. Accept a stage when the settlement rate has dropped below 0.02 mm/minute and check that total settlement stays under 25 mm (p. 3).
4. Unload and reload a second cycle if confirmation of the loading behaviour is needed; the paper's field curves include an unload showing plastic deformation.
5. After the test, sample the soil beneath to measure in-place unit weight and moisture content for correlation.

## Decision rules

- Use stress in the 50-150 kPa range when the data will feed the elastic-modulus formula (Eq. 1).
- Compare wet-side, OWC and dry-side results separately - settlement rises with compaction water content.

## Checks

- Settlement rate below 0.02 mm/min before ending a stage.
- Total settlement under 25 mm.
- Post-test density and moisture confirm the layer met compaction targets (at least 95% of modified maximum dry unit weight in the paper's practice).

## Common errors

- Ending a load stage before the settlement rate criterion is met.
- Testing layers whose field water content has drifted outside OWC plus/minus 2%, which changes stiffness markedly.

## Caveats

- The settlement-time schedule and criteria follow the Thai standard the authors cite alongside ASTM D 1194; ASTM D 1194 itself has been withdrawn by ASTM (not stated in the paper).
- Findings derive from loess and lateritic-loess clayey sands in Thailand; transfer to other soils needs judgement.

## Standards cited

ASTM D 1194-94, ASTM D 1557-12, ASTM D 1556/D1556M-15e1, ASTM D 698-12, ASTM D 854-14, ASTM D 422-63, ASTM D 4318-17e1

notes.title: Run Benkelman Beam deflection lots under R44 Ed 3
notes.body:
# Run Benkelman Beam deflection lots under R44 Ed 3

> **Source:** `R044_E3_R15.pdf` (Clause 7.4.2 and Annexure R44/A6 (Ed 3 Rev 15)), held in the local reference library — see
> [[Reference library]]. This note is a paraphrased working aid, not the
> document. Values, clauses and criteria must be read from the source before
> they are relied on, and engineering conclusions need qualified review.

**Outcome.** Formation deflection lots are laid out, tested and assessed to the Ed 3 rules, including its distinct minimum lot length and annexure-based formula.

## Inputs

- Annexure R44/A6 characteristic deflection limits and equation parameters
- Formation lot layout and homogeneity assessment
- Deflection test data (T199)

## Procedure

1. Confirm Benkelman testing is invoked in Annexure R44/A6, then test at the underside and top of the Selected Material Zone (or underside of pavement if no SMZ) per T199, within 3 days of compaction (Clause 7.4.2).
2. Define each lot as a continuous length of formation with a minimum length of 300 m (reducible by the Principal in constrained/urban areas) and at least a carriageway width, homogeneous, with field-marked boundaries.
3. Obtain the characteristic deflection from the equation in Annexure R44/A6 and compare against the annexure limit.
4. Apply the scatter rules: standard deviation cap when the required characteristic deflection is at or below the stated threshold, coefficient-of-variation cap above it.
5. On exceedance, re-examine lot boundaries and homogeneity, re-nominate and retest; observe the witness point for testing under the first pavement layer and the hold point before placing each SMZ/pavement lot (submissions 3 working days ahead).

## Decision rules

- Testing outside the 3-day post-compaction window invalidates the lot unless the Principal approved a delay.
- Exceeding either the deflection limit or the scatter caps blocks the hold point release.
- Proof rolling results accompany the Benkelman witness notification - they are companion, not alternative, checks.

## Checks

- Surface prepared for deflection monitoring during SMZ trimming
- Test coverage over the SMZ plan area plus any Principal-directed areas
- Lot boundaries physically identifiable in the field

## Common errors

- Using the current-edition in-body formula/f-values instead of the Ed 3 Annexure A6 equation
- Defining short convenience lots below the minimum length without Principal agreement
- Skipping underside-of-SMZ testing when it is required (later editions waive it over drainage layers; check what this contract says)

## Caveats

- Superseded edition - verify it is the contract-incorporated version before applying.
- Contract documents and completed annexures override.

## Standards cited

RMS T199, RMS T198, RMS Q

notes.title: Run proof rolling and Benkelman Beam deflection acceptance under R44
notes.body:
# Run proof rolling and Benkelman Beam deflection acceptance under R44

> **Source:** `r044.pdf` (Clause 7.6, with limits per Annexures R44/A4 and A5 (Ed 5 Rev 1)), held in the local reference library — see
> [[Reference library]]. This note is a paraphrased working aid, not the
> document. Values, clauses and criteria must be read from the source before
> they are relied on, and engineering conclusions need qualified review.

**Outcome.** Formation stability is demonstrated by proof rolling and, where specified, quantified by Benkelman Beam deflection, releasing the hold point for placing the Selected Material Zone or pavement.

## Inputs

- Lot layout for surfaces within 1.5 m of the underside of the Selected Material Zone
- Moisture verification against Annexure R44/A5
- Annexure R44/A4 characteristic deflection limit and f-value (if Benkelman testing specified)
- Prior conformity evidence (density, survey) for the layer

## Procedure

1. Proof roll per T198 where directed: all embankment lots and surfaces within 1.5 m below the Selected Material Zone must withstand it; give the witness-point notice (at least 1 working day) with verification the layer otherwise conforms (Clause 7.6.1).
2. Roll test paths over the full width and length of the lot immediately after compaction, with moisture still inside the A5 range; watch for deformation, rutting, yielding or instability.
3. If proof rolling is repeated later, recondition moisture, re-verify density and survey, and apply the minimum number of preliminary roller passes stated in Clause 7.6.1 before the proof pass.
4. Where Annexure R44/A4 specifies it, Benkelman Beam test per T199 at the underside and top of the Selected Material Zone (top only if a drainage layer sits directly beneath), within 3 days of compaction (Clause 7.6.2).
5. Compute characteristic deflection as mean plus f times standard deviation and compare with the A4 limit; check the spread rule - standard deviation cap when the required deflection is at or below the stated threshold, coefficient-of-variation cap above it.
6. Submit deflection results, survey report and lot conformity at least 3 working days before placing the Selected Material Zone - this is a hold point.

## Decision rules

- Visible deformation, rutting or yielding under the proof roller fails the surface regardless of density results.
- Characteristic deflection above the A4 value triggers re-examination of lot boundaries and homogeneity, then re-nomination and retesting.
- Excessive scatter (SD or CoV beyond the caps) requires corrective action even if the mean looks acceptable.

## Checks

- Benkelman lot is a continuous, homogeneous length at least one carriageway wide with field-marked boundaries
- Testing done within the 3-day window or with documented Principal approval for delay
- Witness/hold point notices lodged with the specified lead times

## Common errors

- Proof rolling a dried-back or re-wetted surface without reconditioning
- Testing only wheelpaths instead of full lot coverage
- Ignoring the standard deviation cap because the characteristic deflection passed
- Placing Selected Material before the deflection hold point release

## Caveats

- Verify the spec edition is current; the deflection formula location and lot rules changed between editions.
- Contract documents and completed annexures override.

## Standards cited

TfNSW T198, TfNSW T199, TfNSW Q

## Related

Proof roll per T198 where directed: all embankment lots and surfaces within 1.5 m below the Selected Material Zone must withstand it; give the witness point notice (at least 1 working day) with verification the layer otherwise conforms (Clause 7.6.1). 2. Roll test paths over the full width and length of the lot immediately after compaction, with moisture still inside the A5 range; watch for deformation, rutting, yielding or instability. 3. If proof rolling is repeated later, recondition moisture, re verify density and survey, and apply the minimum number of preliminary roller passes stated in Clause 7.6.1 before the proof pass. 4. Where Annexure R44/A4 specifies it, Benkelman Beam test per T199 at the underside and top of the Selected Material Zone (top only if a drainage layer sits directly beneath), within 3 days of compaction (Clause 7.6.2). 5. Compute characteristic deflection as mean plus f times standard deviation and compare with the A4 limit; check the spread rule standard deviation cap when the required deflection is at or below the stated threshold, coefficient of variation cap above it. 6. Submit deflection results, survey report and lot conformity at least 3 working days before placing the Selected Material Zone this is a hold point. Decision rules Visible deformation, rutting or yielding under the proof roller fails the surface regardless of density results. Characteristic deflection above the A4 value triggers re examination of lot boundaries and homogeneity, then re nomination and retesting. Excessive scatter (SD or CoV beyond the caps) requires corrective action even if the mean looks acceptable. Checks Benkelman lot is a continuous, homogeneous length at least one carriageway wide with field marked boundaries Testing done within the 3 day window or with documented Principal approval for delay Witness/hold point notices lodged with the specified lead times Common errors Proof rolling a dried back or re wetted surface without reconditioning Testing only wheelpaths instead of full lot coverage Ignoring the standard deviation cap because the characteristic deflection passed Placing Selected Material before the deflection hold point release Caveats Verify the spec edition is current; the deflection formula location and lot rules changed between editions. Contract documents and completed annexures override. Standards cited TfNSW T198, TfNSW T199, TfNSW Q Related Library RMS and TfNSW specifications Skills

notes.title: Run staged monitoring and hold points for supported excavation
notes.body:
# Run staged monitoring and hold points for supported excavation

> **Source:** `gtd-2020-001.pdf` (Ground anchors, instrumentation and monitoring, thresholds and hold points sections (GTD 2020/001)), held in the local reference library — see
> [[Reference library]]. This note is a paraphrased working aid, not the
> document. Values, clauses and criteria must be read from the source before
> they are relied on, and engineering conclusions need qualified review.

**Outcome.** An instrumentation, trigger and hold-point regime that keeps an adjacent-to-road excavation verified stage by stage.

## Inputs

- Wall type and retained height
- Agreed movement trigger values shown on drawings
- Inclinometer/piezometer layout and survey system
- Construction staging (rows of anchors/supports)

## Procedure

1. Decide if instrumentation is required (asset proximity; cantilever walls over the height threshold, propped/anchored walls over theirs).
2. Install at least the minimum inclinometers below wall toe level, plus piezometers where groundwater sits above final excavation level; add total-station monitoring as warranted.
3. Take duplicate independent baseline readings before significant site work, then monitor at each defined stage: after wall construction, after excavation to each support row (before installing it), at base level, after de-stressing/removal of each row, and a closing reading one month after completion or after three stable weekly readings.
4. Have a geotechnical professional review each stage's results and certify performance against design intent before the stage hold point is released; certification at each hold point is by a chartered professional engineer covering as-built conformance, geotechnical conditions matching the report, and anchor testing.
5. Operate the alert/action/alarm regime and inform the authority immediately when triggers are exceeded; de-stress and disconnect temporary anchors at the end.

## Decision rules

- Instrumentation typically required for cantilever walls retaining over 3 m and propped/anchored walls over 6 m (gtd-2020-001 instrumentation section).
- Minimum two inclinometers installed at least 3 m below wall toe level (gtd-2020-001 instrumentation section).
- Alert: movements under 80% of agreed values - continue. Action: 80-100% - notify authority within 24 hours, review data, increase frequency, have the trigger action response plan ready. Alarm: over 100% - notify immediately and suspend excavation until the response plan is implemented (gtd-2020-001 thresholds section).
- Ground anchors in the road reserve: temporary only, no more than 75% of tendon ultimate tensile strength under working or test load, no part shallower than 1.5 m below surface, and anchors needed beyond 18 months must be designed as permanent (gtd-2020-001 ground anchors section).

## Checks

- Two independent consistent baseline sets before any works.
- Hold point certifications explicitly compare encountered geotechnical conditions to the investigation report and record corrective actions.
- Monitoring continues until the defined stability criterion (post-completion month or three stable weekly readings) is met.

## Common errors

- Installing a support row before taking the pre-installation monitoring reading for that stage.
- Treating nails and bolts as outside the anchor rules (they are treated the same).
- Stopping monitoring at base excavation level instead of through de-stressing and the closing period.

## Caveats

- Verify currency; trigger values are agreed case-by-case with the authority and their agreement overrides defaults.
- DA conditions and work method statements agreed with the authority override.

## Standards cited

AS 5100.3, AS 2159

## Related

- [[AS 2159 piling]]
- [[Groundwater observations]]
- [[Skills]]

notes.title: Run the AEMC soil resistivity test (Wenner method) to the STS SOP
notes.body:
# Run the AEMC soil resistivity test (Wenner method) to the STS SOP

> **Source:** [Google Drive — Field Resistivity Test/SOP - AEMC Resistivity Test.pdf](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1Se7pAZ8SfcW7Omjd5WZeUPuJaSAI3e4U/view) (Full 3-page STS SOP 'AEMC Resistivity Test - Wenner' covering equipment, terminal connections, layout, setup, measurement, storage and shutdown). Reconstructed from STS's own
> field records on Google Drive — completed forms, labelled photos and
> scans, catalogued in [[Field records catalogue]]. It shows what the
> records evidence, not necessarily the current approved procedure —
> confirm against the current STS form and procedure before treating it
> as the standard method.

**Outcome.** A set of stored apparent soil resistivity measurements at multiple electrode spacings using the AEMC Model 6471, per the STS standard operating procedure.

## Inputs

- AEMC Model 6471 ground resistance tester
- 2x 150+ m lead reels and 2x 50+ m lead reels
- Four electrodes
- Straight, unobstructed test line long enough for the largest spacing

## Procedure

1. Connect the four electrodes to the tester: terminal H (Z) to current electrode C1, S (Y) to potential electrode P1, ES (Xv) to potential electrode P2, E (X) to current electrode C2; ensure all leads are secure.
2. Install the four electrodes in a straight line at equal spacing 'a'; electrode penetration depth should be less than one twentieth of the electrode spacing where practicable.
3. Instrument setup: inspect instrument and leads, verify battery condition, connect all four leads, turn the rotary switch to ρ (Soil Resistivity) — the instrument automatically recognises the connected electrodes.
4. Select measurement method: press Hz/OPTIONS until 'W' (Wenner) appears; if 'S' (Schlumberger) shows, change to Wenner before testing.
5. Program electrode spacing: press DISTANCE, use the arrow buttons to enter the spacing, confirm; the tester uses this for automatic resistivity calculation. Typical spacings in the SOP: 1, 2, 4, 8, 15, 30, 75, 100 m.
6. Press START — the instrument injects current, measures voltage, calculates resistance and apparent resistivity (ρ). Wait until the reading stabilises; display shows resistance, soil resistivity, test frequency and electrode status.
7. Press MEM to save, storing test number, electrode spacing and soil resistivity (the 6471 stores up to 512 measurements).
8. Repeat: increase the spacing, reposition all four electrodes maintaining equal spacing, and re-run for each required spacing.
9. Press DISPLAY to cycle additional readouts if needed: resistance, resistivity, test voltage, test current, test frequency, electrode resistance.
10. On completion: turn selector to OFF, disconnect leads, remove electrodes, clean equipment, recharge the instrument if required.

## Decision rules

- 'W' on the display is the gate to proceed — never record with 'S' (Schlumberger) selected.
- Keep all four electrodes equally spaced at every spacing step; the programmed distance must match the actual layout or the auto-calculated resistivity is wrong.
- Keep electrode depth < a/20 where practicable.

## Checks

- Battery condition verified before starting
- All four leads connected and recognised by the instrument
- Reading stable before saving
- Electrode status display checked for poor contacts
- Each stored record carries test number, spacing and resistivity

## Common errors

- Testing in Schlumberger mode by not checking the W/S indicator
- Programmed spacing not updated after moving electrodes
- Electrodes driven too deep relative to close spacings
- Not waiting for the reading to stabilise before pressing MEM

## Caveats

- This one is an actual STS SOP rather than a reconstructed practice, so it can be treated as the documented method — but check for a newer revision (the copy carries no revision number)
- The SOP's step numbering is internally inconsistent ('Repeat Steps 7-9' where steps are numbered 1-8); the sequence above follows the document order
- No field record sheet for resistivity results was among the retrieved files — recording format is not evidenced

## Standards cited

None cited in the source passage.

## Related

- [[Field records catalogue]]
- [[Skills]]

notes.title: Run the slake durability test through two cycles and record the masses for the durability index
notes.body:
# Run the slake durability test through two cycles and record the masses for the durability index

> **Source:** [YouTube — Slake Durability Test: Procedure, Measurements, Calculations, Classification](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=x86l8_gHlhQ&t=0s) (00:00-11:46). A YouTube lecture — learning
> material, not an approved design procedure. Equations and numbers were
> heard through auto-captions; read them off the video before use, and
> verify anything design-relevant against the standard and the project
> specification. Engineering conclusions need qualified review.

**Outcome.** A complete set of drum-and-sample mass records over two wet-dry abrasion cycles, ready for computing the second-cycle slake durability index used for durability classification

## Inputs

- About 450-500 g of rock in roughly ten lump pieces of 40-60 g each, not too angular
- Slake durability drum, motorised trough, tap water, oven, scale

## Procedure

1. Check each lump's mass falls in the 40-60 g band (43 g and 57 g pieces both acceptable in the demo)
2. Weigh the empty drum (842.2 g in the demo)
3. Load the rock and weigh drum plus rock (1285.5 g), then fit and secure the lid
4. Mount the drum in the trough and fill with tap water to about 20 mm below the drum axis
5. Rotate at about 20 revolutions per minute for 10 minutes; fines migrate into the water and it turns muddy
6. Remove the drum, take off the lid, and oven-dry drum and retained rock for about 6 hours
7. Weigh the dry drum plus retained rock — this closes cycle one (1244.6 g in the demo)
8. Repeat the whole wet-rotate-dry-weigh sequence for a second cycle, topping up water first (final dry mass 1237.1 g in the demo)
9. Use the second-cycle retained dry mass data to compute the second-cycle slake durability index and classify the rock's durability

## Decision rules

- The classification is based on the second-cycle index, so the test is not complete after one cycle
- Follow the Franklin and Chandra testing procedure (named by the lecturer) for the setup details

## Checks

- Water level set at the pre-marked height about 20 mm below the drum axis before each cycle
- Drum connections secure before rotation
- All four masses recorded: empty drum, drum+rock initial, drum+rock after cycle 1 drying, drum+rock after cycle 2 drying

## Common errors

- Stopping after the first cycle and classifying from the first-cycle loss
- Using highly angular fragments, which abrade differently from the intended lump shape
- Skipping or shortening the roughly 6-hour drying stage so the retained mass includes moisture

## Caveats

- YouTube lecture — learning material, not an approved design procedure; verify against project specification and current standards
- The index formula itself is not spoken aloud — equation shown on screen — read from the video; it is derived from the retained dry mass ratios of the recorded weighings
- The durability classification bands for the second-cycle index are also shown on screen rather than narrated

## Standards cited

Franklin and Chandra slake durability procedure (authors named by lecturer; specific publication not cited on audio)

## Related

notes.title: Screen a tunnel for squeezing using the rock-mass-strength to in-situ-stress ratio
notes.body:
# Screen a tunnel for squeezing using the rock-mass-strength to in-situ-stress ratio

> **Source:** [YouTube — Tunnel Squeezing: Predicting and Estimating Ground Deformation](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=hVgGXjpDYXg&t=0s) (00:00-04:57). A YouTube lecture — learning
> material, not an approved design procedure. Equations and numbers were
> heard through auto-captions; read them off the video before use, and
> verify anything design-relevant against the standard and the project
> specification. Engineering conclusions need qualified review.

**Outcome.** An estimate of expected tunnel strain and squeezing severity class for a tunnel in weak rock, from an empirical strength/stress chart

## Inputs

- Rock mass strength (given or separately estimated; low values typify shale, mudstone, sheared flysch)
- Tunnel depth below surface
- Rock unit weight (assume an average of 27 kN/m3, i.e. 0.027 MPa per metre, when unmeasured)
- Empirical chart relating strength/stress ratio to tunnel strain and squeezing severity

## Procedure

1. Compute the in-situ vertical stress as unit weight times depth; with the average-rock assumption use 0.027 times depth in metres to get MPa (example: 44 m depth gives about 1.19 MPa)
2. Form the ratio of rock mass strength to in-situ stress (example: 0.17 / 1.19 = 0.14)
3. Enter the empirical chart at that ratio and read the expected strain percentage (example: slightly above 5 percent)
4. Classify the squeezing severity from the strain band the reading falls in (strain between about 5 and 10 percent indicated very severe squeezing problems in the example)

## Decision rules

- Low strength/stress ratios mean high strain: the lower the ratio, the more severe the squeezing class
- Very severe classes flag risk of local tunnel collapse and demand support design attention
- Fine-grained weak rocks (shale, mudstone, flysch) are the candidate lithologies to screen

## Checks

- Confirm unit consistency: 0.027 times depth in metres yields MPa directly
- Confirm the strength value used is rock mass strength, not intact rock strength

## Common errors

- Using intact UCS instead of rock mass strength in the ratio, which greatly understates squeezing
- Unit errors mixing kPa and MPa in the stress estimate

## Caveats

- YouTube lecture — learning material, not an approved design procedure; verify against project specification and current standards
- The strain vs ratio chart and its severity bands are shown on screen — read from the video
- Only vertical gravitational stress is considered; tectonic or horizontal stress effects are not addressed

## Standards cited

None cited in the source passage.

notes.title: Screen Hawkesbury Sandstone durability with sodium sulphate soundness before exposed or marine use
notes.body:
# Screen Hawkesbury Sandstone durability with sodium sulphate soundness before exposed or marine use

> **Source:** `substanceAndMassPropertiesForTheDesignOfEngineeringStructuresInTheHawkesburySandstone.pdf` (Sections 2.5 (durability, Tables 7 and grading; pp 8-9) and 2.6 (creep; pp 9-10)), held in the local reference library — see
> [[Reference library]]. This note is a paraphrased working aid, not the
> document. Values, clauses and criteria must be read from the source before
> they are relied on, and engineering conclusions need qualified review.

**Outcome.** A durability grading of sandstone for breakwater, cladding or dimension-stone applications based on sodium sulphate soundness loss, cross-checked against wet/dry strength ratio and expansive clay content.

## Inputs

- Sodium sulphate soundness test results (e.g. 15 cycles in 14% solution per AS/NZS 4456.10)
- Wet and dry UCS for the same stone (wet/dry ratio)
- Methylene blue adsorption / expansive clay mineral content where available
- Intended exposure (marine, aggressive, domestic, restoration)

## Procedure

1. Run the sodium sulphate soundness test as the primary index of physico-chemical breakdown resistance; the Maritime Services Board breakwater study found it the most useful discriminator.
2. Grade dimension stone per Spry (2000): A grade under 1% loss (restoration, thin cladding, aggressive environments), B grade 1-4% (high-grade construction), C grade 5-9% (domestic), D grade over 10% (less aggressive, less critical uses).
3. Cross-check with the wet/dry strength ratio, which correlates with sulphate loss, and with methylene blue adsorption as an index of expansive clay content.
4. Note that the ISRM slake durability test proved insufficiently severe to discriminate between these sandstones; do not rely on it alone.
5. For sustained high load ratios, consider creep and static-fatigue behaviour: strength decreases with log time-to-failure, and model footings loaded at 85-90% of ultimate showed time-dependent failures.

## Decision rules

- Low saturated strength combined with high sulphate loss flags unsatisfactory field performance (the exposed Botany Bay case: ~6 MPa saturated UCS with very high loss failed in service).
- Porosity strongly influences dimension-stone performance; measure it under standard conditions (ASTM C97 approach).

## Checks

- Test method and cycle count recorded with every soundness result.
- Grading matched to actual exposure aggressiveness.

## Common errors

- Substituting slake durability for sulphate soundness in these sandstones.
- Grading on dry strength while the service condition is saturated.
- Ignoring long-term creep at high sustained stress ratios.

## Caveats

- Grading thresholds come from a dimension-stone context; adapt with judgement for other applications.
- Design reference only: gradings and thresholds must be verified against the source and reviewed by a qualified engineer before use.

## Standards cited

AS/NZS 4456.10 sodium sulphate soundness, ASTM C97 (porosity/absorption of dimension stone), ISRM slake durability method (noted as insufficiently severe here)

Run the sodium sulphate soundness test as the primary index of physico chemical breakdown resistance; the Maritime Services Board breakwater study found it the most useful discriminator. 2. Grade dimension stone per Spry (2000): A grade under 1% loss (restoration, thin cladding, aggressive environments), B grade 1 4% (high grade construction), C grade 5 9% (domestic), D grade over 10% (less aggressive, less critical uses). 3. Cross check with the wet/dry strength ratio, which correlates with sulphate loss, and with methylene blue adsorption as an index of expansive clay content. 4. Note that the ISRM slake durability test proved insufficiently severe to discriminate between these sandstones; do not rely on it alone. 5. For sustained high load ratios, consider creep and static fatigue behaviour: strength decreases with log time to failure, and model footings loaded at 85 90% of ultimate showed time dependent failures. Decision rules Low saturated strength combined with high sulphate loss flags unsatisfactory field performance (the exposed Botany Bay case: ~6 MPa saturated UCS with very high loss failed in service). Porosity strongly influences dimension stone performance; measure it under standard conditions (ASTM C97 approach). Checks Test method and cycle count recorded with every soundness result. Grading matched to actual exposure aggressiveness. Common errors Substituting slake durability for sulphate soundness in these sandstones. Grading on dry strength while the service condition is saturated. Ignoring long term creep at high sustained stress ratios. Caveats Grading thresholds come from a dimension stone context; adapt with judgement for other applications. Design reference only: gradings and thresholds must be verified against the source and reviewed by a qualified engineer before use. Standards cited AS/NZS 4456.10 sodium sulphate soundness, ASTM C97 (porosity/absorption of dimension stone), ISRM slake durability method (noted as insufficiently severe here) Related Rock strength classes Borehole log conventions Library salinity and sodic soils Skills

notes.title: Screen laboratory and field soil results against published typical ranges before design use
notes.body:
# Screen laboratory and field soil results against published typical ranges before design use

> **Source:** `Correlations of Soil Properties.pdf` (Carter & Bentley (1991), whole-book pointer; typical-value tables within each property chapter), held in the local reference library — see
> [[Reference library]]. This note is a paraphrased working aid, not the
> document. Values, clauses and criteria must be read from the source before
> they are relied on, and engineering conclusions need qualified review.

**Outcome.** Early detection of implausible test results or data gaps by comparing site values with the typical property ranges per soil class compiled in Carter & Bentley.

## Inputs

- Site laboratory/field results (densities, permeabilities, strengths, compressibility indices, CBR, swelling indices)
- Soil classifications for the tested samples
- Carter & Bentley typical-value tables for the corresponding soil classes

## Procedure

1. Classify each tested sample and identify the corresponding typical range in the book's property chapters (density, permeability/grading, consolidation, shear strength, CBR, shrink/swell).
2. Flag any site result falling well outside the published range for its class and investigate (test error, misclassification, or genuinely unusual material).
3. Use the ranges to fill gaps only for preliminary design or small projects, marking such values as estimates.
4. Where frost susceptibility or swelling potential cannot be measured directly, use the book's indirect correlations as screening indicators only.

## Decision rules

- An out-of-range result is a trigger for investigation, not automatic rejection.
- Never let range-derived estimates govern final design of significant structures without confirmatory testing.

## Checks

- Classification of the sample confirmed before the range comparison.
- Screening outcomes documented in the ground model.

## Common errors

- Comparing results against ranges for the wrong classification system (USCS vs AASHTO tables differ).
- Treating typical ranges as statistical bounds rather than indicative spreads.

## Caveats

- OCR of this excerpt is largely unreadable; chapter identification is from headings only and all content must be taken from the printed book.
- Design reference only: verification against the source and qualified review are required before use.

## Standards cited

USCS and AASHTO classification systems (covered in the book's Chapters 1-2)

notes.title: Screen trenchless crossing for authority review
notes.body:
# Screen trenchless crossing for authority review

> **Source:** `TS 02088_0.00_Trenchless Excavation within the easement of Roads and Maritime infrastrucutre.pdf` (Scope and Figure 1 (issued as GTD 2018 002, 25 July 2018)), held in the local reference library — see
> [[Reference library]]. This note is a paraphrased working aid, not the
> document. Values, clauses and criteria must be read from the source before
> they are relied on, and engineering conclusions need qualified review.

**Outcome.** A quick, defensible decision on whether a proposed trenchless under-road crossing needs formal roads-authority review.

## Inputs

- Proposed bore diameter
- Effective ground cover from road surface to obvert
- Ground quality along the alignment (consistency/density, presence and thickness of bedrock)
- Proximity to bridges, retaining walls or other major infrastructure

## Procedure

1. Confirm the crossing is within the covered scope (diameters up to 1.2 m using cased auger boring, microtunnelling, pipe jacking or HDD); larger bores require direct contact with the authority.
2. Apply the screening flowchart: reject proposals with insufficient minimum cover outright; then branch on ground quality, diameter and cover-to-diameter ratios.
3. Where any asset such as a bridge or retaining wall could be affected, refer for review regardless of screening outcome.

## Decision rules

- Effective ground cover below 1.5 m is not acceptable at all (TS 02088 Figure 1).
- In stiff/medium-dense-or-better ground: diameter up to 250 mm passes without review; larger diameters pass if cover is at least 7 diameters including at least 2 diameters of bedrock, or at least 10 diameters of cover (TS 02088 Figure 1).
- Ground softer/looser than stiff/medium dense: review is required (with the 10-diameter cover branch as the only exemption path) (TS 02088 Figure 1).
- Crossings affecting bridges, retaining walls or major infrastructure are assessed case-by-case regardless (TS 02088 screening section).

## Checks

- Ground quality claim is backed by boreholes/test pits at entry, exit and at most 30 m spacing.
- Cover measured to the excavation obvert, not the pipe crown after lining.

## Common errors

- Screening on pipe diameter rather than excavation diameter.
- Assuming the screening exemption removes the need to meet the technical requirements (loads, settlement limits, geometry) - it only removes the review step.

## Caveats

- Verify the direction is still current under TfNSW; review dates have passed since issue.
- Authority concurrence conditions and contract documents override.

## Standards cited

AS 1726, AS 5100, AS/NZS 2566.1, ASTT trenchless guidelines

## Related

notes.title: Select a rock excavation method (dig, rip or blast) from a strength-spacing chart
notes.body:
# Select a rock excavation method (dig, rip or blast) from a strength-spacing chart

> **Source:** [YouTube — How to Choose Rock Excavation Methods — Digging, Ripping or Blasting](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=9W1vB1dhc5w&t=0s) (00:00-04:34). A YouTube lecture — learning
> material, not an approved design procedure. Equations and numbers were
> heard through auto-captions; read them off the video before use, and
> verify anything design-relevant against the standard and the project
> specification. Engineering conclusions need qualified review.

**Outcome.** The most economical open-excavation method for a rock mass, chosen from point load strength and discontinuity spacing

## Inputs

- Unconfined compressive strength (or point load index directly)
- Discontinuity frequency from field mapping (joints per metre)
- Excavation assessment chart with digging / ripping / blasting zones plotted on point load index vs discontinuity spacing axes

## Procedure

1. Map discontinuities on site and count joints per metre; compute average spacing as the reciprocal (example: 8 joints per metre gives 0.125 m)
2. Convert UCS to point load index using the general correlation UCS = 24 times point load index unless a rock-specific correlation exists (example: 60 MPa / 24 = 2.5 MPa)
3. Plot the point (point load index, spacing) on the chart
4. Read the zone the point falls in: digging (cheapest), ripping (intermediate cost and plant), or blasting (hardest, most technical and costly); zone labels also guide equipment choice (example fell in easy ripping)

## Decision rules

- Prefer a site- or rock-specific UCS to point-load correlation over the general factor of 24 when one has been established
- Method cost and complexity escalate from digging to ripping to blasting — the chart zone drives plant selection and project cost planning

## Checks

- Verify axis scales (both often logarithmic) before plotting
- Confirm the spacing used is an average from mapping, not a single measurement

## Common errors

- Plotting UCS directly on a point load index axis without converting
- Inverting the spacing (using joints per metre instead of metres per joint)

## Caveats

- YouTube lecture — learning material, not an approved design procedure; verify against project specification and current standards
- The chart and its zone boundaries are shown on screen — read from the video

## Standards cited

None cited in the source passage.

## Related

- [[Rock strength classes]]
- [[Skills]]

notes.title: Select a soil parameter correlation and record its provenance using Carter and Bentley
notes.body:
# Select a soil parameter correlation and record its provenance using Carter and Bentley

> **Source:** `Correlations of Soil Properties.pdf` (Carter & Bentley (1991), whole-book pointer; consult the chapter for the relevant property family), held in the local reference library — see
> [[Reference library]]. This note is a paraphrased working aid, not the
> document. Values, clauses and criteria must be read from the source before
> they are relied on, and engineering conclusions need qualified review.

**Outcome.** A defensible preliminary soil parameter chosen from the Carter & Bentley compendium, with its class basis, applicability limits and citation documented, and with the value explicitly flagged as an estimate pending testing.

## Inputs

- Soil classification data (grading, Atterberg limits, USCS/AASHTO class)
- The target parameter (e.g. density, permeability, compressibility, shear strength, CBR, swelling potential)
- Carter & Bentley, Correlations of Soil Properties (Pentech Press, 1991)

## Procedure

1. Locate the chapter covering the target parameter (the book is organised by property family: classification systems; natural and compacted density; permeability and grading; consolidation and settlement; shear strength; California Bearing Ratio; shrinkage and swelling).
2. Check the stated region of applicability of the candidate correlation (soil type, plasticity range, stress state) before adopting it.
3. Take typical values or correlation outputs as preliminary estimates only; the authors state such predictions can never substitute for proper testing.
4. Record the exact table/figure, page and edition alongside the adopted value, plus the classification inputs used.
5. Plan confirmation testing for any parameter that ends up governing design.

## Decision rules

- Prefer correlations tied to classification tests actually performed for the site over generic typical-value tables.
- Where two correlations disagree materially, carry the range forward rather than picking the favourable end.

## Checks

- Correlation applicability limits verified against the site soils.
- Every correlation-derived value distinguishable from measured values in the design record.

## Common errors

- Using typical-value tables outside the soil class they describe.
- Letting a correlation-derived parameter silently become a 'measured' value in later reports.
- Skipping confirmation testing on design-governing parameters.

## Caveats

- The OCR of this excerpt is heavily garbled (large sections mirrored/scrambled), so no numeric content from the extract should be trusted; use the printed book.
- Design reference only: any adopted value requires verification against the source tables and qualified review before use.

## Standards cited

BS/ASTM classification test methods referenced within the book

notes.title: Select an axial design method for a rock socket: elastic, side-slip, or non-linear
notes.body:
# Select an axial design method for a rock socket: elastic, side-slip, or non-linear

> **Source:** `The Design Of Socketed Piles In Rock by pells.pdf` (Pells, 8th ANZ Geomechanics Conf, Hobart 1999, pp 1-307 to 1-314; Sections 3-4 and 6 intro; ROCKET comparison Figures 5-7 and Table 2), held in the local reference library — see
> [[Reference library]]. This note is a paraphrased working aid, not the
> document. Values, clauses and criteria must be read from the source before
> they are relied on, and engineering conclusions need qualified review.

**Outcome.** A justified choice among the three accepted socket design families (elastic; Rowe & Armitage side-slip; non-linear/ROCKET-type), matched to construction quality, data availability and whether sidewall slip may be mobilised.

## Inputs

- Rock mass moduli adjacent to sidewall and beneath base (Es, Eb)
- Average UCS at sidewall and base
- Sidewall roughness class and cleanliness assurance
- For fundamental-parameter methods: the 8 ROCKET inputs (rock c and phi, residual friction, diameter, mass modulus, Poisson's ratio, roughness geometry, initial normal stress)

## Procedure

1. Confirm the three prerequisites of all modern methods: equivalent Young's moduli, average UCS, and sidewall roughness knowledge.
2. If sidewall slip is not to be mobilised (or end-bearing capacity is uncertain), use the conservative elastic method.
3. If slip may be mobilised with assured cleanliness and R2+ roughness, use the Rowe & Armitage chart method - the author's recommended state of practice - or the equivalent Carter & Kulhawy closed-form equations.
4. Consider non-linear fundamental-parameter analysis (ROCKET, successor to the Williams method) only with good knowledge of all 8 input parameters and their sensitivities; the program was primarily calibrated on Melbourne Mudstone and gave mixed first-pass predictions even in well-characterised Hawkesbury Sandstone.
5. For roughness-based computations, use the asperity angle at a chord length of about twice the design displacement (e.g. ~20 mm chords for 10 mm displacement).
6. Cross-check: in a reviewed Sydney CBD socket, Rowe & Armitage, Carter & Kulhawy and ROCKET gave practically identical settlements (6-10 mm), while the elastic method demanded double the socket length.

## Decision rules

- Sockets needing base resistance require full sidewall slip; all the safety margin then sits in end bearing.
- R2 or better roughness is required for the non-brittle (elasto-plastic) sidewall assumption underpinning the slip methods.
- Without confidence in the 8 fundamental parameters, chart-based methods give a better 'feel' and are quicker for design.

## Checks

- Same mass modulus basis used consistently across side shear, settlement and load-sharing calculations.
- ROCKET results checked for its computational truncation quirks (displacement capped at half the roughness chord length; chord lengths limited to 10% of diameter).

## Common errors

- Treating ROCKET as broadly calibrated outside Melbourne-mudstone-like materials.
- Using slip-based designs where construction QC of cleanliness is not assured.
- Reading shear resistance from asperity data at the wrong chord length.

## Caveats

- Reflects 1999 state of practice; check subsequent literature for ROCKET calibration progress.
- Design reference only: the method choice and parameters must be verified against the source and reviewed by a qualified engineer before use.

## Standards cited

Rowe & Armitage (1984); Carter & Kulhawy (1987); Seidel & Haberfield (1995/1999), AS 2159-1995

## Related

- [[AS 2159 piling]]
- [[Rock strength classes]]

notes.title: Select and interpret soil tests for water movement and corrosivity
notes.body:
# Select and interpret soil tests for water movement and corrosivity

> **Source:** `booklet3siteinvestigationsforurbansalinity (2).pdf` (Phase 2 'Soil Tests for Urban Salinity' pp. 9-10; Phase 3 interpretation pp. 13-14; Appendices 2-3 pp. 22-25), held in the local reference library — see
> [[Reference library]]. This note is a paraphrased working aid, not the
> document. Values, clauses and criteria must be read from the source before
> they are relied on, and engineering conclusions need qualified review.

**Outcome.** A test suite and interpretation that establishes how water (and therefore salt) moves through the site and how aggressive the soil/groundwater will be to concrete and steel.

## Inputs

- Representative soil samples per horizon/landform unit and groundwater samples
- Lab capability for permeability, CEC, ESP, Emerson class, sulphate, pH, chloride, resistivity and EC
- AS 2159 durability tables (and DIN 4030 if magnesium/ammonium are of interest)

## Procedure

1. Run the water-movement suite: permeability (controlled by texture, structure, compaction, sodicity, impermeable layers), cation exchange capacity (needed to compute sodicity), sodicity as ESP = exchangeable Na / CEC x 100, and dispersibility by the Emerson aggregate test (AS 1289.3.8.1-1997).
2. Run the corrosivity suite: sulphate (report as % by weight of soil for direct comparison with AS 2159), soil pH (AS 1289.4.3.1-1997), chloride (report as ppm or mg/L in water for AS 2159 comparison), and resistivity in ohm.cm (AS 1289.4.4.1-1997) for steel corrosion.
3. Interpret sodicity against ESP bands used in the booklet: below 5 non-sodic, 5-15 sodic, above 15 highly sodic (p. 14); consider depth and thickness of sodic layers, not just presence.
4. Interpret Emerson classes: classes 1-2 prone to tunnelling erosion; class 3 stable and water-holding when compacted; classes 4-6 highly aggregated and poor at holding water even compacted; classes 7-8 non-slaking, split on swelling.
5. Compare corrosivity results with AS 2159 exposure classification tables, DIN 4030 limits (which add carbonic acid, ammonium and magnesium in mg/L), and manufacturers' specifications.
6. Note that AS 2159 flags (without quantifying) that magnesium and ammonium ions increase sulphate aggressiveness on concrete — use DIN 4030 only as a guide since it reflects German soils and practice.

## Decision rules

- AS 2159 distinguishes soil condition classes: (A) high-permeability soils below groundwater vs (B) low-permeability soils and all soils above groundwater; in urban settings where leaks and perched water tables can raise groundwater, the precautionary path is to adopt the more conservative condition-A classification.
- Where water flow can be concentrated (through-flow layers, pale-coloured horizons), expect concentrated salt — corrosivity sampling should target these zones.
- Salinity (EC) itself is not a corrosivity parameter in this framework; use it for landscaping/plant tolerance decisions and use sulphate/pH/chloride/resistivity for aggressivity.

## Checks

- Units match the comparison standard exactly: sulphate as % soil weight, chloride as ppm or mg/L, resistivity as ohm.cm — otherwise the AS 2159 tables cannot be applied directly.
- EC results labelled as EC1:5, EC1:2 or ECe with conversion factors stated.
- Dispersibility considered alongside sodicity: low-sodium soils with poor structure and low organic matter can still be highly dispersive.

## Common errors

- Comparing raw EC1:5 against ECe-based criteria (underestimates salinity by roughly a texture factor of 14 for sandy loam to 6 for heavy clay).
- Assuming compacted wet dispersive fill will hold water regardless of Emerson class (classes 4-6 do not).
- Ignoring magnesium/ammonium when sulphate is present.
- Treating an arbitrary ECe threshold as a building-damage predictor — damage depends on salt type, water supply and wetting/drying cycles.

## Caveats

- Classification and aggressivity calls must be verified against the current editions of AS 2159/AS 3600 and the project specification — the booklet's extracts reference superseded editions.

notes.text: Select and interpret soil tests for water movement and corrosivity Source: booklet3siteinvestigationsforurbansalinity (2).pdf (Phase 2 'Soil Tests for Urban Salinity' pp. 9 10; Phase 3 interpretation pp. 13 14; Appendices 2 3 pp. 22 25), held in the local reference library — see Reference library. This note is a paraphrased working aid, not the document. Values, clauses and criteria must be read from the source before they are relied on, and engineering conclusions need qualified review. Outcome. A test suite and interpretation that establishes how water (and therefore salt) moves through the site and how aggressive the soil/groundwater will be to concrete and steel. Inputs Representative soil samples per horizon/landform unit and groundwater samples Lab capability for permeability, CEC, ESP, Emerson class, sulphate, pH, chloride, resistivity and EC AS 2159 durability tables (and DIN 4030 if magnesium/ammonium are of interest) Procedure 1. Run the water movement suite: permeability (controlled by texture, structure, compaction, sodicity, impermeable layers), cation exchange capacity (needed to compute sodicity), sodicity as ESP = exchangeable Na / CEC x 100, and dispersibility by the Emerson aggregate test (AS 1289.3.8.1 1997). 2. Run the corrosivity suite: sulphate (report as % by weight of soil for direct comparison with AS 2159), soil pH (AS 1289.4.3.1 1997), chloride (report as ppm or mg/L in water for AS 2159 comparison), and resistivity in ohm.cm (AS 1289.4.4.1 1997) for steel corrosion. 3. Interpret sodicity against ESP bands used in the booklet: below 5 non sodic, 5 15 sodic, above 15 highly sodic (p. 14); consider depth and thickness of sodic layers, not just presence. 4. Interpret Emerson classes: classes 1 2 prone to tunnelling erosion; class 3 stable and water holding when compacted; classes 4 6 highly aggregated and poor at holding water even compacted; classes 7 8 non slaking, split on swelling. 5. Compare corrosivity results with AS 2159 exposure classification tables, DIN 4030 limits (which add carbonic acid, ammonium and magnesium in mg/L), and manufacturers' specifications. 6. Note that AS 2159 flags (without quantifying) that magnesium and ammonium ions increase sulphate aggressiveness on concrete — use DIN 4030 only as a guide since it reflects German soils and practice. Decision rules AS 2159 distinguishes soil condition classes: (A) high permeability soils below groundwater vs (B) low permeability soils and all soils above groundwater; in urban settings where leaks and perched water tables can raise groundwater, the precautionary path is to adopt the more conservative condition A classification. Where water flow can be concentrated (through flow layers, pale coloured horizons), expect concentrated salt — corrosivity sampling should target these zones. Salinity (EC) itself is not a corrosivity parameter in this framework; use it for landscaping/plant tolerance decisions and use sulphate/pH/chloride/resistivity for aggressivity. Checks Units match the comparison standard exactly: sulphate as % soil weight, chloride as ppm or mg/L, resistivity as ohm.cm — otherwise the AS 2159 tables cannot be applied directly. EC results labelled as EC1:5, EC1:2 or ECe with conversion factors stated. Dispersibility considered alongside sodicity: low sodium soils with poor structure and low organic matter can still be highly dispersive. Common errors Comparing raw EC1:5 against ECe based criteria (underestimates salinity by roughly a texture factor of 14 for sandy loam to 6 for heavy clay). Assuming compacted wet dispersive fill will hold water regardless of Emerson class (classes 4 6 do not). Ignoring magnesium/ammonium when sulphate is present. Treating an arbitrary ECe threshold as a building damage predictor — damage depends on salt type, water supply and wetting/drying cycles. Caveats Classification and aggressivity calls must be verified against the current editions of AS 2159/AS 3600 and the project specification — the booklet's extracts reference superseded editions. ESP banding (5/15) is one example scheme; other rating schemes exist. DIN 4030 limits are for mainly natural waters under German conditions — guide only. notes.title: Select class-based end bearing, shaft adhesion and modulus design values for Sydney sandstone and shale
notes.body:
# Select class-based end bearing, shaft adhesion and modulus design values for Sydney sandstone and shale

> **Source:** `Pells Paper on Foundations on sandstone and shale in The Sydney Region.pdf` (Section 4.3 and Tables 5a-5b (pp 23-25); boundary footing guidance p 24), held in the local reference library — see
> [[Reference library]]. This note is a paraphrased working aid, not the
> document. Values, clauses and criteria must be read from the source before
> they are relied on, and engineering conclusions need qualified review.

**Outcome.** Ultimate and serviceability end-bearing pressures, ultimate shaft adhesion and typical mass modulus chosen by rock class for limit state design of pads and sockets, with boundary-footing adjustments where needed.

## Inputs

- Rock class (I-V) established by the three-criteria classification
- Substance UCS (several serviceability entries are expressed as 0.5 x qu with class caps)
- Footing/socket geometry and proximity to property boundaries or excavations
- Confirmation of clean sockets with roughness R2 or better where shaft adhesion is used

## Procedure

1. Classify the rock, then read ultimate end bearing, serviceability end bearing (pressure for settlement under 1% of minimum footing dimension), ultimate shaft adhesion, and typical mass modulus from Table 5a (sandstone) or 5b (shale) on pp 24-25 of the paper; do not quote values from memory.
2. Note the table footnotes: ultimate end-bearing values occur only at large settlements (over ~5% of minimum footing dimension); adhesion values presume clean R2+ sockets, and shale values may need reduction for smear.
3. Use ultimate values only within a limit state check with the recommended geotechnical reduction factors; use serviceability values for settlement-governed sizing.
4. For footings near property boundaries where uniform settlement is desired, reduce boundary-footing pressure to about 60% of that for remote footings (boundary footing defined by centre-to-boundary distance less than the footing width normal to the boundary).
5. Where an adjacent excavation exists below footing level, check kinematic failure of joint-bounded blocks; in the Sydney CBD the dominant joint set strikes NNE dipping 65-90 degrees, making N-S faces particularly prone.

## Decision rules

- End bearing is usually settlement-controlled, so arbitrary nominal boundary reductions are illogical; use the settlement-equalising 60% guideline or explicit analysis.
- Pick modulus within the class range according to whether the rock sits at the upper or lower bound of the class.

## Checks

- Class assignment satisfies all three criteria (strength, defect spacing, seams).
- Load-displacement linearity assumption valid up to the serviceability values used.
- Adhesion only claimed where inspection confirms cleanliness and roughness.

## Common errors

- Using ultimate end-bearing values at working-load settlements.
- Applying sandstone adhesion values to smeared shale sockets.
- Ignoring kinematic block failure next to deep excavations.

## Caveats

- Table values in the OCR contain obvious character corruption; always read the numbers from the published tables, not this extract.
- Design reference only: values must be verified against the source tables and reviewed by a qualified engineer before use.

## Standards cited

AS 2159-1995 (piling, limit state), NSW Ordinance 70 (superseded practice discussed for context)

## Related

- [[AS 2159 piling]]
- [[Weathered siltstone]]
- [[Rock strength classes]]

- [[Soil description order]]
