notes.title: Select, document and maintain landslide risk mitigation measures (AGS 2007)
notes.body:
# Select, document and maintain landslide risk mitigation measures (AGS 2007)

> **Source:** `42_1_4_amend.pdf` (AGS Practice Note 2007, Sections 9-10, Appendices D and G), held in the local reference library — see
> [[Reference library]]. This note is a paraphrased working aid, not the
> document. Values, clauses and criteria must be read from the source before
> they are relied on, and engineering conclusions need qualified review.

**Outcome.** A mitigation plan that brings landslide risk to tolerable levels, with design life, maintenance regime, responsibilities and reporting that satisfy AGS 2007 minimum standards and survive regulator scrutiny.

## Inputs

- Completed risk estimation with hazards exceeding tolerable criteria identified
- Development proposal and constraints; regulator approval conditions
- Applicable design-life expectations (e.g. AS 2870, AS 4678, AS 3600 ranges — Section 9.3.1)

## Procedure

1. Identify feasible options per hazard and quantify the residual risk of each: accept (only if tolerable), avoid (relocate/redesign/abandon), reduce frequency (re-profile, surface and subsurface drainage, retaining/anchored structures), reduce consequence (defensive works such as catch fences, relocation), manage (monitoring and warning systems with workable response time), transfer (insurance/other authority), or postpone pending better data (Section 9.1.1).
2. Prefer engineered, robust options that reduce uncertainty; apply ALARP within the tolerable band and adopt cheap risk reductions even below tolerable where practicable (Section 9.1.2).
3. Detail the adopted measures in a mitigation plan: stakeholder responsibilities, costs, programme, inspection regime, performance measures, and an emergency plan with defined trigger levels and actions where monitoring is relied on (Section 9.1.3).
4. Specify site-specific development conditions split across detailed design, construction (sequencing, temporary works) and maintenance stages, sufficient to allow later certification (Section 9.2).
5. State design life on the drawings; where a component's effective performance life (e.g. timber crib walls, subsoil drains, stressed anchors) is shorter, prescribe an inspection/repair/replacement regime to bridge the gap (Section 9.3).
6. Establish the maintenance plan and make it durable — register mitigation/maintenance obligations on the land title so future owners inherit them (Sections 9.1.3, 9.4.3).
7. Report to the Section 10 standard: data sources, methods and limitations, scaled plan and sections, factual logs, past-performance evidence, hazard-by-hazard likelihoods, and transparent logic from data to conclusion; use the Appendix D forms where the regulator requires them.
8. Monitor and review risk during option assessment, implementation and ongoing operation; reassess when new data emerges (Section 9.1.4).

## Decision rules

- Risk cannot be removed, only reduced — if no option reaches tolerable levels, development should not proceed or must be radically conditioned.
- Monitoring/warning counts as consequence reduction only when the warning-to-action time is realistically sufficient.
- Postponement means the risk is being temporarily accepted — permissible only where further investigation will genuinely improve the assessment.
- Owner (and successors) hold responsibility for maintaining mitigation measures; the practitioner confirms approval conditions are fulfilled.

## Checks

- Residual risk after mitigation recalculated and shown to meet the criteria — not asserted.
- Design life stated on drawings; shortfall components covered by an explicit maintenance regime.
- Mitigation plan reviewed for workability; land-title annotation or equivalent enforcement mechanism in place.

## Common errors

- Recommending measures without recomputing residual risk.
- Emergency/monitoring plans with warning times too short for evacuation or response.
- Maintenance obligations that die with the first owner because nothing was registered on title.
- Treating LRM as a documentation exercise rather than designed, constructed and maintained works.

## Caveats

- Design-life figures quoted are pointers to Section 9.3.1 and the underlying codes — verify current code editions.
- Regulator-specific policies may impose stricter conditions than the Practice Note.

## Standards cited

AS 4678 (earth retaining structures), AS 2870 (residential slabs and footings), AS 3600 (concrete), AGS 2007e GeoGuides (maintenance and record keeping)

## Related

- [[AS 2870 residential site classification]]
- [[Library - RMS and TfNSW specifications]]
- [[Skills]]

notes.title: Select field density test method by oversize
notes.body:
# Select field density test method by oversize

> **Source:** `b030.pdf` (Clauses 6.4.1 and 6.4.3, Table B30.5), held in the local reference library — see
> [[Reference library]]. This note is a paraphrased working aid, not the
> document. Values, clauses and criteria must be read from the source before
> they are relied on, and engineering conclusions need qualified review.

**Outcome.** A valid in-situ density / relative compaction result using the test method appropriate to the material's oversize fraction and layer thickness.

## Inputs

- Percentage by mass retained on the 37.5 mm sieve for the fill
- Layer thickness
- Material type (cohesive, cohesionless, one-size or gap-graded)

## Procedure

1. Determine the oversize fraction retained on the 37.5 mm sieve for the lot.
2. Choose the density method from the applicability table: nuclear gauge or sand replacement for low-oversize material; sand replacement only for moderate oversize; fixed-volume extractive method for fine-medium cohesionless, one-size or gap-graded materials.
3. Compute relative compaction per the ratio test method and report the characteristic value per the quality-system spec.

## Decision rules

- Oversize <= 20%: nuclear gauge or sand replacement permitted; 20-40%: sand replacement only (no nuclear gauge); > 40%: relative compaction is invalid - report only the oversize percentage (b030 Table B30.5).
- Do not use the nuclear gauge where layer thickness exceeds 300 mm (b030 Clause 6.4.3).

## Checks

- Field moisture methods T121/T180 only used after correlation against the oven method for the materials being compacted.
- Results rounded to nearest 0.1% and characteristic value computed per RMS Q.

## Common errors

- Reporting a relative compaction number for material with more than 40% oversize.
- Nuclear gauge probe depths mismatched to layer thickness.
- Using an uncorrelated rapid moisture method.

## Caveats

- Verify edition currency; the same logic appears in other RMS earthworks specs but limits must be confirmed per contract.
- Contract documents override.

## Standards cited

RMS T119, RMS T165, RMS T166, RMS T173, RMS Q

## Related

- [[Library - RMS and TfNSW specifications]]
- [[Skills]]

notes.title: Select geotextile strength and filtration class
notes.body:
# Select geotextile strength and filtration class

> **Source:** `RMS Spec D & C R63.pdf` (Clauses 2.1-2.2, 4.1 and Annexure R63/E (Ed 2 / Rev 0, May 2013)), held in the local reference library — see
> [[Reference library]]. This note is a paraphrased working aid, not the
> document. Values, clauses and criteria must be read from the source before
> they are relied on, and engineering conclusions need qualified review.

**Outcome.** The correct geotextile strength class and filtration class for a separation/filtration application, matched to fill size, subgrade strength and soil fines.

## Inputs

- Application category (separation under embankments unsaturated/saturated, trench/edge drains, drainage behind structures, under rock revetment)
- Nominal maximum stone size D90 of the fill or revetment
- Subgrade CBR and saturation state
- Site soil grading (D15, D50, coefficient of uniformity, fines content)

## Procedure

1. Classify the application into the specification's category system (G1-G5).
2. Pick the strength class (A-E) from the application table using fill D90 and, for drains/drainage layers, depth or subgrade CBR; saturated/soft-ground applications demand higher classes for the same stone size.
3. Pick filtration requirements (equivalent opening size, permittivity, flow rate) from the soil-type columns based on the fines fraction and permeability of the site soil.
4. Confirm survivability considering subgrade condition, fill particle size and construction/placement process, not just the table lookup.

## Decision rules

- Strength class escalates with larger D90 and weaker/saturated subgrades; some large-stone saturated cases are simply not permitted with any class (RMS Spec D&C R63 Annexure R63/E Table E.1 notes).
- Filtration EOS ceilings tighten as soil fines increase (finer soils need smaller opening sizes) with matching minimum flow/permittivity values (Annexure R63/E Table E.1).
- UV stability requires at least 50% retained strength after 500 hours exposure testing (Clause 2.1.3).

## Checks

- Application-specific site details (D90, CBR, soil type) recorded in the project annexure table.
- High-strength basal reinforcement under embankments on soft ground is outside this spec - use the appropriate reinforcement spec.

## Common errors

- Selecting on strength alone and ending up with an opening size that clogs or pipes in fine soils.
- Using the unsaturated-ground category for a working platform on soft saturated subgrade.
- Applying this separation/filtration spec to reinforcement functions.

## Caveats

- Verify edition currency; the D&C variant mirrors base spec R63 Ed 4.
- Project deed documents and design drawings override.

## Standards cited

AS 3706 series, AS 1289.3.6.1

notes.title: Select layered rockfall protection measures for a rock slope
notes.body:
# Select layered rockfall protection measures for a rock slope

> **Source:** [YouTube — How to Protect Slopes from Rock Falls — Effective and Inexpensive Methods](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ZD7aTftDZn4&t=0s) (00:00-09:33). A YouTube lecture — learning
> material, not an approved design procedure. Equations and numbers were
> heard through auto-captions; read them off the video before use, and
> verify anything design-relevant against the standard and the project
> specification. Engineering conclusions need qualified review.

**Outcome.** A practical, cost-conscious combination of scaling, benches, fence or barrier, ditch and drapery mesh that contains future rockfalls on a loose-rock slope

## Inputs

- Site walkover observations: loose rocks at the crest, fallen rocks on benches and at the toe
- Presence and condition of existing benches
- Value and proximity of infrastructure at the toe (building, highway) that needs protection
- Typical falling-rock sizes, from inspection or simulation

## Procedure

1. Start with a site investigation / rockfall hazard assessment to map loose rocks at the crest, on benches, and at the toe
2. Scale the slope first: remove all loose rocks — presented as one of the most effective and cheapest measures, and standard practice before anything else
3. Assess existing benches as rock catchment; a bench that already holds fallen rocks is demonstrably working, with only some rocks bouncing over
4. Where rocks can still reach the toe, choose between a fence/barrier and a ditch depending on the importance of the infrastructure being protected and the budget; simulate fence performance in rockfall software if needed
5. Design the ditch width and depth from slope inclination and height (a separate design method), and use a gravel bed in the ditch to absorb kinetic energy so rocks cannot bounce out
6. Hang drapery mesh over source areas so falling rocks stay constrained against the face instead of bouncing outward; multiple mesh panels can cover separate source zones
7. Leave the bottom edge of drapery mesh open so contained rocks can fall through and accumulate on the bench or in the ditch for later cleanout

## Decision rules

- Scaling comes first on essentially any slope with rockfall potential
- Spend on high-capacity fencing only when large rock sizes or high-value infrastructure justify it; modest rock sizes may need only an inexpensive fence
- Never fix drapery mesh closed at the bottom: trapped rocks accumulate behind it, have nowhere to go, and progressively damage the mesh

## Checks

- After design, confirm each hazard path is addressed: crest sources (scaled/meshed), mid-slope trajectories (bench/mesh), toe run-out (fence, barrier or ditch)
- Plan periodic cleanout of benches and ditches as part of the scheme

## Common errors

- Installing barriers or mesh without scaling, leaving the loose-rock source in place
- Closing the drapery mesh at the toe, causing rock accumulation and mesh damage
- Omitting the gravel bed so rocks bounce out of the ditch

## Caveats

- YouTube lecture — learning material, not an approved design procedure; verify against project specification and current standards
- Ditch sizing and fence capacity design are only referenced, not derived, in this lecture — they need the companion methods or project-specific design

## Standards cited

None cited in the source passage.

notes.title: Select loading stages, plate size and reaction load for a plate load test
notes.body:
# Select loading stages, plate size and reaction load for a plate load test

> **Source:** `f69406cd-07d7-4d53-bf33-79a48c9c755b.pdf` (Single-sheet loading-stage table with footnotes), held in the local reference library — see
> [[Reference library]]. This note is a paraphrased working aid, not the
> document. Values, clauses and criteria must be read from the source before
> they are relied on, and engineering conclusions need qualified review.

**Outcome.** The engineer can pick the plate diameter and jack capacity that suit the target bearing pressure, set out a compliant six-stage loading schedule, and size the reaction weight.

## Inputs

- Required maximum normal stress for the test
- Available plates (300 / 600 / 762 mm) and jack capacity (100 kN, or non-standard 200 kN)
- Available reaction mass (truck, roller, excavator)

## Procedure

1. Check the plate/jack combination can reach the target stress: maximum bearing capacities are about 1.4 MPa for 300 mm/100 kN, 0.4 MPa for 600 mm/100 kN, 0.2 MPa for 762 mm/100 kN, and roughly double with a 200 kN jack (bottom table).
2. Adopt the recommended six-stage schedule for the chosen plate - e.g. 300 mm/100 kN: preload 0.010 then 0.080/0.160/0.250/0.330/0.420/0.500 MN/m2, held 30 s for preload and 60 s per stage; unload via 0.250 and 0.125 back to 0.010; reload through 0.080-0.420 MN/m2 for the second cycle.
3. Follow the DIN principle behind the table: at least 6 approximately equal increments to maximum stress, each load change completed within one minute, unloading in 3 stages to 50%, 25% and about 2% of maximum, and a second cycle taken only to the penultimate first-cycle stage (DIN18134-2012 clause 7.5.2, quoted in the sheet).
4. Convert between jack load and plate stress with the plate factor (kN per MN/m2): 70.68 for 300 mm, 282.76 for 600 mm, 456.05 for 762 mm.
5. Provide a reaction load at least 10 kN greater than the maximum test load (DIN18134-2012 clause 5.2); prefer unsprung reaction masses such as rollers or excavators, since a sprung truck lifting off its springs demands extra margin (Anix remark).

## Decision rules

- Larger plates suit weaker ground and lower target stresses; the 300 mm plate is needed for high-pressure verification.
- 200 kN devices fall outside DIN 18134 - their stage values are recommendations only.
- DIN itself fixes no stage list; the tabulated stages are a recommendation satisfying the standard's rules.

## Checks

- Maximum stage load plus 10 kN does not exceed the reaction mass available.
- Stage loads divided by the plate factor reproduce the intended stresses.

## Common errors

- Using a sprung truck with barely sufficient mass, so it lifts off its springs during peak load.
- Carrying the second cycle to full maximum load instead of stopping at the penultimate stage.

## Caveats

- The sheet itself stresses these stages are recommendations, not fixed by DIN 18134.
- Some tabulated loads (e.g. 762 mm column) imply stresses rounded to the nearest 0.005-0.01 MN/m2; use the factors for exact conversion.

## Standards cited

DIN 18134

## Related

- [[Library - plate load testing]]
- [[Skills]]

notes.title: Select rock mass and defect parameters for numerical modelling in Hawkesbury Sandstone and Sydney shale
notes.body:
# Select rock mass and defect parameters for numerical modelling in Hawkesbury Sandstone and Sydney shale

> **Source:** `substanceAndMassPropertiesForTheDesignOfEngineeringStructuresInTheHawkesburySandstone.pdf` (Sections 3.1-3.2 and Tables 10-11 (pp 10-12)), held in the local reference library — see
> [[Reference library]]. This note is a paraphrased working aid, not the
> document. Values, clauses and criteria must be read from the source before
> they are relied on, and engineering conclusions need qualified review.

**Outcome.** A parameter set (mass modulus, strength, permeability, GSI, defect normal and shear stiffness, defect friction) for numerical analysis of Sydney-region excavations, drawn from the Bertuzzi & Pells (2002) tables with data-provenance understood.

## Inputs

- Rock class or ground description (sandstone/shale, Class I/II through IV/V groupings)
- Defect descriptions: type (bedding, cross-bed parting, erosional plane, joint), infill thickness and nature
- Tables 10 (mass parameters) and 11 (discontinuity parameters) of the paper
- Any site-specific back-analysis or large-scale test data

## Procedure

1. Read class-grouped substance strength, substance modulus, unit weight, mass modulus, permeability (log-mean and range) and GSI from Table 10; use GSI with Hoek-Brown methods to derive stress-dependent c' and phi'.
2. For shale substance modulus, apply the moisture-dependent relationship attributed to Won (1985) given in the table notes.
3. Read defect friction angle and normal/shear stiffness by defect type and infill thickness from Table 11.
4. Where infill data exist, estimate defect normal stiffness kn from the infill modulus divided by infill thickness, and take shear stiffness ks as about 0.10 x kn at normal stresses above ~1 MPa (Bandis et al 1983) in the absence of specific data.
5. Prefer parameters back-figured from monitored excavations (deep basements, tunnel convergence, instrumented pile tests such as Glebe Island Bridge) over generic correlations; the sandstone mass modulus database is comparatively strong, the shale database weaker.

## Decision rules

- The foundation classification is a communication tool, not a design tool, for non-foundation works: tunnels, slopes and basements must be designed by applied mechanics with these parameters, not by class alone.
- Where kn/ks matter to results, run sensitivity analyses; the authors flag a paucity of data for these.

## Checks

- Adopted mass modulus consistent with field-measured benchmarks (e.g. ~800-1100 MPa for borderline Class III sandstone at Lucas Heights; ~1200 MPa Class III from the Glebe Island pile test).
- Elastic ks/kn expectation (0.33-0.5) recognised as unconservative relative to the observed ~0.1 recommendation.

## Common errors

- Treating Table 10/11 as consensus values; the authors state other practitioners may reasonably differ, especially on defect stiffness.
- Applying dry substance moduli where saturated behaviour governs.
- Using class-based parameters across dykes and faults.

## Caveats

- Table values in the OCR show alignment corruption; read parameters from the published tables.
- Design reference only: parameters must be verified against the source and reviewed by a qualified engineer before use.

## Standards cited

Hoek et al (1995) GSI / Hoek-Brown framework, Bertuzzi & Pells (2002) Geotechnical Parameters of Sydney Sandstone and Shale

## Related

- [[Weathered siltstone]]
- [[Rock strength classes]]
- [[Borehole log conventions]]
- [[Library - Pells papers on Sydney sandstone and shale]]
- [[Soil description order]]
- [[Skills]]

notes.title: Select surface treatments for pavements by salt content before sealing
notes.body:
# Select surface treatments for pavements by salt content before sealing

> **Source:** `Techniques-to-use-on-roads-affected-by-salinity.pdf` (Section 5.2-5.3.2 and Table 2, pp. 8-10), held in the local reference library — see
> [[Reference library]]. This note is a paraphrased working aid, not the
> document. Values, clauses and criteria must be read from the source before
> they are relied on, and engineering conclusions need qualified review.

**Outcome.** A seal/prime strategy chosen from measured salt content of pavement fines, preventing salt crystallisation from blistering and destroying thin bituminous surfacings.

## Inputs

- Base material samples for salt testing (fines fraction passing 2.36 mm)
- Salt content test capability (gravimetric on dried saturation extract; RTA Test Method T200 for chloride content of roadbase)
- Sealing options: prime, primerseal, final seal, asphalt, concrete

## Procedure

1. Suspect salt when a bituminous surface shows eruptions of small blisters; test the uppermost base material rather than assuming.
2. Determine salt content of the fines (% passing the 2.36 mm sieve, measured gravimetrically by drying the saturation extract) — note the criterion applies to fines, not the whole sample.
3. Apply the treatment ladder (after Januszke 1984, Table 2 of the paper, p. 9): roughly 0-1.5% salt, a prime is acceptable; about 1.6-2.5%, apply a primerseal followed as quickly as possible by the final seal; about 2.6-3.0%, a swept sacrificial primed surface then primerseal and final seal may work, otherwise treat as the highest band; above 3.0%, special investigation is required and no single method is assured.
4. For the mid band (<2.5%), the cited practice is a primerseal with size 10 aggregate and AMC4 primer binder at about 1.8 L/m2.
5. Specify low-salt aggregates and construction water for sealing work (cited RTA limits: ~600 ppm chloride, ~400 ppm sulphate maximums).
6. Prefer substantial seal treatments over light primes/primerseals in saline areas, since light treatments are the most salt-vulnerable; concrete and well-designed asphalt surfaces are generally the most salt-durable.

## Decision rules

- Light treatments (primes, primerseals) left exposed in saline conditions will distress — minimise the time between primerseal and final seal.
- If salt exceeds ~3% in fines, do not proceed on a standard method; investigate (source of salt, moisture regime) and trial treatments.
- Salt can also crystallise beneath seals over fine crushed rock bases, 'blowing up' the seal into potholes — treat promptly when blisters appear.

## Checks

- Salt content measured on the correct fraction (fines) and reported as % with method stated.
- Aggregate and water salt certificates reviewed before sealing.
- Post-sealing surveillance for blistering in the first seasons.

## Common errors

- Priming a salty base and losing the prime to crystallisation before sealing.
- Testing whole-sample salt content and comparing against fines-based thresholds.
- Attributing seal blisters to bitumen quality rather than underlying salt.

## Caveats

- Classification and aggressivity calls must be verified against the source document and the current road agency specification — thresholds derive from 1984 South Australian work and RTA-era methods that may have been updated.
- Salt content bands are for thin bituminous surfacings on unsealed/granular pavements; they do not size asphalt or concrete solutions.
- Companion (OCR-corrupted) source roads-and-salinity.pdf cites related limits work in Australian Road Research 20(4) 1990 — verify against a clean copy.

## Standards cited

RTA Test Method T200 Chloride Content of Roadbase (2002), RTA/Austroads sprayed sealing guides (2001-2003 era), Januszke & Booth (1984) Soluble Salt Damage to Sprayed Seals on the Stuart Highway, 12th ARRB Conference

## Related

- [[Library - salinity and sodic soils]]
- [[Library - RMS and TfNSW specifications]]
- [[Skills]]

notes.title: Select the correct field density test method for an R44 earthworks lot
notes.body:
# Select the correct field density test method for an R44 earthworks lot

> **Source:** `r044.pdf` (Clause 7.3, Table R44.9 (Ed 5 Rev 1)), held in the local reference library — see
> [[Reference library]]. This note is a paraphrased working aid, not the
> document. Values, clauses and criteria must be read from the source before
> they are relied on, and engineering conclusions need qualified review.

**Outcome.** The field density method matches the material's oversize content and layer thickness, so relative compaction results are valid and defensible.

## Inputs

- Particle size data - % by mass retained on the 37.5 mm AS sieve
- Material description (cohesive vs fine/medium cohesionless, gap graded)
- Layer thickness

## Procedure

1. Screen the material against Table R44.9: with low oversize (up to the first threshold) either nuclear gauge (T173) or sand replacement (T119) is allowed; in the intermediate oversize band only sand replacement is allowed; above the upper threshold report only the oversize percentage because relative compaction is invalid.
2. For fine to medium grained cohesionless, one-size or gap-graded materials, use the fixed volume extractive method (T165).
3. Reject nuclear gauge use where the layer exceeds 300 mm thickness (Clause 7.3.3).
4. At each location run the field density test and take a companion sample for laboratory maximum density and field moisture (T120 primary; T121/T180 only after correlation checks per Clause 7.3.5).
5. Apply the oversize correction to the laboratory maximum density per the nominated T105 appendix procedure and compute relative compaction via T166.

## Decision rules

- One test method per lot - choose before testing starts and do not mix (Clause 7.3.4).
- If oversize exceeds the upper Table R44.9 threshold, do not report relative compaction at all; the lot needs a procedure-based approach (e.g. rock fill rules) instead.
- Microwave/other rapid moisture methods are conditional on prior calibration against the oven method.

## Checks

- Smooth surface prepared at each sampling location
- Companion sample taken from the correct zone relative to the density test
- Oversize proportion and density determined for every sample, whatever the field method

## Common errors

- Nuclear gauge used on 20-40% oversize material or thick layers
- Relative compaction reported on very rocky fill where the result is meaningless
- Skipping the oversize adjustment of laboratory maximum density

## Caveats

- Verify the spec edition is current for the project; test method suites differ between R44 editions.
- Contract documents override.

## Standards cited

TfNSW T105, TfNSW T119, TfNSW T120, TfNSW T165, TfNSW T166, TfNSW T173

notes.title: Sequence R44 hold points from stripping through to formation cover-up
notes.body:
# Sequence R44 hold points from stripping through to formation cover-up

> **Source:** `r044.pdf` (Annexure R44/C schedules; Clauses 2.3.3, 2.4, 3.2, 3.4, 4.2, 4.6.1, 6.1, 6.2, 7.5, 7.6.2 (Ed 5 Rev 1)), held in the local reference library — see
> [[Reference library]]. This note is a paraphrased working aid, not the
> document. Values, clauses and criteria must be read from the source before
> they are relied on, and engineering conclusions need qualified review.

**Outcome.** Earthworks proceed without breaching any of the staged inspection gates, keeping lots releasable and payment claims clean.

## Inputs

- Annexure R44/C schedules
- Earthworks program and lot plan
- Survey reports (joint surveys where Annexure R44/A1 requires)

## Procedure

1. Before disturbing any surveyed surface, close out the post-topsoil-strip survey hold point (Clause 2.3.3): submit the survey report and set-out notification with the required lead time.
2. At each foundation exposure, observe the inspection holds: presentation of each embankment foundation lot (Clause 3.2) and each floor-of-cutting lot (Clause 3.4), with CBR/PI results where required.
3. Where unsuitable material is directed out, hold before replacing each lot so the Principal can inspect and possibly direct further removal (Clause 2.4).
4. In rock cuttings, present cleaned batter and bench/floor surfaces for geotechnical inspection before proceeding (Clause 4.2); for blasting, clear the management sub-plan and per-blast details holds (Clause 4.6.1).
5. For the Upper Zone of Formation and verges, clear the material-source holds - including proof that site-won sources are exhausted before importing (Clauses 6.1, 6.2) - and the stockpiled Selected Material conformity hold before placement, then the lot conformity hold before covering (Clause 6.1.2).
6. Before placing Selected Material Zone or pavement, clear the deflection/survey hold (Clause 7.6.2); for rock fill, clear the trial-section hold (Clause 7.5).

## Decision rules

- Imported material for the upper zone is blocked until available suitable site-won material is used or assigned - importing early is a nonconformance with payment consequences.
- Any surface that ruts, yields or shows distress must be notified promptly even between formal gates (Clause 2.4.1).
- Witness points (rock fill trials, proof rolling, Benkelman testing) require the stated advance notice but not release; hold points require release evidence.

## Checks

- Identified records per R44/C3 retained (Earthworks Plan, spoil/borrow records, blasting records, deflection results)
- Joint surveys done where Annexure R44/A1 nominates them
- Notice periods (typically 1-3 working days, 10 for stockpile/borrow concurrence) tracked in the program

## Common errors

- Stripping or excavating past a surveyed surface before the survey hold release
- Backfilling over unsuitable-material excavations without inspection
- Importing select material while site-won sources remain unassigned
- Covering the Selected Material Zone before the final conformity hold

## Caveats

- Verify the spec edition is current for the project.
- Project-specific annexures and the contract may add, delete or re-time hold points.

## Standards cited

TfNSW Q, TfNSW G71, TfNSW G36

notes.title: Set serviceability bearing pressures on Sydney rock from allowable settlement and class-based mass modulus
notes.body:
# Set serviceability bearing pressures on Sydney rock from allowable settlement and class-based mass modulus

> **Source:** `PELLS MOSTYN WONG (2019) CLASSIFICATION OF SANDSTONES AND SHALES IN THE SYDNEY.pdf` (Section 4.1 and Tables 3-5 (pp 33-36); serviceability equations on p 35), held in the local reference library — see
> [[Reference library]]. This note is a paraphrased working aid, not the
> document. Values, clauses and criteria must be read from the source before
> they are relied on, and engineering conclusions need qualified review.

**Outcome.** A footing bearing pressure derived explicitly from the structure's allowable settlement using class-based mass modulus, instead of blind adoption of the tabulated 1%-settlement guideline values.

## Inputs

- Rock class per the Pells classification (sandstone or shale)
- Allowable settlement for each footing from the structural engineer
- Footing geometry (rigid circular diameter D, or rectangular L by B) and rigidity
- Design Young's modulus and Poisson's ratio ranges from Tables 3 (sandstone) and 4 (shale) of the 2019 paper

## Procedure

1. Establish the rock class, then select design modulus and Poisson's ratio from Tables 3 and 4, taking lower values where strength, spacing or seam content sits at the bottom of the class range.
2. Compute serviceability bearing pressure from the allowable settlement using the rigid-footing elastic equations given in the paper (from Poulos & Davis 1974; Whitman & Richart 1967), or numerical analysis for complex cases.
3. Check the computed pressure against the second-column limits of approximately linear settlement-versus-pressure behaviour (expressed as multiples of UCS per class) before relying on elastic theory.
4. For simple sites where all footings are similar in size and 1% settlement is acceptable, the tabulated bearing-pressure guideline values in Tables 3 and 4 may be adopted directly.
5. For socketed footings mobilising both side shear and end bearing, switch to socket-specific settlement methods (Rowe & Armitage 1984; Pells 1999; Randolph 2003).

## Decision rules

- If proposed pressures exceed the tabulated guidelines substantially, the designer must confirm the adopted moduli by site-specific investigation and construction verification, including spoon testing of all footings.
- Where footing sizes differ widely, do not use the 1% guideline pressures uncritically; equal pressures on an 800 mm and a 4500 mm footing produce very different settlements and can cause unacceptable differential movement.
- Recessed-footing settlement reduction factors from elasticity theory should be treated with caution because tensile fracturing and bedding effects can invalidate them.

## Checks

- Computed settlement stays within the approximately linear pressure range for the class.
- Semi-infinite-mass elastic equations recognised as potentially conservative.
- Differential settlement between adjacent footings assessed, not just individual settlements.

## Common errors

- Treating the guideline table values as universal allowables regardless of footing size or structure sensitivity.
- Adopting upper-bound modulus values for rock at the lower end of a class.
- Applying pad-footing pressures to sockets without socket interaction analysis.

## Caveats

- Modulus ranges are broad; validity of computed settlements depends entirely on the adopted mass modulus.
- Some equation symbols were garbled in OCR; retrieve the exact expressions from the published paper before calculating.
- Design reference only: all values must be verified against the source tables and reviewed by a qualified engineer before use.

## Standards cited

Poulos & Davis (1974) elastic solutions, Rowe & Armitage (1984) socket design, AS 2159 limit state piling framework (via the 1998 companion paper)

notes.title: Set up the plate load test loading train under a reaction counterweight
notes.body:
# Set up the plate load test loading train under a reaction counterweight

> **Source:** `050-Setup Proceedure for PLT Draft 4 Feb 2024.pdf` (Section D Steps 1-4 and Section E, pp. 2-4), held in the local reference library — see
> [[Reference library]]. This note is a paraphrased working aid, not the
> document. Values, clauses and criteria must be read from the source before
> they are relied on, and engineering conclusions need qualified review.

**Outcome.** The engineer can position a reaction weight, prepare the bearing surface, and assemble the plate, load cell, hydraulic cylinder and ball joint ready for loading.

## Inputs

- A stable reaction counterweight (e.g. loaded backhoe or truck)
- Loading plate / load cell module, hydraulic cylinder, extensions, magnetic ball joint
- Hydraulic pump and hoses
- Trowel or spatula, brush, hand level
- Fine to medium grained bedding sand

## Procedure

1. Park the counterweight over the test location, leaving clearance greater than 600 mm to fit the loading device beneath the jacking point (p. 2).
2. Drop a little sand or loose soil from the jacking point to mark where the plate centre must sit (p. 2).
3. Prepare a test area large enough for the plate, trim it to a smooth level plane with a trowel or spatula checked against a hand level, and brush away loose material.
4. Seat the loading plate / load cell module by pressing it down with a slight twisting motion; on rough surfaces first spread a thin layer of fine to medium bedding sand to improve contact.
5. Place the hydraulic cylinder on the plate module and fix the magnetic ball joint to a stable point on the counterweight.
6. Pump the hydraulics only until the piston just touches the upper ball joint without applying load, keeping the ball joint bolt from jamming in the piston; fit extensions to the piston if the gap requires them.
7. Set up the pump: confirm the hydraulic coupling is fully closed with its cap nut, crack open the bleed/fill cover part of a turn, use the discharge valve (counterclockwise to lower, clockwise to stop) to retract the piston as needed, then return the bleed/fill cover to its prescribed position.

## Decision rules

- Use bedding sand only when the prepared surface is rough (p. 3).
- Use piston extensions when the cylinder cannot otherwise reach the ball joint (p. 3).

## Checks

- The sand-drop mark confirms the plate is centred under the jacking point.
- The piston contacts the ball joint with no load registered and no jamming of the ball joint bolt.

## Common errors

- Applying load while bringing the piston up to the ball joint.
- Jamming the ball joint bolt in the piston.
- Leaving loose material or an uneven surface under the plate.

## Caveats

- No minimum counterweight mass is stated in this document (the companion Anix loading-stage sheet gives a reaction-load rule).
- Some pump-setup details are placeholders awaiting training photos, so field verification against the equipment manual is advisable.

## Standards cited

None cited in the source passage.

notes.title: Set up the reference beam and zero the PLT sensors
notes.body:
# Set up the reference beam and zero the PLT sensors

> **Source:** `050-Setup Proceedure for PLT Draft 4 Feb 2024.pdf` (Sections F-G, pp. 4-6), held in the local reference library — see
> [[Reference library]]. This note is a paraphrased working aid, not the
> document. Values, clauses and criteria must be read from the source before
> they are relied on, and engineering conclusions need qualified review.

**Outcome.** The engineer can install the displacement reference beam clear of the loaded zone, align the transducer on the plate centre, and zero both displacement and force channels before loading.

## Inputs

- Folding reference beam with adjustable feet and star knobs
- Displacement transducer and holder
- Electronic measuring box
- Assembled plate / cylinder / ball joint loading train

## Procedure

1. Unfold the reference beam and place it roughly 1.5 m from the loading plate (p. 4).
2. Mount the displacement transducer in its holder and align the beam so the transducer tip sits at the centre of the loading plate, handling the transducer carefully.
3. Free the knob on the front L-shaped arm so the arm can travel up and down, level the beam with the adjustable feet, and fine-align the front support arm using its bubble level.
4. Confirm every star knob is tight.
5. Put the bubble level indicator near the outer edge of the loading plate and adjust it until the bubble is centred, so plate tilt during the test will be visible.
6. Position the electronic box near the operator, mechanically adjust the displacement sensor to read approximately zero (near fully retracted) using the star knob and display, then set it to zero electronically.
7. Confirm there is slack between the hydraulic cylinder/extensions and the counterweight so the load cell carries no force, then zero the force channel on the electronic box.
8. Route and clip the cables tidily along the reference beam.
9. Recheck the plate bubble level indicator is still centred before starting the load sequence (p. 6).

## Decision rules

- Zero the force sensor only while the cylinder is demonstrably unloaded (visible flex in the train) (p. 6).

## Checks

- Transducer tip is at the plate centre and nearly fully retracted at zero.
- Plate bubble remains centred at the end of setup.
- All star knobs tight; cables clipped so they cannot snag.

## Common errors

- Damaging the displacement transducer during beam alignment.
- Zeroing the force sensor while residual load is on the cylinder.
- Leaving star knobs loose so the beam shifts during the test.

## Caveats

- Steps 5-7 of the test-performance section are blank in this draft, so the loading sequence itself must come from the AX01a manual.
- The 1.5 m beam offset is given as approximate; the document does not state a tolerance.

## Standards cited

None cited in the source passage.

notes.title: Simulate rockfall trajectories and bench effectiveness in RocFall
notes.body:
# Simulate rockfall trajectories and bench effectiveness in RocFall

> **Source:** [YouTube — Rockfall Analysis using RocFall — Barriers and Ditch Analysis](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1H6aQIb9TBM&t=0s) (00:00-10:53). A YouTube lecture — learning
> material, not an approved design procedure. Equations and numbers were
> heard through auto-captions; read them off the video before use, and
> verify anything design-relevant against the standard and the project
> specification. Engineering conclusions need qualified review.

**Outcome.** A statistical picture of where falling rocks end up on a benched rock slope, used to judge whether a bench catches rocks or lets them reach the toe

## Inputs

- Slope geometry coordinates from site investigation (or drawn manually with length/angle feedback)
- Slope material with normal restitution coefficient (from the built-in material library or custom, e.g. a custom sandstone)
- Rock properties: density (reference values by geology, e.g. basalt around 2700 kg/m3) or measured/estimated mass, or a shape assumption (e.g. sphere of given radius)
- Seeder location and initial horizontal velocity of the falling rocks

## Procedure

1. Set view limits to match the coordinate extent of the slope being analysed
2. Draw the slope profile (including any bench) using Slope > Add Slope, finishing with a right-click
3. Assign a slope material via the material library; add a custom material if your investigation data differ from the presets, and set the normal restitution coefficient
4. Add a statistical distribution (typically normal) with a standard deviation to the restitution coefficient so all simulated rocks are not identical; the same can be done for friction angle and tangential restitution
5. Assign the material to the entire slope, or assign different materials to different slope segments
6. Place a seeder at the most dangerous location — rocks sitting right at the crest edge — and set the number of rocks (e.g. 50) rather than a single rock
7. Give the seeder an initial horizontal velocity with a normal distribution and standard deviation; rotational velocity can also be varied
8. Define the rock type: set density from the geology reference or enter a measured mass, again with a distribution
9. Run the analysis and open Graphs > End Points to see the distribution of final resting positions
10. Use the animation of individual rock paths to understand bounce behaviour for specific rocks

## Decision rules

- If most rocks stop on the bench, the bench is effective; rocks that bounce over the bench and run to the toe drive the need for further protection
- Rocks that come to rest close to the bench edge should be treated as a future hazard — rain or wind can move them over the edge later
- The higher the normal restitution coefficient, the more the rocks bounce

## Checks

- Always simulate a population of rocks with distributed parameters, not a single deterministic rock
- Compare simulated behaviour with observed fallen-rock positions on site where available

## Common errors

- Using a single rock with fixed properties, which hides the spread of outcomes
- Forgetting to assign the material to the slope after defining it in the library

## Caveats

- YouTube lecture — learning material, not an approved design procedure; verify against project specification and current standards
- Specific coefficient and distribution values in the demo are illustrative, not recommendations; use site-specific data where possible

## Standards cited

None cited in the source passage.

notes.title: Size a rock socket with the elastic chart method when sidewall slip is not permitted
notes.body:
# Size a rock socket with the elastic chart method when sidewall slip is not permitted

> **Source:** `The Design Of Socketed Piles In Rock by pells.pdf` (Section 6.1 with Figures 8-9 and worked example (pp 1-315 to 1-316)), held in the local reference library — see
> [[Reference library]]. This note is a paraphrased working aid, not the
> document. Values, clauses and criteria must be read from the source before
> they are relied on, and engineering conclusions need qualified review.

**Outcome.** A conservative socket length and diameter satisfying strength and serviceability limit states with all behaviour kept elastic, using the load-proportion and settlement-influence charts.

## Inputs

- Strength limit state load S* and long-term serviceability load
- Serviceability settlement limit (typically 5-15 mm at pile head if unspecified)
- Ultimate side shear, elastic-limit end bearing and ultimate end bearing stresses
- Pile modulus Ep and rock mass modulus Er (with reduction factor for serviceability)

## Procedure

1. Select a trial diameter D and compute the socket length that would carry all of S* in side shear alone (Lmax).
2. On the elastic load-distribution chart (base load proportion vs L/D for various Ep/Er), draw the straight line from 100% base load to Lmax/D; every point on it satisfies the side-shear limit.
3. Intersect that line with the curve for the assessed mean Ep/Er to obtain the design L/D and the base load proportion.
4. Read the settlement influence factor from the companion chart and compute settlement as rho = (P I) / (Er D) form given in the paper, applying the serviceability modulus reduction factor and the serviceability load.
5. Check the serviceability base pressure stays below the linear-elastic end-bearing limit.
6. Compute ultimate geotechnical strength Rug from ultimate side shear plus ultimate end bearing, and verify phi_g x Rug >= S*.
7. Repeat quickly for other diameters to optimise.

## Decision rules

- Adopt this method when sidewall slip must not occur, or when end-bearing capacity is too uncertain to rely on; expect materially longer sockets than slip-based design (6.9 m vs 4.7 m in the worked example).
- Charts shown assume uniform rock modulus; use the extended chart sets for differing base/shaft moduli or recessed sockets.

## Checks

- Chart axes and Ep/Er curve selection consistent with the assessed moduli.
- Settlement computed with the serviceability load, not S*.

## Common errors

- Using the strength load in the settlement check.
- Skipping the linear-elastic base-pressure check at serviceability.
- Forgetting the modulus reduction factor for long-term settlement.

## Caveats

- Chart figures are not legible in the OCR; the method requires the published charts or equivalent equations.
- Design reference only: chart readings and factors must be verified against the source and reviewed by a qualified engineer before use.

## Standards cited

Rowe & Pells (1980) theoretical basis, AS 2159-1995 phi_g framework (Section 5 of the same paper)

This note is a paraphrased working aid, not the document. Values, clauses and criteria must be read from the source before they are relied on, and engineering conclusions need qualified review. Outcome. A conservative socket length and diameter satisfying strength and serviceability limit states with all behaviour kept elastic, using the load proportion and settlement influence charts. Inputs Strength limit state load S and long term serviceability load Serviceability settlement limit (typically 5 15 mm at pile head if unspecified) Ultimate side shear, elastic limit end bearing and ultimate end bearing stresses Pile modulus Ep and rock mass modulus Er (with reduction factor for serviceability) Procedure 1. Select a trial diameter D and compute the socket length that would carry all of S in side shear alone (Lmax). 2. On the elastic load distribution chart (base load proportion vs L/D for various Ep/Er), draw the straight line from 100% base load to Lmax/D; every point on it satisfies the side shear limit. 3. Intersect that line with the curve for the assessed mean Ep/Er to obtain the design L/D and the base load proportion. 4. Read the settlement influence factor from the companion chart and compute settlement as rho = (P I) / (Er D) form given in the paper, applying the serviceability modulus reduction factor and the serviceability load. 5. Check the serviceability base pressure stays below the linear elastic end bearing limit. 6. Compute ultimate geotechnical strength Rug from ultimate side shear plus ultimate end bearing, and verify phi g x Rug = S . 7. Repeat quickly for other diameters to optimise. Decision rules Adopt this method when sidewall slip must not occur, or when end bearing capacity is too uncertain to rely on; expect materially longer sockets than slip based design (6.9 m vs 4.7 m in the worked example). Charts shown assume uniform rock modulus; use the extended chart sets for differing base/shaft moduli or recessed sockets. Checks Chart axes and Ep/Er curve selection consistent with the assessed moduli. Settlement computed with the serviceability load, not S . Common errors Using the strength load in the settlement check. Skipping the linear elastic base pressure check at serviceability. Forgetting the modulus reduction factor for long term settlement. Caveats Chart figures are not legible in the OCR; the method requires the published charts or equivalent equations. Design reference only: chart readings and factors must be verified against the source and reviewed by a qualified engineer before use. notes.title: Size a rockfall catch ditch with the Ritchie chart
notes.body:
# Size a rockfall catch ditch with the Ritchie chart

> **Source:** [YouTube — Rockfall Catch Ditch Design — Ritchie Chart Method](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Eof-qGDKfWo&t=0s) (00:00-05:51). A YouTube lecture — learning
> material, not an approved design procedure. Equations and numbers were
> heard through auto-captions; read them off the video before use, and
> verify anything design-relevant against the standard and the project
> specification. Engineering conclusions need qualified review.

**Outcome.** Required width and depth of a catch ditch at the toe of a rock slope, from slope height and slope angle

## Inputs

- Slope height from site survey
- Slope angle, computed from height and horizontal setback if not measured directly (tan alpha = height / horizontal distance)
- Ritchie ditch design chart (introduced by Ritchie, 1963)

## Procedure

1. Estimate slope height during site investigation (example: 20 m)
2. Compute the slope angle from geometry (example: tan alpha = 20/22.2 giving about 42 degrees)
3. Enter the Ritchie chart with slope height and slope angle and locate the design point
4. Read the required ditch width from the dashed-line family (example result: 4.57 m)
5. Read the required ditch depth from the solid-line family (example result: 1.83 m)
6. Where the point falls between chart lines, interpolate between the adjacent width values and the adjacent depth values
7. Detail the ditch base with soft material such as gravel to absorb impact energy of falling rocks

## Decision rules

- Width and depth both increase with slope height and depend on slope angle; always read both line families
- If the design point does not sit on chart lines, interpolate rather than rounding to the nearer line

## Checks

- Verify the computed slope angle against the chart axis range before reading values
- Confirm the ditch geometry is buildable at the site (excavation depth of the order of 1.8 m in the example)

## Common errors

- Reading only one line family and reporting width for depth or vice versa
- Skipping interpolation when the point falls between lines

## Caveats

- YouTube lecture — learning material, not an approved design procedure; verify against project specification and current standards
- Chart values quoted (4.57, 1.83, 2.13, 6.1 m) are imperial-derived line labels read on screen — read from the video
- Geology does not enter the chart; only slope height and inclination are used

## Standards cited

Ritchie (1963) ditch design chart (named by lecturer)

notes.title: Size and embed reinforced soil wall
notes.body:
# Size and embed reinforced soil wall

> **Source:** `r057.pdf` (Clause 4.5, Tables R57.5 and R57.6, Figures R57.3-R57.5), held in the local reference library — see
> [[Reference library]]. This note is a paraphrased working aid, not the
> document. Values, clauses and criteria must be read from the source before
> they are relied on, and engineering conclusions need qualified review.

**Outcome.** RSW geometry (reinforcement length, embedment depth, toe berm) meeting the roads-authority minimum dimensions before detailed design starts.

## Inputs

- Mechanical height H and facing height of the wall
- Application type (abutment vs non-abutment, trapezoidal or stepped section)
- Slope of ground at the toe
- Foundation quality assessment (sound rock or otherwise) by a geotechnical engineer

## Procedure

1. Establish mechanical height H per the specification figures and set the bottom reinforcement length from the minimum-dimensions table (a function of H, larger minima for abutments).
2. Set toe embedment from the embedment table as a function of toe slope and application, measured to the definitions figure.
3. Where the toe slope exceeds the threshold angle, provide a toe berm of the specified minimum width with crossfall for drainage, and measure embedment from the berm.
4. Confirm trapezoidal or stepped sections satisfy the additional geometric restrictions and reinforcement-spacing ratios, and analyse them via the specified transformed-section rules.

## Decision rules

- Minimum reinforcement length: the greater of 2 m or (0.6H + 1) m for non-abutment walls; the greater of 7 m or (0.6H + 2) m for bridge abutments (r057 Table R57.5).
- Minimum embedment ranges from H/20 (level ground, non-abutment) to H/5 (steep toe slope), never less than 0.3 m; abutments on level ground require H/10 (r057 Table R57.6).
- Toe slope steeper than 18 degrees triggers a berm at least 2 m wide (r057 Clause 4.5).
- Trapezoidal sections are prohibited unless founded by excavation into sound rock (slightly weathered or better, medium strength or better per AS 1726) and are never allowed under sill beams (r057 Clause 4.5).

## Checks

- Confirm weak or soft foundation soils have been considered for deeper embedment on the geotechnical engineer's advice.
- Confirm lengthened top reinforcement layers for impact loading have not been misclassified as a trapezoidal section.

## Common errors

- Measuring embedment from the wrong reference when a berm is present.
- Using a trapezoidal section on a soil foundation.
- Applying the embedment table to slender walls (it applies to L/H greater than 0.6 in good ground).

## Caveats

- Verify the edition is current; contract documents override.
- Embedment values assume good ground and adequate slenderness; site-specific assessment governs otherwise.

## Standards cited

AS 1726, AS 5100.3

## Related

- [[AS 1726 soil and rock description]]
- [[Rock weathering classes]]
- [[Skills]]

notes.title: Size and position a rockfall barrier by iterative capacity testing in RocFall
notes.body:
# Size and position a rockfall barrier by iterative capacity testing in RocFall

> **Source:** [YouTube — Rockfall Analysis using RocFall — Barriers and Ditch Analysis](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1H6aQIb9TBM&t=653s) (10:53-14:30). A YouTube lecture — learning
> material, not an approved design procedure. Equations and numbers were
> heard through auto-captions; read them off the video before use, and
> verify anything design-relevant against the standard and the project
> specification. Engineering conclusions need qualified review.

**Outcome.** A barrier location, height and energy capacity that actually stops the simulated rock population, found by iteration rather than a single guess

## Inputs

- A completed RocFall trajectory model of the slope and rock population
- Candidate barrier position (distance from the slope toe) and height
- Barrier capacity options: vendor product presets (the library includes manufacturers such as Geobrugg and Maccaferri) or a custom capacity in joules/kilojoules

## Procedure

1. Add a barrier near the toe (e.g. 1-2 m from the toe) and set its height (e.g. about 2 m); the barrier can be dragged to adjust position
2. Open the barrier properties library and either select a vendor product with predefined properties or define a custom barrier by energy capacity
3. Run the analysis and check whether rocks pass through the barrier
4. If rocks pass through, increase the capacity stepwise (the demo iterates from roughly 0.1 kJ through 1000 kJ and beyond) and re-run
5. If increasing capacity alone does not work, move the barrier to a different position and re-run; iterate capacity and position together until the design stops the rocks

## Decision rules

- A cheap low-capacity fence is acceptable only if the simulation shows it stops the expected rock sizes and energies
- If neither realistic capacity nor repositioning stops the rocks, revisit the overall protection concept rather than forcing the barrier

## Checks

- Re-run the full rock population after every barrier change; a barrier that stops some trajectories may still be bypassed by others
- Check the animation to confirm rocks are stopped rather than bouncing over

## Common errors

- Selecting a barrier capacity without simulating impact energies, so rocks pass straight through
- Fixing capacity but ignoring position — a stronger barrier in the wrong place still fails

## Caveats

- YouTube lecture — learning material, not an approved design procedure; verify against project specification and current standards
- Barrier capacities in the demo are deliberately unrealistic starting points used for teaching iteration; real designs use vendor-certified capacities and impact energy statistics

## Standards cited

None cited in the source passage.

## Related

notes.title: Specify construction and supervision requirements for socketed bored piles in Sydney rock
notes.body:
# Specify construction and supervision requirements for socketed bored piles in Sydney rock

> **Source:** `Bored Piles Socketed Into Shale And Sandstone by pells.pdf` (Walker & Pells, Australian Geomechanics Dec 1998, pp 31-33; Sections 1, 2, 4, 5 and Appendix A draft clauses), held in the local reference library — see
> [[Reference library]]. This note is a paraphrased working aid, not the
> document. Values, clauses and criteria must be read from the source before
> they are relied on, and engineering conclusions need qualified review.

**Outcome.** Contract documents that lock in the workmanship (cleanliness, roughness, concreting, inspection regime) required for modern high-capacity socket design values to be valid.

## Inputs

- Project design method and assumed side-shear/end-bearing parameters
- The paper's Draft Specification Clauses (Appendix A) as a template
- Ground conditions and construction method (dry, tremie under water, drilling mud)
- Site investigation scope (cored boreholes, strength testing, per-footing proving)

## Procedure

1. Start from the Draft Specification Clauses in Appendix A of the paper and edit them to suit the specific project and contract; minimal alteration is expected for most Sydney cases.
2. Define the 'engineer' role (designer or supervising authority) consistently with the contract terminology.
3. Require site investigation by cored boreholes with strength testing, plus proving of individual foundation locations; allow for extra investigation during construction if design-stage data is inadequate for approval purposes.
4. Specify that socket inspection and approval is done or supervised by experienced geotechnical personnel employed by the principal, not the contractor.
5. Add project-specific clauses for setting out, reinforcement and concreting; treat underwater (tremie) concreting as a specialist operation requiring proven contractor experience and on-site familiarity.
6. Require inspection documentation limited to certifying that inspections occurred and that piles are considered built to design assumptions and accepted practice.

## Decision rules

- If tremie placement under water is proposed, only accept it where the engineer is satisfied socket cleanliness is achieved and the contractor has proven underwater concreting experience.
- If high side-shear/end-bearing values are not economically achievable through the specified workmanship, do not invoke them in design.

## Checks

- Specification clauses are consistent with the actual design assumptions (roughness class, cleanliness limits, inspection method).
- Contractual independence of the inspector from the piling contractor.
- Reporting items align with the paper's Clause A6.2 list.

## Common errors

- Copying the draft clauses verbatim without reconciling them with the project's design method and contract terms.
- Letting construction practice default to what suits old code-level capacities while the design assumes modern high capacities.
- Omitting proving requirements at individual footing locations.

## Caveats

- Appendix A clause text was not included in the OCR extract read here; obtain the full paper before drafting a specification.
- Design reference only: clause content and acceptance limits must be verified against the source document and reviewed by a qualified engineer before contractual use.

## Standards cited

Pells & Rowe (1983); Rowe & Armitage (1989); Williams & Pells (1981)

- [[Bored pier inspection]]
- [[Weathered siltstone]]
- [[Rock strength classes]]
- [[Borehole log conventions]]

notes.title: Specify, install and quality-control working platform material
notes.body:
# Specify, install and quality-control working platform material

> **Source:** `Working Platforms for tracked plant.pdf` (Sections 3.3, 3.4 and Chapter 4 (Installation)), held in the local reference library — see
> [[Reference library]]. This note is a paraphrased working aid, not the
> document. Values, clauses and criteria must be read from the source before
> they are relied on, and engineering conclusions need qualified review.

**Outcome.** A platform built from suitable granular (or approved recycled) material, placed and compacted to specification with records proving it, including correctly installed geosynthetics.

## Inputs

- Design specification including required material strength and acceptable variation
- Candidate platform material data: grading, maximum particle size, strength, durability, crushability, geochemical properties
- Geosynthetic type and function (separation/filtration fabric vs strengthening geogrid) and manufacturer lapping requirements
- Operational constraints (e.g. pile positional tolerance driving a smaller maximum particle size)

## Procedure

1. Specify material for compactibility, durability, trafficability and drainage; set maximum particle size to suit operations (a smaller max size is needed where tight pile positional tolerance applies — see Section 3.3); exclude organic matter and clay; avoid materials that crush significantly under trafficking.
2. Review geochemical properties: sulfate attack risk on substructure concrete (especially if the platform becomes permanent works), and hazards in unsorted demolition rubble (asbestos, rebar, plaster).
3. Distinguish geosynthetic functions: geofabrics to separate/filter a granular platform from cohesive subgrade; geogrids to strengthen. Place strengthening reinforcement at or near the platform base; follow overlap requirements.
4. Protect geosynthetics from damage in storage, handling and installation; place an adequate thickness of material over them before compaction, and a protective granular layer beneath where the subgrade could damage them.
5. Place and compact in accordance with the specification with competent supervision; observe placement for revealed subgrade weak areas needing removal, treatment or design change.
6. Run quality-control tests and sample the material at suitable frequencies; keep records certifying installation as specified (Section 1.6).
7. Use plate load tests to indicate platform adequacy, choosing a plate size as close to the plant track size as practicable to replicate the loading.
8. Compact and level the finished surface; mark permissible working area boundaries and provide service markers and any interceptor ditches/drainage.

## Decision rules

- If platform material is excavated and re-used elsewhere on site, re-check it still meets the design assumptions before re-use.
- On cohesive formations in wet conditions, provide a granular filter layer or geofabric to stop upward fines migration degrading the platform.
- If quality-control results fall outside the specified acceptable variation, stop and refer to the platform designer.

## Checks

- Certification that the platform was installed as specified, backed by supervision and test records.
- Small plate tests recognised as unrepresentative — plate size versus track size documented.
- Geosynthetic cover thickness before compaction plant traffics over it.

## Common errors

- Using unsorted demolition rubble containing plaster, asbestos or rebar.
- Compacting directly on exposed geogrid/geofabric and damaging it.
- Confusing separation fabric with structural reinforcement and claiming a thickness reduction from a non-structural layer.
- No sampling regime, so degraded or variable material goes undetected.

## Caveats

- OCR noise present; verify particle-size limits and any test frequencies against the original document before specifying.
- Material availability and specification practice differ by country — adapt to local specifications (e.g. TfNSW/TMR) while keeping the performance intent.

## Standards cited

BRE BR 470 (2004), BS 6031:1981 (earthworks), Highways Agency Specification for Highway Works, CIRIA SP123 (geosynthetics)

## Related

- [[Library - plate load testing]]
- [[Library - RMS and TfNSW specifications]]
- [[Skills]]

notes.title: Specify reinforced fill for soil wall
notes.body:
# Specify reinforced fill for soil wall

> **Source:** `r057.pdf` (Clauses 5.2 and 5.3, Tables R57.9 and R57.10), held in the local reference library — see
> [[Reference library]]. This note is a paraphrased working aid, not the
> document. Values, clauses and criteria must be read from the source before
> they are relied on, and engineering conclusions need qualified review.

**Outcome.** A reinforced fill specification (grading, plasticity, durability, strength parameters) that will realise the design friction angle in the constructed wall.

## Inputs

- Candidate fill sources and their test histories
- Soil reinforcement type (steel or geosynthetic) and design life
- Applicable construction specification (companion R58/R59 chemical and electrical limits)

## Procedure

1. Restrict fill to inert, hard, durable granular soil, decomposed rock or crushed rock, free of organics, synthetics, contaminants and combustible material.
2. Exclude argillaceous rock (shales, claystones) and any material prone to breakdown to friable fines.
3. Determine the constant-volume friction angle on pretreated samples (repeated-compaction pretreatment, plus artificial wet/dry weathering for index tests as specified) and adopt zero effective cohesion.
4. Check grading envelope, uniformity coefficient, liquid limit and plasticity index against the fill property table, with maximum particle size limited by reinforcement type and lift thickness.
5. For steel reinforcement, apply the sacrificial-thickness corrosion allowance table by structural location and design life, on top of the minimum galvanizing requirement; verify chemical/electrical properties under the companion construction spec.

## Decision rules

- Fill fails if grading, uniformity coefficient, liquid limit or plasticity index fall outside Table R57.10 limits (r057 Clause 5.3).
- Maximum particle dimension differs for steel vs geosynthetic reinforcement and must not exceed one third of the lift thickness (r057 Table R57.10 note).
- Environments more aggressive than the tabulated cases (or with stray currents) require corrosion allowances assessed by investigation rather than the table (r057 Table R57.9 notes).

## Checks

- Confirm index tests were run on pretreated samples per the specified test-method sequence, not raw feed.
- Confirm the adopted design friction angle is not greater than the tested value and respects the 34/36 degree caps.
- Confirm electrolytic compatibility or insulation between dissimilar metallic components.

## Common errors

- Accepting shale-derived fill that meets grading at the crusher but degrades after compaction and weathering.
- Claiming cohesion for the reinforced fill in design.
- Ignoring the reduced sacrificial-thickness regime below the water table or 1-year flood level.

## Caveats

- Verify edition currency; chemical/electrical limits live in the companion R58/R59 specs and must be checked there.
- Contract documents override.

## Standards cited

AS/NZS 4680, AS 3678, AS 4671, Q181C, RMS T102/T103/T108/T109

notes.title: Specify salt-resistant masonry, damp-proof courses and membranes
notes.body:
# Specify salt-resistant masonry, damp-proof courses and membranes

> **Source:** `building-in-saline-environment-080145.pdf` (pp. 9-15 (Bricks Resistant to Salt and Water; Preventing Water and Salt Moving into the Building; Damp Proof Membranes; Building Codes)), held in the local reference library — see
> [[Reference library]]. This note is a paraphrased working aid, not the
> document. Values, clauses and criteria must be read from the source before
> they are relied on, and engineering conclusions need qualified review.

**Outcome.** Masonry and moisture-barrier specifications (brick class, mortar, DPC height and continuity, under-slab membrane) that meet BCA/AS requirements for saline sites and avoid the common DPC failure modes.

## Inputs

- Site salinity risk assessment (existing or potential)
- Building type and floor system (slab-on-ground vs suspended)
- Local council building policy requirements
- BCA and relevant Australian Standards

## Procedure

1. Specify exposure-class bricks where salt attack is possible: BCA lists them as suitable for severe local conditions including below the DPC in salt-affected ground; classification follows AS 3700 via the AS 4456.1 salt-attack test (bricks surviving 40 wet/dry salt cycles with less than 0.4 g mass loss, or demonstrated saline-environment history). Within a brick style, exposure-grade often costs no more than general purpose.
2. Consider low initial salt content products using the AS 4456.6 efflorescence-potential test as an extra precaution (not a BCA requirement).
3. Use the BCA-specified mortar mix for exposure-class brickwork and do not use raked mortar joints with exposure-class bricks.
4. Detail the DPC as a continuous barrier: nominal 150 mm above finished ground, reducible to 100 mm on sandy well-drained ground or 50 mm where adjoining paving/concrete slopes away under a verandah.
5. Guard against DPC failure modes: chemical breakdown, cracking/puncture at installation, breakage by differential settlement, incorrect installation, and bridging (render or pointing carried over the DPC, raised garden beds, paving, mortar droppings in the cavity, later renovations such as replacing a timber floor with sand and slab without a separating barrier).
6. For slab-on-ground in NSW/SA, specify a high-impact-resistant 0.2 mm polyethylene damp-proof membrane continuous under the slab and wrapped around footings to ground level (NSW BCA state variation since May 2004); some councils also require/recommend ~50 mm of sand under the membrane against puncture and capillary rise.
7. For salt-prone areas consider pier-and-beam construction: less material in ground contact, ventilation and evaporation occur in the soil, damage is inspectable, less cut and fill (minimum 400 mm subfloor clearance where termite inspection applies).

## Decision rules

- If salinity status is unknown, exposure-grade bricks and a damp-proof (not vapour) membrane are cheap insurance relative to repair cost — Australia-wide, most urban sites have some water source capable of mobilising salts.
- Existing NSW council policies in saline areas typically add: 50 mm sand under slab, 32 MPa concrete, seven days curing, plus the high-impact membrane — check the local policy since councils may exceed but not relax the BCA.
- Distinguish damp-proof membranes (high impact resistance) from vapour barriers (low impact resistance): both look identical laid face-down, so specify and verify the product, not the colour.

## Checks

- DPC continuity verified around the full perimeter and above finished ground/paving at the specified height.
- Membrane laps, penetration sealing and extension to ground level inspected before the pour (it is hidden early in construction).
- Landscaping plans checked for future DPC bridging (garden beds, paths against walls).

## Common errors

- Render, pointing or paving bridging the DPC after handover, defeating an otherwise sound barrier.
- Substituting a low-impact vapour barrier where a damp-proof membrane is required.
- Using general-purpose bricks below the DPC on a saline site when exposure-grade was available at the same price.
- Assuming extra subfloor vents can fix salt damage driven by high groundwater (barriers and salt-resistant materials are usually needed instead).

## Caveats

- Classification and aggressivity calls must be verified against the source document, current BCA/NCC editions and the project spec — this booklet is 2008 and code clause numbers have since changed.
- Membrane requirements are state-specific (NSW/SA variation described); confirm the current jurisdictional position.
- Membrane detailing requirements merged from INDUSTRY_GUIDE_T56_Residential_Slabs_and_Footings_in_Saline_Environments.pdf Section 6.6 (20 mm sand layer minimum, 200 mm laps, sealed penetrations, extend to ground level) — note the sand layer figure differs between sources (20 mm in T56 vs 50 mm in NSW council policies).

## Standards cited

Building Code of Australia Vol 2 (damp/weatherproofing, NSW state variation on damp-proof membranes), AS 3700 Masonry Structures; AS 4456.1 (salt attack resistance test); AS 4456.6 (efflorescence potential), AS 2870 Residential Slabs and Footings (membrane, DPC detailing clauses)

## Related

- [[Library - salinity and sodic soils]]
- [[Library - RMS and TfNSW specifications]]
- [[Soil description order]]
- [[Skills]]

notes.title: Stabilise road subgrades with lime in saline and wet conditions
notes.body:
# Stabilise road subgrades with lime in saline and wet conditions

> **Source:** `Techniques-to-use-on-roads-affected-by-salinity.pdf` (Sections 5.3.2 (Table 3) and 5.5, pp. 10 and 13-14), held in the local reference library — see
> [[Reference library]]. This note is a paraphrased working aid, not the
> document. Values, clauses and criteria must be read from the source before
> they are relied on, and engineering conclusions need qualified review.

**Outcome.** A lime-stabilised subgrade that is drier, stiffer, less moisture-reactive and lower-permeability, reducing water and salt movement into the pavement and watertable.

## Inputs

- Subgrade characterisation: clay content, PI, CBR (soaked/unsoaked), organic matter, seasonal moisture behaviour
- Binder choice: quicklime or hydrated lime (or cementitious/polymer alternatives)
- Mixing plant capable of at least two-pass mixing

## Procedure

1. Use lime stabilisation of clay subgrades to: increase subgrade stiffness, reduce PI, improve volumetric stability, stiffen subbase layers, and create a temporary construction platform.
2. Understand the two-stage mechanism: calcium cation exchange first agglomerates clay fines and 'dewaters' the clay; then at pH above about 12, pozzolanic reactions form calcium silicates/aluminates that gel, bind and slowly crystallise — strength gain is temperature-dependent and can continue for months (trackable by CBR).
3. Mix thoroughly with a minimum of two mixing passes per stabilisation best practice; allow reaction time before trafficking.
4. Rely on the permeability benefit: strongly modified clay shows decreased permeability (void occlusion by reaction products, per Stocker's ARRB work), so less water enters, less salt diffuses in, and subgrade strength loss is diminished.
5. Use lime to bind seasonally shrink-swell subgrades so cracks do not propagate into pavement or footpaths and admit more water.
6. For very weak subgrades (CBR under 3% at construction), the common convention is to ignore the structural gain of light lime/cement stabilisation and design at CBR 3%, unless using explicit stabilised-subgrade design procedures.

## Decision rules

- Choose modification vs bound behaviour deliberately (indicative Austroads bands: modified 0.7-1.5 MPa UCS; lightly bound 1.5-3.0 MPa; bound above 3.0 MPa) — bound layers cut water entry but crack and must have cracks sealed (crack sealing, SAMI or crumb rubber seals).
- Organic matter in the soil, even in small quantities, can reduce the lime reaction's effectiveness — test and adjust.
- No evidence is cited that salt degrades lime-stabilised material, but the paper notes the salt effect on cementitious/bituminous stabilised strength was unquantified — treat high-salt cases with trials rather than assumption.

## Checks

- Lime spread rate and mixing uniformity verified (two-pass minimum).
- Strength gain tracked over time with CBR/UCS testing rather than assumed at 7 days.
- Shrinkage cracks in bound layers sealed promptly after appearing.

## Common errors

- Single-pass mixing leaving unreacted clay pockets.
- Expecting full strength quickly in cold weather (crystallisation is temperature-dependent).
- Treating lime stabilisation as a substitute for subsurface drainage instead of a complement.
- Ignoring organics that quench the pozzolanic reaction.

## Caveats

- Classification and aggressivity calls must be verified against the source document, current Austroads stabilisation guides and the project spec — the UCS class bands cited were from a draft guide.
- The absence of evidence for salt degrading lime-stabilised layers is not evidence of absence; the author explicitly calls for Australian research on strength loss at various salt levels.
- Wyndham City standard configurations (lime-stabilised clay subgrades under granular/asphalt pavements by traffic tier) are context for expansive, not necessarily saline, subgrades.

## Standards cited

Austroads Guide to Stabilisation in Roadworks (draft 2004c) and Guide to Best Practice for Construction of Insitu Stabilised Pavements (2003), AustStab Technical Note 1 Lime Stabilisation Practice, Stocker (1972) ARRB Special Report 8 (diffusion and cementation in lime/cement stabilised clays)

## Related

- [[Library - salinity and sodic soils]]
- [[Library - RMS and TfNSW specifications]]
